title: Web Exploitation
content:
Web Exploitation Field Notes Start with a signal. Confirm it. Identify the parser. Then choose the payload.
Manual reference for CTF challenges and labs. Payloads are ready to adapt in a browser, Burp Repeater, or a request editor. No generated solver is needed to follow the workflows. Availability of notes and tools during your event depends on its rules.
Pick your starting point What you have / what you see Open this First question A new URL or source archive First 10 minutes Where does each input go? Exposed backups, Git files, debug traces Source / backup leaks Can source reveal the actual sink and flag location? Search, login, sorting, numeric ID SQL injection Can I change a query condition? Confirmed SQLi, unknown database Database fingerprinting Which engine actually executed the query? MySQL / MariaDB MySQL Current schema → tables → columns → data PostgreSQL PostgreSQL Current schema → catalog → text casts SQLite SQLite Read sqlite_schema and CREATE TABLE definitions Microsoft SQL Server SQL Server DB_NAME → sys.tables → sys.columns Oracle Oracle DUAL → USER_TABLES → USER_TAB_COLUMNS SQLi confirmed, no rows displayed Blind / error SQLi What reliable true/false signal exists? A greeting / preview evaluates expressions SSTI Server evaluation or browser rendering? Which engine? JSON login, MongoDB operators NoSQL injection Does the app accept an object where it expects a string? Input becomes HTML or JavaScript XSS Which exact browser context contains the input? Ping, convert, archive, DNS tools Command injection Shell string or direct argument list? Filename, download, language/include Traversal / LFI Can I read a known file outside the intended directory? URL fetcher, webhook, PDF generator SSRF Which request does the server itself make? XML, SOAP, SVG upload XXE Does the parser resolve entities? Upload form / attachment API File upload Accepted, stored, served, interpreted: which stages work? Object IDs, roles, reset links Auth / IDOR Does the server enforce ownership and workflow state? Three-part bearer token JWT What is verified, with which key and algorithm? Serialized cookie / import Deserialization Which format and which server-side classes? Deep object merge / JS config Prototype pollution Can input alter inherited properties? GraphQL endpoint GraphQL Schema, resolver authorization, hidden arguments Cookie-authenticated state changes CSRF / CORS Can another origin send or read this request? OAuth login / account linking OAuth Are callback, identity, state, and session bound correctly? Live socket messages WebSockets Which message changes state, and when is completion reported? Coupon, payment, repeated claim Business logic / races Which invariant should hold after two requests? Proxy, cache, suspicious framing HTTP / cache issues Do two HTTP components disagree? PHP loose checks, arrays, hashes PHP quirks Which types and PHP version participate in the check? Directory/XML query syntax LDAP / XPath What grammar and boolean oracle does the sink expose? Redirect / return URL Open redirect What hostname does the consuming parser actually use? Blocked words / changed payloads Encoding / filters What bytes reach the final parser? Need prepared Python helpers Reusable snippets Byte transforms, JWT, or a confirmed boolean oracle? The loop for every technique Baseline request → one small probe → matching negative control → repeat the difference → fingerprint the parser / engine → select the matching payload → enumerate actual names / paths → read the challenge resultAn error is a clue; repeatable controlled behavior is evidence. A 200 OK, accepted upload, or login redirect alone does not prove success.
Payload notation Notation Meaning ctf.invalid Placeholder challenge host; replace it YOUR-LAB-HOST Your permitted callback host, if callbacks are part of the challenge users, flags, flag, /flag.txt Example names; enumerate actual names first -- - SQL line comment with a trailing space after the two dashes NULL,NULL,EXPR Example three-column UNION; adapt count, types, and reflected position 1' ... -- - Complete example input for a single-quoted query value SELECT ... in an engine page Standalone query fragment; insert it into your confirmed injection %XX URL-encoded bytes; do not encode twice unless two decoding stages exist Many pages deliberately show raw payloads. In Burp’s decoded parameter editor, enter the raw payload; in an actual URL/form body, encode transport-sensitive characters. JSON, URL forms, HTML, and shell quoting are different layers. See encoding.
Keep a tiny evidence record Route / method: Parameter and content type: Baseline response: True probe / false probe: Observed difference: Engine evidence: Working payload: Next step / result:The reference links at the end of each page are optional further reading. The workflow and payloads are included here for offline use. Examples are not a claim that every payload works on every version or has been tested against your event’s environment.
Tool map and other artifact types Burp → capture/replay exact requests. Chrome → inspect DOM, network and storage. CyberChef recipes → decode evidence. Python snippets → repeat confirmed operations.
Network · Steganography · Reversing · All 39 tools.

title: Network Exploitation
content:
Network Field Notes Flow: identify the transport → identify the application → reconstruct the conversation → extract the actual object → verify the result.
Use the supplied capture, service description, source, memory dump, or protocol specification as your starting evidence. A port number is a hint; the bytes and negotiated protocol determine the next action.
Choose your starting point What the challenge provides Start here First useful result PCAP / PCAPNG with no context Packet triage Hosts, times, protocols, candidate streams Web requests, uploads, downloads HTTP and streams Correct request/response and saved object Many DNS queries / odd hostnames DNS Ordered labels and decoded bytes TLS / HTTPS / SSH TLS and SSH Metadata; determine whether matching secrets exist A TCP/UDP host and port TCP/UDP sessions Exact framing, status semantics, persistent session 802.11 / radiotap / EAPOL Wi-Fi SSID, station/AP pair, security mode, usable handshake CAN log / cannelloni endpoint CAN bus IDs, frame changes, protocol-defined state transition FTP / mail / ICMP / SMB Other protocols Transfer channel, messages, attachments, or file objects Need a ready offline helper Python snippets TCP conversation or ordered DNS reconstruction Approved tool route These links point to this notebook’s supplied tournament tool list. Actual event rules still control which features and existing snippets you can use.
Task Approved tool page Practical operation Visual packet inspection Wireshark Follow stream, protocol tree, export objects Repeatable packet extraction TShark Display filters, field export, conversation statistics Connection / application summaries Zeek Offline logs for capture triage Encoding and byte inspection CyberChef, HxD, xxd Decode only the selected payload bytes Script a known protocol Python 3 Standard-library sockets, struct, base64, hashlib Certificate / TLS checks OpenSSL Parse certificates, inspect supplied endpoint TLS SSH keys in memory OpenSSH recovery Match memory-derived key material to the connection CAN frames over IP cannelloni Preserve tunnel and local receiving path Local CAN observe / replay can-utils candump, cansend, canplayer Linux command environment WSL Run supplied CLI tools; kernel/network constraints apply No aircrack suite, unrestricted scanner, or extra packet library is assumed by these pages.
First five minutes Keep the original capture unchanged. Record its name, byte size, and hash. Open it in Wireshark; check Statistics → Protocol Hierarchy and Conversations. Check capture time span, interfaces, dropped/truncated packet clues, and link-layer type. Select one candidate stream and follow both directions. Decide whether you have plaintext, an encoded application field, encrypted transport, or an incomplete capture. Export the smallest relevant object while preserving the original stream/packet references. A capture containing no plaintext flag can still disclose a filename, hostname, session identity, request ID, key-log hint, or archive password.
Keep an evidence record Input: challenge.pcapng SHA-256: ... Candidate: tcp.stream 7 Packet range: 140–188 Client/server: 192.0.2.10:51514 -> 192.0.2.20:8080 Why selected: POST /upload followed by binary response Saved artifact: objects/payload.zip Next check: file signature, archive contents, password source Verified result: ...Stream numbers belong to the particular capture and dissector processing. Preserve the input when citing them.
Distinguish the layers Ethernet / 802.11 -> IPv4 / IPv6 -> TCP stream / UDP datagrams -> TLS or application framing -> HTTP / DNS / FTP / custom protocol -> Base64 / compression / archive / fileBase64 decoding a TLS record does not decrypt it. Concatenating TCP payloads does not automatically reconstruct HTTP bodies. A UDP packet boundary can be an application boundary, but a protocol may split its own message across several datagrams.
When the obvious attempt fails Observation Check before changing the payload No HTTP dissector output Correct port, Decode As, TLS, HTTP/2, capture completeness Exported file corrupt Direction, transfer framing, reassembly, compression, missing bytes DNS reconstruction garbled Retry handling, sequence labels, encoding, suffix stripping Service responds once then stops Protocol state, message framing, authentication, EOF vs timeout ACK but no flag Required setup, message semantics, asynchronous status CAN tunnel sends but receives nothing Local interface, UDP return port, VPN/WSL routing Wi-Fi key known but traffic unreadable Correct AP/SSID, handshake, cipher support, session key material Final verification Reopen exported artifacts using an appropriate approved tool. Confirm magic bytes and length rather than trusting an extension. Decode a candidate value and compare it with its source field. For live stateful tasks, keep the same connection/tunnel alive until the service reports the objective. Record the final flag/result immediately; avoid extra speculative actions after success. Next: Packet triage or TCP/UDP sessions.

title: Steganography
content:
Steganography field notes Inspect the container before guessing the hidden algorithm. A file can hold a message in metadata, trailing bytes, pixels, sound samples, document objects or text code points.
These notes use tools already covered in the approved-tool reference. Optional Python packages are explicitly marked: Python being available does not mean Pillow, NumPy or Matplotlib is installed or allowed by your event.
Pick the evidence you have Evidence / clue Read next First useful action Unknown artifact or misleading extension Triage Magic, metadata, strings, dimensions, embedded signatures Lossless image, “least significant” hint Image LSB and bit planes Identify actual image mode and test one channel PNG/JPEG with odd size or broken structure Image containers Parse chunks/markers; distinguish pixels from compressed coefficients Appended ZIP, archive inside image Archives and carving Establish offset and length, list entries before extraction WAV, repeating tones, strange noise Audio Channels/sample format, waveform, spectrogram, sample bits PDF, DOCX, presentation PDF and documents Visible text, metadata, attachments, XML/media members Invisible characters, odd spacing Text and Unicode Escaped code points and symbol counts Need reusable offline extraction tools Python snippets Download helpers and choose explicit extraction settings Ordered route Original file + hash → inspect metadata / strings / format → inspect visible content or listen at a comfortable level → identify a specific hidden channel → extract exact bytes to a new file → classify the extracted payload → decode / decompress only the indicated layer → verify full message, checksum or valid nested formatFast toolbox map Task Existing notes Metadata and thumbnails ExifTool Readable data and byte offsets strings, xxd Hex inspection / precise selection HxD Embedded format candidates binwalk PNG/BMP bitstream candidates zsteg QR / barcode ZBar PDF text / internals pdftotext, qpdf Decompression / custom extraction xz, Python Encodings / XOR / visual decode CyberChef Keep these distinctions clear A ZIP signature is a candidate offset, not a validated archive. A decoder finding a short printable word in random bits is not a confirmed message. PNG compressed file bytes are not the image’s decoded pixel bytes. JPEG coefficient hiding is different from PNG pixel-LSB hiding. A visually hidden object may still be ordinary document text. A QR may give a hint while a different layer contains the result. Extraction record Original filename and SHA-256: Container / dimensions / encoding: Clue: Tool and version: Offset / member / channel / bit plane: Pixel or sample order / packing / skip: Extracted filename and SHA-256: Next layer: Verified full message:Write down the exact settings that worked. “LSB” alone is insufficient to reproduce a result.

title: Reverse Engineering
content:
Reverse Engineering Field Notes Identify the format. Find the real check. Recover the exact bytes. Verify them in the original program.
Offline manual workflows and reusable Python for authorized CTF binaries. Every tool link below leads to the existing supplied-tool notes. Optional extensions and Z3 are separate from that list; inclusion here does not establish tournament permission.
Original workflow diagram, not a captured tool screenshot.
Choose by evidence What you see Start here Next move Unknown file / wrong architecture Triage Format, ABI and runnable status Native binary, no source Ghidra cheatsheet Strings → references → check function Complex native logic Static analysis Types, widths, branch and data flow Decrypted data only in memory Dynamic debugging Break after transform, dump exact length UTF-16 / hex / XOR array Strings and encodings Extract bytes, confirm decoding layer XOR/rotate/hash/VM Crypto and obfuscation Recognize then model exact operations Managed Windows executable .NET dnSpyEx metadata, resources and IL Need repeatable byte operations Python snippets Download stdlib tools and test fixtures Need stronger Ghidra tooling Ghidra plugins Built-ins first, explicit compatibility checks Pick the right tool Task Supplied-tool notes Native static analysis Ghidra, objdump Linux runtime GDB Windows native runtime x64dbg Windows managed code dnSpyEx Bytes, offsets, patches HxD, xxd Assembly experiments LLVM MC Data transforms Python, CyberChef Static text strings Three flag shapes Stored: plaintext/resource/encoded bytes already exist. Follow references and verify the live printing path; decoys are common. Checked: input is transformed and compared. Recover preprocessing, transforms, constants and exact length; invert or solve the resulting model. Computed: input/state drives decryption or flag construction. A patched “success” branch may still produce garbage because the decryption key depends on valid state. Keep a small evidence card SHA-256 / original filename: Format / architecture / ABI: Native tool / managed tool: Input source and newline rules: Success and failure references: Check function / address / RVA: Expected data address and length: Transform widths / signedness / byte order: Candidate / forward-model result: Original unpatched program result:A patched success popup is a useful experiment, not proof that the recovered input is correct. Finish by running the candidate through the original unmodified validator when the challenge permits execution.

Preserve the original bytes and record their hash. Identify the input format from bytes, not only its extension. Choose one evidence-led operation. Inspect the actual output bytes / message / file. Save the recipe or command and continue only when the result supports the next step. Examples use synthetic flag{demo} data. External plugins and optional Python packages are labeled separately; appearing in a note does not establish tournament approval.

title: CTF Writeups
content:
CTF Writeups Challenge notes with the commands, code, and intermediate bytes needed to repeat the solve. Each writeup records what was tested and any part that still depends on an assumption.
Categories Category Writeups Reversing Native binaries, obfuscation, and flag decryption

title: A Matter of Time
content:
A Matter of Time This crackme builds its AES key from a Windows account name. Its IV depends on a file timestamp and the executable’s PE timestamp. The code is split across jump trampolines and duplicated blocks, which makes the first decompiler output misleading.
The useful break was CBC itself: the IV affects only the first plaintext block. Once the right username decrypted the remaining blocks, I could work on the first block separately.
Item Value Event Crackmes.one Reverse Engineering CTF 2026, identified by the program’s banner File a_matter_of_time.exe Format Windows PE32+, x86-64 Image base in IDA 0x140000000 Tools used IDA, Python, Capstone, Unicorn, PyCryptodome Result Readable candidate, reproduced by the original AES routine; no external acceptance result There is one unresolved part: the IV below was inferred from a readable first block. I did not recover the original timestamp pair that generated it. Replaying AES confirms the bytes for that IV, but does not prove the first block is unique. Section 8 shows the ambiguity directly.
1. Check the file and the IDA database Start by identifying the file:
file a_matter_of_time.exe sha256sum a_matter_of_time.exeOutput:
a_matter_of_time.exe: PE32+ executable for MS Windows 6.00 (console), x86-64, 7 sections bc8583d082c42efa9ad0959792af49c063368db0241dabccb9138fa29ef5e7dc a_matter_of_time.exeThe solve started with an IDA database already supplied for this file. The database reported the same input SHA-256. Its mapped segments were:
.text 0x140001000 - 0x14000b000 .idata 0x14000b000 - 0x14000b480 .rdata 0x14000b480 - 0x140011000 .data 0x140011000 - 0x140012000 .pdata 0x140012000 - 0x140013000 .ch 0x140015000 - 0x140029000The .ch mapping matters. The supplied database has code and layout that differ from the raw file’s section layout. The scripts here use that database image. This writeup starts from the supplied IDB; it does not include an independently recovered unpacking step. Opening only the raw EXE in a fresh database may therefore give different results at the addresses below.
Use the attached mapped segments to reproduce this analysis, or export the corresponding segments from the supplied IDB with export_ida.py. Edit its output path, then run it through IDA’s File → Script file.
The exported JSON maps each segment’s virtual address to its Base64-encoded bytes. It is input for the analysis scripts, not a runnable PE file.
Prepare the helpers Download analysis-tools.zip, extract it, and enter that directory:
unzip analysis-tools.zip -d a-matter-of-time cd a-matter-of-time python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install pycryptodome unicorn capstonePyCryptodome is enough for the final solve.py. Unicorn runs the original machine code. Capstone is used by the control-flow helper.
2. Find main through the CRT startup The entry point is 0x140009188. Decompiling it immediately produced a stack warning and jumps into .ch. That was a reason to inspect the instructions before trusting the pseudocode.
I followed references to __p___argv. One startup path contains:
1400219fe call __p___argv 140021a03 mov rbx, [rax] 140021a06 call __p___argc 140021a0b mov r8, rdi 140021a0e mov rdx, rbx 140021a11 mov ecx, [rax] 140021a13 call 0x140004290The Windows x64 argument registers are RCX, RDX, and R8. The caller is passing the argument count, argument vector, and another startup argument into 0x140004290. This identifies the main routine despite its missing function boundary.
At 0x140004290, the first two instructions are:
140004290 jp 0x14001ceb9 140004296 jnp 0x14001cef3One branch is taken when the parity flag is set, and the other when it is clear. There is no executable fallthrough after the pair. Both destinations contain copies of the main prologue and converge at 0x1400042c2.
The same pattern appears elsewhere:
14001d306 jo 0x14000453b 14001d30c jno 0x14000453bHere both outcomes reach the same address. Bytes following the pair are junk, even if decoding linearly makes them look like instructions.
Other transfers use a register:
140004858 push rsi 140004859 lea rsi, [rip + 0x19276] 140004860 jmp rsiThe lea resolves to 0x14001dad6. That destination starts with pop rsi, restoring the saved register. A normal direct-jump-only walk would miss this block.
Walk reachable instructions Run the helper from the download:
python recover_cfg.py 0x140004290 > main.asm python recover_cfg.py 0x140001000 > startup.asm python recover_cfg.py 0x14000326c > aes-cbc.asmIt follows direct branches, complementary branch pairs, and the nearby lea/register and lea/ret trampolines used here. It keeps both branch destinations instead of assuming every duplicated block is equivalent.
The output is sorted by address for reference; it is not execution order. Follow the branch targets to move between .text and .ch. The helper also stops at calls, so run it again with a callee’s address when tracing into another routine. It is specific to these patterns and does not resolve arbitrary indirect jumps or exception paths.
3. Recover the ciphertext from the initializer The main routine eventually reads a C++ string at 0x140011d98. Searching the raw file for a readable flag was not useful because the string is constructed during startup.
The initializer starts at 0x140001000 and transfers into a block at 0x14001f415. It loads encrypted constants into a stack buffer, then applies:
lea eax, [rcx - 0x28] xor byte ptr [rbp + rcx - 0x19], al inc rcx cmp rcx, 0x60The transform is:
decoded = bytes( byte ^ ((index - 0x28) & 0xff) for index, byte in enumerate(encrypted) )The comparison with 0x60 gives 96 decoded bytes. These are ASCII hex characters, so they represent 48 bytes of ciphertext.
Rather than transcribe every stack constant, I ran just this initializer in Unicorn. The extraction hook stops at 0x140007bc4, before the C++ string-copy helper executes. At that point:
RCX = destination std::string RDX = decoded stack-buffer address R8 = string length, 96The attached extract.py performs that extraction:
python extract.pyRelevant output:
Ciphertext hex: 4c4635258cf6eca5d80b8e050a9e5b04f1a9c979bc55f3f4773971ed2f81a96967bb3569fa002f549cc970a18779b3a7 Ciphertext bytes: 48 Time source: C:\\Windows\\System32\\winevt\\Logs\\System.evtxThe decoded path has doubled backslashes, as printed above; elsewhere on this page I show it with single path separators for readability. The script also writes ciphertext.hex. It stops before library calls in each extraction path, so it does not need to emulate Windows or the full C++ runtime.
4. Identify AES and the CBC loop At this stage the important functions are:
Address What the code does 0x1400010b0 Expands an AES-128 key into 44 words 0x140001498 Applies AES inverse rounds to one 16-byte block 0x14000326c Decrypts a byte vector using CBC chaining 0x1400033b4 Gets the Windows account name and converts it to UTF-8 0x140003734 Reads the loaded module’s PE timestamp 0x140003750 Gets the last-write time of System.evtx 0x1400034f8 Converts the file-time value to seconds through a chrono helper 0x140003d98 Formats a string with zero fill and width 16 0x140007034 Converts an unsigned 32-bit integer to decimal text The key expansion copies 16 key bytes, uses the substitution and round-constant tables, and expands to 0x2c words. The inverse cipher then operates on 16-byte blocks. The surrounding loop establishes the mode: it saves each ciphertext block, decrypts the block, XORs it with the previous ciphertext block or initial IV, and carries the saved ciphertext forward.
In pseudocode:
previous = iv for offset in range(0, len(ciphertext), 16): current = ciphertext[offset:offset + 16] plaintext_block = xor(aes_decrypt_block(key, current), previous) previous = currentThis is AES-128-CBC. The original inverse cipher at 0x140001498 is also used in the final machine-code verification.
5. Trace the key back to the account name The routine at 0x1400033b4 calls:
GetCurrentProcess OpenProcessToken GetTokenInformation(TokenUser) LookupAccountSidWIt gets the account name associated with the process token. The following conversion makes that UTF-8 text available to the key-building code.
The formatter at 0x140003d98 uses width 0x10 and fill byte 0x30. For the short strings relevant here, its behavior is equivalent to:
formatted = text.rjust(16, "0")There is hexadecimal stream formatting nearby, but the operand is a string. That does not turn nicetryboogeyman into the ASCII string 6e696365.... The bytes passed to AES remain the formatted account-name bytes.
The PDB path gives a username worth testing:
0x14000d5a8 C:\Users\nicetryboogeyman\cmo\x64\Release\cmo.pdbThat name is exactly 16 ASCII bytes:
key = b"nicetryboogeyman" assert len(key) == 16A PDB path alone would only be a lead. The next step checks the key against ciphertext without guessing the IV.
6. Decrypt the blocks that do not need the IV For CBC decryption:
P1 = AES_DEC(K, C1) XOR IV P2 = AES_DEC(K, C2) XOR C1 P3 = AES_DEC(K, C3) XOR C2Only P1 depends on the IV. The ciphertext already supplies the chaining bytes for the later blocks.
Run this from the directory containing the extracted ciphertext.hex:
from pathlib import Path from Crypto.Cipher import AES ciphertext = bytes.fromhex(Path("ciphertext.hex").read_text()) key = b"nicetryboogeyman" intermediate = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB).decrypt(ciphertext) for offset in range(16, len(ciphertext), 16): decrypted = intermediate[offset:offset + 16] previous = ciphertext[offset - 16:offset] block = bytes(a ^ b for a, b in zip(decrypted, previous)) print(offset // 16 + 1, repr(block))Output:
2 b't0_l34rn_fr0M_n0' 3 b'T_t0_l1V3_1n}\x03\x03\x03'The suffix reads t0_l34rn_fr0M_n0T_t0_l1V3_1n}. Three trailing 0x03 bytes are valid PKCS#7 padding for a 45-byte plaintext.
Together, the readable suffix and padding strongly support the username as the AES key. Padding by itself would be much weaker evidence.
7. Check what the time code actually reads My first notes described the time input as the current clock. Inspecting the code more closely showed a file lookup instead.
At 0x140003750, another XOR-decoded stack string resolves to:
C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\System.evtxextract.py stops at 0x140009a80, after that decode and before the library work, and reads the path through R13. The subsequent filesystem-stat call at 0x140009bbc requests the last-write-time field. Main converts the returned file time, keeps its low 32 bits, and XORs that with the loaded module’s PE timestamp before calling the decimal formatter.
The PE timestamp reader is short enough to recognize directly:
xor ecx, ecx call GetModuleHandleW mov rcx, rax movsxd rax, dword ptr [rax + 0x3c] mov eax, dword ptr [rax + rcx + 8]0x3c is the DOS header’s e_lfanew. The final read gets the COFF TimeDateStamp at NT headers +8.
The IV-building path can be described as:
# Model of the data flow, not an exact replacement for the chrono conversion. file_seconds = convert_last_write_time(system_event_log) value = (file_seconds & 0xffffffff) ^ loaded_module_pe_timestamp iv_text = str(value).rjust(16, "0")There are also warnings based on 0x698fbb00, corresponding to 2026-02-14 UTC. The elapsed-hour calculation uses a multiply by 0x91a2b3c5 followed by a 43-bit shift. Those warning paths converge before decryption; reaching the CTF date window is not sufficient to identify the IV.
The current raw EXE has a zero PE timestamp. That does not tell us the original System.evtx time or establish which timestamp pair the author used when encrypting the flag. The solve therefore does not claim to have reproduced the intended Windows environment.
8. Reconstruct the first block, and keep the uncertainty visible With the key known, decrypting the first ciphertext block without CBC XOR gives:
from Crypto.Cipher import AES ciphertext = bytes.fromhex( "4c4635258cf6eca5d80b8e050a9e5b04" "f1a9c979bc55f3f4773971ed2f81a969" "67bb3569fa002f549cc970a18779b3a7" ) decrypted_first = AES.new(b"nicetryboogeyman", AES.MODE_ECB).decrypt( ciphertext[:16] ) print(decrypted_first.hex())Output:
737d7f4b0558036a430363426701466cThe readable suffix suggests the sentence “the past is to learn from, not to live in.” A candidate for its first 16 bytes is:
first_block = b"CMO{5h3_p4St_1s_" iv = bytes(a ^ b for a, b in zip(decrypted_first, first_block)) print(iv) print(int(iv))Output:
b'0000000537068053' 537068053That matches the expected IV representation: a zero-padded decimal unsigned 32-bit value. Decrypting with it produces a coherent complete string.
This is still an inference. For example, changing the first-block candidate from ..._1s_ to ..._0s_ produces another decimal-looking IV:
CMO{5h3_p4St_1s_ -> 0000000537068053 CMO{5h3_p4St_0s_ -> 0000000537068153Both preserve the exact same later plaintext blocks and padding. The wording favors the first, but CBC does not authenticate it.
The executable’s success branch is also too weak to settle this. Its relevant comparisons are equivalent to:
if (plaintext[0] == 'C' || plaintext[1] == 'M') { print_success(); print_plaintext(); }At 0x1400048a3, equality with C jumps directly to the success path. If that fails, equality with M at 0x1400048a9 reaches the same path. It does not require the whole CMO{...} prefix or compare the full flag.
So the final result below is a readable candidate corroborated by the machine code. An original timestamp capture or external checker would be needed to remove the remaining first-block ambiguity.
9. Run the solver Save this as solve.py, or use the attached solver:
from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Util.Padding import unpad ciphertext = bytes.fromhex( "4c4635258cf6eca5d80b8e050a9e5b04" "f1a9c979bc55f3f4773971ed2f81a969" "67bb3569fa002f549cc970a18779b3a7" ) key = b"nicetryboogeyman" # Inferred from a readable first block; not an observed runtime timestamp. iv = b"0000000537068053" padded = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv).decrypt(ciphertext) plaintext = unpad(padded, AES.block_size) assert AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv).encrypt(padded) == ciphertext print(plaintext.decode("ascii"))Run:
python solve.pyOutput:
CMO{5h3_p4St_1s_t0_l34rn_fr0M_n0T_t0_l1V3_1n}Keep 5h3 exactly as shown. Substituting a more natural spelling changes the bytes and the inferred IV.
10. Compare with the original AES routine The downloadable solver also supports:
python solve.py --verify-nativeThis calls verify_aes.py, which maps the exported segments and enters the original CBC routine at 0x14000326c.
The emulated call uses the Windows x64 argument registers:
RCX -> ciphertext vector RDX -> key vector R8 -> IV vectorEach vector is represented as three 64-bit pointers:
begin, end, capacity_endFor example, a 48-byte ciphertext at 0x120000 has:
struct.pack("<QQQ", 0x120000, 0x120030, 0x120030)The emulator models four helpers:
Address Emulator replacement 0x140007e08 Supply a scratch allocation and initialize its vector pointers 0x140009fb1 Perform memset 0x140008ef4 Return from the free helper 0x140008c50 Return from the security-cookie check The key expansion, inverse rounds, CBC XOR, and block chaining execute as original machine instructions. No crypto instruction is patched, and the complete application is not launched.
The resulting bytes are:
b'CMO{5h3_p4St_1s_t0_l34rn_fr0M_n0T_t0_l1V3_1n}\x03\x03\x03'The verifier asserts that those 48 bytes match PyCryptodome. The solver also removes the padding and re-encrypts to the extracted ciphertext. These checks confirm the AES model and chosen inputs; they do not independently recover the original IV.
Files Everything needed for the recorded analysis is in analysis-tools.zip. Individual files:
File Purpose solve.py Final decryption and optional machine-code comparison extract.py Recover the ciphertext and hidden file path from the mapped code recover_cfg.py Follow the branch/trampoline patterns used by this binary verify_aes.py Run the original AES-CBC routine in Unicorn export_ida.py Export mapped segments from the supplied IDA database ida_segments.json Segment snapshot used in this solve ciphertext.hex Extracted 96-character ciphertext string The raw challenge EXE is not included in this bundle. The mapped snapshot is enough to replay the recorded initializer and AES routine.

title: 00 · First 10 Minutes
content:
First 10 Minutes 1. Read what the challenge gives you If source is supplied, start there. Find routes, database setup, templates, upload handling, authentication checks, Dockerfile, and the flag placement. Trace input → transformation → guard → dangerous operation → response.
Sink in source Investigate String concatenation / interpolation in SQL SQLi render_template_string, Environment.from_string, template compilation SSTI findOne(req.body), object spread into a database filter NoSQLi exec, shell=True, system, backticks Command injection open, readFile, include using user path LFI / traversal Server HTTP client using user URL SSRF Raw HTML / innerHTML / unescaped template output XSS Object deserialization Deserialization Recursive merge of untrusted JSON Prototype pollution execute("... WHERE id=?", (id,)) is different from constructing the SQL string first. Parameterization protects values; dynamically assembled identifiers, sort directions, or a later query can remain vulnerable.
2. Black-box: inspect before injecting Open page source, DevTools Network, scripts, and storage. Read comments and hidden fields. Inspect redirects and actual API calls, including errors. Note cookies, CSRF tokens, content types, and response fields. Check robots.txt, sitemap.xml, linked JS source maps, and challenge-indicated backups. A 200 might be a catch-all: compare with a random nonexistent path. Map every input: query, form, JSON, path, cookie, headers, upload filename, stored profile fields. Decide where the result likely lives: database row, server file, environment variable, browser/admin bot, or gated workflow. An nginx header does not identify the application or database. Flask suggests Python, but not necessarily Jinja injection. A browser form can still send JSON to an API.
3. Save a baseline in Repeater GET /search?q=apple HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalid Cookie: session=YOUR_SESSION Connection: closeChange one field at a time. Compare status, headers, response length, actual records, error text, timing, and asynchronous job output. Ignore random request IDs and rotating tokens when comparing bodies.
First probe Matching control Potential lead apple' apple and apple'' SQL syntax context; not proof alone 1 AND 1=1 1 AND 1=2 SQL boolean oracle A{{7*7}}B A{{7*8}}B Template evaluation if raw response changes to A49B / A56B JSON object instead of string Original string / wrong operator condition NoSQL or type confusion ../../../etc/hostname Known nonexistent file Traversal / file read 127.0.0.1; printf CTFPROBE Valid original input Shell command execution 4. Follow evidence, not a payload lottery SQL error names database → engine-specific schema queries Template arithmetic in raw HTTP → engine fingerprint → context inspection JSON object changes query semantics → operator injection tests Input appears as literal HTML → inspect browser context before XSS URL fetched by server → inspect SSRF response / redirect behavior Stored input causes later error → test second-order sinkIf every payload produces the same response, check the route, method, session, parameter name, content type, caching, and whether another request actually consumes the input.
5. Common time traps A changed page may be a rate limit, validation failure, expired session, or CSRF rejection. A login 302 may redirect back to the login page. Follow it and inspect the authenticated session. A fragment after # never goes to the HTTP server unless encoded as %23 in a parameter. Browser-only arithmetic can be client-side templating. Compare raw response before calling it SSTI. A WAF rejection is not a database fingerprint. Read backend errors or use controlled engine functions. Do not discard a preview, PDF, canvas, image, or JS response: it can be the actual challenge evidence. For a stateful challenge, keep the session and inspect status/job responses until the final result appears. Next: SQLi · SSTI · Auth / IDOR

title: 01 · Packet Triage
content:
Packet Triage Flow: capture health → protocol hierarchy → conversations → candidate stream → exported evidence.
Tools: Wireshark, TShark, Zeek, Python.
1. Preserve the input and establish scale from pathlib import Path import hashlib p = Path('traffic.pcapng') h = hashlib.sha256() with p.open('rb') as source: for chunk in iter(lambda: source.read(1024 * 1024), b''): h.update(chunk) print(p.name, p.stat().st_size, h.hexdigest())Do not hash text output from tshark; hash the actual input bytes.
In Wireshark, open Statistics → Capture File Properties. Note interfaces, encapsulation, capture length, time range, and packet count. A snap length that cuts off application data limits extraction even if TCP headers are present.
2. Inventory protocols and conversations Commands below use a shell with TShark on PATH. The Windows tool page shows the full executable path.
tshark -r traffic.pcapng -q -z io,phs tshark -r traffic.pcapng -q -z conv,tcp tshark -r traffic.pcapng -q -z conv,udp tshark -r traffic.pcapng -q -z endpoints,ip Output What to prioritize A rare protocol Inspect decoded fields before assuming a tunnel One very large TCP flow File transfer, video, encrypted bulk traffic Many small DNS queries DNS label content, retries, TXT answers Short repeated connections Polling, retries, authentication, application heartbeats UDP with changing binary fields Datagram framing / custom telemetry Large traffic volume does not guarantee relevance. A small request can contain the only password.
3. Look for evidence-bearing protocols Wireshark display filters:
http.request http.response dns ftp || ftp-data smtp || imap || pop smb2 icmp || icmpv6 tls.handshake sshIf a field or protocol name is rejected, use the installed display-filter autocomplete or packet tree. Dissector field names can differ between versions.
tshark -G protocols tshark -G fieldsThese enumerate local capabilities; they do not read the challenge capture.
4. Export a compact timeline tshark -r traffic.pcapng -T fields -E header=y -E separator=/t \ -e frame.number -e frame.time_relative \ -e ip.src -e ipv6.src -e tcp.srcport -e udp.srcport \ -e ip.dst -e ipv6.dst -e tcp.dstport -e udp.dstport \ -e _ws.col.Protocol -e _ws.col.Info > timeline.tsv-r reads a capture; -T fields exports selected decoded fields; -e selects one field; -E controls text output. separator=/t requests a tab separator.
Do not treat an exported field table as a packet capture. It can omit payloads, retransmissions, repeated field values, and interface metadata.
5. Inspect one stream ip.addr == 192.0.2.10 tcp.stream eq 7 udp.stream eq 2tshark -r traffic.pcapng -q -z follow,tcp,ascii,7 tshark -r traffic.pcapng -Y 'tcp.stream eq 7' -w stream7.pcapngThe first command prints a human-readable followed stream. The second saves selected packets as a new capture. Neither is automatically a clean application file.
For an exact binary object, use protocol export or the correct directional Follow Stream → Show data as Raw → Save As workflow. Keep framing bytes in mind.
6. Search carefully frame contains "flag" tcp contains "password" http.request.uri contains "download" dns.qry.name contains "challenge"A packet-byte search can miss strings split across packets, compressed content, or encrypted records. Compare it with stream follow and object export. Check headers, cookies, URLs, request bodies, response bodies, filenames, and metadata.
A literal flag-like string can be a decoy or an example. Trace it to the actual challenge objective.
7. Use Zeek for a second view zeek -r traffic.pcapngRun in a separate output directory: Zeek writes logs into the working directory. Inspect conn.log, then protocol logs actually produced, such as http.log or dns.log. Absent logs can mean encryption, missing handshake, unsupported encapsulation, or a missing analyzer.
Zeek summaries and Wireshark dissections can disagree because they reconstruct and classify traffic differently. Return to the packets to resolve the discrepancy.
8. Health checks before trusting extraction frame.cap_len < frame.len tcp.analysis.retransmission tcp.analysis.lost_segment tcp.analysis.out_of_orderThese are investigation clues. Outbound checksum failures can be capture-offload artifacts; a “previous segment not captured” warning can arise from starting midstream. Do not discard a stream solely because Expert Information reports a warning.
Decision checkpoint Result Next page Web object / request HTTP Suspicious DNS names DNS Encrypted traffic TLS/SSH Unknown binary/text stream TCP/UDP Mail/file-share/ping Protocols Reference: TShark manual for local field and statistics options.

title: Arc4 Decrypt
content:
ida-pattern
for ( i = 0; i < 256; ++i ) v44[i] = i; v8 = a6; v9 = 0; for ( j = 0; j < 256; ++j ) { if ( v8 <= j % v8 ) sub_401710(); p_Block = &Block; v12 = v44[j]; if ( a7 >= 0x10 ) p_Block = (_DWORD **)Block; v9 = (v12 + *((char *)p_Block + j % v8) + v9) % 256; v44[j] = v44[v9]; v44[v9] = v12; }import struct from Crypto.Cipher import ARC4 v36 = [0] * 11 v36[0] = 0x33122A35 v36[1] = 0xB2645787 v36[2] = 0x34A6EF00 v36[3] = 0x3EDEE001 v36[4] = 0x40EC2101 v36[5] = 0xB0691D26 v36[6] = 0x7BB269B0 v36[7] = 0x6EB2256 v36[8] = 0xCB5DF2BE v36[9] = 0x512B0F79 v36[10] = 0x55 ciphertext = b"".join(struct.pack('<I', x) for x in v36) cipher = ARC4.new(b'LLURULDUL') print(cipher.decrypt(ciphertext).decode('utf-8'))

title: CyberChef
content:
Use for: decoding, XOR, compression, hashes, quick crypto experiments.
Run in: Chrome → CyberChef. Browser tool; no install.
Quick start Paste text into Input, or open a file with the input file button. Search operations on the left and drag them into Recipe. Read Output. Operations run from top to bottom. Use the output download button for binary results. Recipes to remember Input clue Recipe to try Base64 text From Base64 Hex byte pairs From Hex %7B, %2F URL Decode &#...; or < From HTML Entity Binary digits From Binary ROT13 clue ROT13 One byte XOR XOR Brute Force Known XOR key XOR → set key format correctly Compressed Base64 From Base64 → Gunzip Unknown encoding Magic → inspect suggestions Walkthrough: two encoding layers Input: 3636366336313637376236343635366436663764 Recipe: From Hex From Hex Output: flag{demo}For AES, select the stated mode, key encoding, IV encoding, input format and padding. A hex key must be interpreted as hex bytes.
Gotchas Magic gives candidates; verify against the challenge format. Keep the original input and save the recipe so the steps are repeatable. Text copied from a binary output can lose bytes; download the result instead. CTF: choose a transform from the evidence Observation Experiment What confirms it Alphabet ends with = From Base64 Structured bytes/text after decoding Only hex digits, even length From Hex Recognizable signature or coherent text Many %xx escapes URL Decode A URL/query/string with valid syntax Base64URL token sections From Base64 using URL-safe alphabet JSON header/payload for a JWT Random-looking short bytes XOR with known key / XOR Brute Force Matching prefix plus meaningful remainder 1F 8B after decoding Gunzip Complete decompressed data 78 9C or 78 DA clue Zlib Inflate Successful decompression and valid output These are hypotheses. For example, many ordinary strings fit the Base64 alphabet.
CTF: decode a JWT without validating it Split the token into its dot-separated sections. Take the header or payload section. Use From Base64 with the URL-safe alphabet; handle omitted padding if required. Inspect the JSON, including algorithm, expiry, role and identifiers. Preserve the full original token for request reproduction. Decoding a payload does not verify its signature or prove the server accepts changes.
CTF: decrypt AES from explicit parameters Input: the challenge ciphertext Recipe: From Base64 # only when input is Base64 text AES Decrypt Key: supplied value, correct Hex/UTF8/Base64 representation IV: supplied value, correct representation Mode: CBC/CTR/etc. as specified Input: Raw after From Base64 Output: RawAES-128 uses a 16-byte key; AES-256 uses 32 bytes. A 32-character hex string represents 16 bytes. CBC’s IV is 16 bytes. Password-derived keys require reproducing the given KDF rather than typing the password into a raw key field.
CTF: repeating-key XOR Load ciphertext as bytes, using From Hex or From Base64 if needed. Add XOR and enter the key in its actual format. Inspect output as both text and hex. Check the entire message or embedded file structure. For a one-byte key, XOR Brute Force gives candidates. For a known plaintext prefix, use Python to calculate candidate key bytes and test repetition.
Process many encoded lines Use Fork around a per-line recipe when each input line is independent. Keep a small known example first. Applying a single Base64 decoder to several concatenated values can silently change boundaries.
Recover binary output correctly If output starts with PK, PNG magic or another file signature, download it as a file. Check the resulting bytes in xxd/HxD. Copy/pasting through a text field can alter NULs, line endings or encoding.
When the output looks wrong Symptom Likely next check Readable prefix, broken remainder Wrong XOR key length or truncation AES error Key/IV representation, mode, length or padding Empty decompression Wrong wrapper: gzip vs zlib vs raw DEFLATE Unexpected extra layer Continue one transformation at a time Plausible but meaningless result Check original clue; avoid unbounded random recipes Save the recipe and record which inputs are text versus raw bytes at each step.
Reference: official project and usage.
Related playbooks Visual CyberChef recipes Reusable byte helpers

title: CyberChef · Visual Recipes
content:
CyberChef Visual Cheatsheet Input bytes → ordered recipe → inspect output → save exact bytes. Start with one transformation suggested by the data. Magic is a hypothesis generator, not proof of a correct decode.
Existing CyberChef tool note · Official app · Official project / offline release.
1. Know the four panels Actual browser screenshot captured during this update, using only synthetic demo input. UI layout may differ on the tournament’s installed build.
Area What to do What to watch Operations, left Search operation name, drag it into Recipe Similar names can mean different formats Recipe, middle Arrange operations top to bottom Each operation consumes the previous output Input, top right Paste text or load a file Raw file bytes differ from text spelling of hex Output, bottom right Inspect text/hex, download output Copying binary as text may alter bytes Use Step to inspect one stage at a time. Disable/enable a recipe operation to locate where data stops making sense. Save the recipe before trying a different hypothesis.
2. Choose the first operation Input clue First operation Control / verification Even count of hex digits, optional separators From Hex Re-encode with To Hex; compare bytes Base64 alphabet, possible = padding From Base64 Valid bytes / expected file signature, not alphabet alone - / _ in JWT sections From Base64, URL-safe alphabet Header/payload should parse as JSON %xx URL Decode Identify percent encoding vs form + rules &#...;, < From HTML Entity Check resulting browser/text context 01000110... From Binary Confirm grouping and bit order Decimal byte values From Decimal Confirm separator and 0–255 byte interpretation Letter-only substitution clue ROT13 / ROT47 as appropriate Coherent full output, not one matching word Repeating XOR clue XOR / XOR Brute Force Correct key encoding and known prefix Decoded 1f 8b Gunzip Complete decompression with valid output Decoded zlib wrapper Zlib Inflate Correct wrapper and full output Raw DEFLATE bytes Raw Inflate No gzip/zlib header expected 3. Base64, hex, and multiple layers One Base64 layer Input: ZmxhZ3tkZW1vfQ== Recipe: From Base64 Output: flag{demo}One hex layer Input: 666c61677b64656d6f7d Recipe: From Hex Output: flag{demo}Two hex layers Input: 3636366336313637376236343635366436663764 Recipe: From Hex From Hex Output: flag{demo}At the intermediate stage the output is the ASCII text 666c61677b64656d6f7d. It is not already the decoded flag bytes. This distinction matters when chaining AES, XOR, and decompression.
Reproducible Python control import base64 assert base64.b64decode('ZmxhZ3tkZW1vfQ==') == b'flag{demo}' layered = '3636366336313637376236343635366436663764' assert bytes.fromhex(bytes.fromhex(layered).decode()) == b'flag{demo}'4. XOR: specify bytes, not appearances Input: 242e23253926272f2d3f Recipe: From Hex XOR Key format: Hex Key: 42 Output: flag{demo}42 in Hex mode is one byte 0x42. 42 in UTF-8 mode is two bytes 0x34 0x32. A key of ICE in UTF-8 mode is the same bytes as 494345 in Hex mode.
For repeating-key XOR:
known plaintext prefix + ciphertext prefix → XOR the two byte sequences → candidate key bytes → test candidate repetition against whole ciphertextFor single-byte XOR, XOR Brute Force enumerates a one-byte keyspace. It does not solve an arbitrary AES key or a long repeating XOR key. Score full structure and save the actual key, not just the most readable preview.
5. Compression: identify the wrapper Base64 text → From Base64 → inspect magic → Gunzip / Zlib Inflate / Raw Inflate Hex text → From Hex → inspect magic → correct decompressorDo not feed ASCII hex into a decompressor. 1f 8b is a gzip clue; zlib headers include common 78 01, 78 9c, 78 da combinations but header validation is stronger than matching two bytes. A ZIP container needs archive extraction, not simply Gunzip.
If decompression fails, verify whether the stream is truncated, begins at a nonzero offset, has a password/container layer, or is not compressed at all. Keep binary output as a download.
6. AES: a parameter checklist Parameter What you need Key Actual bytes or an explicitly specified KDF/password derivation Mode ECB, CBC, CTR, GCM, etc.; modes are not interchangeable IV / nonce Correct length and bytes for that mode Ciphertext representation Raw / Hex / Base64 Padding PKCS#7, none, or another specified scheme GCM tag / AAD Required authenticated inputs where applicable Output representation Raw bytes first, then display as needed Example workflow when the challenge explicitly supplies a CBC key and IV:
From Base64 # if ciphertext input is Base64 text AES Decrypt Key: actual key, with correct Hex/UTF8 representation IV: actual IV, with correct representation Mode: CBC Input: Raw (because From Base64 already decoded it) Padding: the challenge's actual paddingAES-128/192/256 keys have 16/24/32 bytes. A 32-character hex string encodes 16 bytes. CBC has a 16-byte IV. A readable first block does not prove the whole decrypt is correct; check all plaintext, padding and any authentication tag.
CyberChef versions expose crypto parameters differently. If the needed mode/tag/derivation is not supported in your build, use the event-permitted Python cookbook and exact parameters rather than substituting a different mode.
7. JWT inspection Preserve the full token. Split its three JWS sections at .. Decode the first and second with Base64URL alphabet and compatible padding. Parse JSON and read alg, kid, sub, role, audience, issuer, and time claims. Do not modify/re-sign until the application’s verification behavior is understood. A five-part encrypted token is a different structure. Decoding a token is not signature verification. Continue with JWT testing.
8. Per-line transforms with Fork Input: ZmxhZw== e2RlbW99 Recipe: Fork (split by newline) From Base64Expected decoded lines: flag and {demo}. Keep each original record boundary unless the challenge says to concatenate. Applying one decoder to a concatenation of separately padded Base64 strings can discard or misinterpret later records.
9. Regex and extraction Use Regular expression to extract an evidence-supported format, for example:
flag\{[^}\r\n]+\}The event’s actual flag prefix may differ. Regex over binary may hide NULs or line-ending details. For a PCAP stream, first reconstruct the correct stream and direction with TShark, then transform the extracted application data.
10. Save a reproducible recipe Save/export the recipe and record input format, key format, mode, and intermediate result. A deep link may embed the entire input and recipe in the URL. Avoid sharing live tokens/keys in links; use the synthetic sample when taking screenshots. Download CyberChef’s offline release before the event if permitted. Verify the downloaded package opens without network access; a bookmarked online tab alone is not an offline copy. Preserve binary output using the download button. Confirm its hash/length in Python, HxD, or xxd. Troubleshooting Wrong output Check next Decoder error Alphabet, omitted padding, truncation, copy artifacts Coherent prefix, wrong suffix Incorrect key length/alignment, partial bytes, wrong mode AES padding error Key/IV bytes, CBC mode, full ciphertext, real padding Decompression error Wrapper, start offset, complete stream Output looks like another encoding Inspect then add one justified stage Magic offers many candidates Validate clue, signature, full message and round-trip Download differs from copied text Binary/text conversion; use exact download bytes References: official CyberChef getting started, official operation source.

title: Dmp Hunt4c2
content:
DMP Hunt4C2 — .NET Memory Dump Analysis This walkthrough follows a .NET application from its call stack to its heap objects, then recovers an encrypted message from a Google Calendar event stored in memory.
The workflow:
Identify the .NET runtime → Find application objects and crypto fields → Recover the application assembly → Decompile the message-handling code → Read a Calendar event description from the heap → Decrypt the recovered messageThe addresses below come from this dump. For another dump, use the addresses returned by your own commands. Names such as CRYPTO_OBJECT_ADDRESS and BASE_ADDRESS are placeholders to replace before running a command.
1. Set up WinDbg and SOS Open the dump in WinDbg. Run these commands in the command box, one at a time:
.symfix .reload !eeversion !clrstack Command Purpose .symfix Configure the Microsoft symbol server. .reload Reload symbols using the configured symbol path. !eeversion Display runtime and SOS version information; a successful response also confirms that SOS is responding. !clrstack Display the current thread’s managed call stack. If WinDbg cannot find the SOS commands, try loading SOS beside CoreCLR:
.loadby sos coreclr !eeversion !clrstackThis loading method requires sos.dll to be available beside coreclr.dll. If it fails, load your installed SOS extension using its actual path:
.load C:\path\to\sos.dllThe stack contains coreclr and System.Private.CoreLib, which identify a modern .NET runtime. We use SOS to inspect managed memory and ILSpy or dnSpy to inspect the application code.
2. Find application objects Start with a summary of the managed heap:
!dumpheap -statLook for application-specific types among the framework types. In this dump, two useful leads are:
CSG2025_RC_Crypto CSG2025_RC_ComSearch for objects whose type names contain CSG:
!dumpheap -type CSGThe object rows include an Address column and an MT column. Use the object address with !do:
!do CRYPTO_OBJECT_ADDRESSUse the Address column here. MT is the MethodTable address, which identifies the object’s type; it is not the address of that object instance.
Read the crypto fields Inspecting the Crypto object revealed these fields:
key iv xorKeyFollow each field’s reference from the Value column. For a byte-array field, inspect its elements with:
!dumparray ARRAY_OBJECT_ADDRESSFor a string field, use:
!do STRING_OBJECT_ADDRESSThe heap contains the values present at the time of capture. We can recover those runtime values before understanding how the application originally encoded or decoded them.
For the final AES decryption in this walkthrough, the recovered values are:
key = b"rA8fT6YzX2pQ4eM9vW1kLdB3" iv = b"uJ7nP0xR3aH5bG2q"The supplied notes do not include an xorKey value. It is not needed by the final decryption script shown below.
3. Locate the application method Inspect the native stack and the managed stack:
k !clrstackThe relevant native stack excerpt is:
# Child-SP RetAddr Call Site 03 00000088`3979e8f0 00007ffd`a216580a ws2_32!recv+0xc1 04 00000088`3979e990 00007ffd`a21651f0 System_Net_Sockets!Interop.Winsock.recv+0xca 05 00000088`3979ea60 00007ffd`a2164def System_Net_Sockets!System.Net.Sockets.Socket.Receive+0x180 06 00000088`3979eae0 00007ffd`a2164b63 System_Net_Sockets!System.Net.Sockets.NetworkStream.Read+0x9f 07 00000088`3979eb60 00007ffe`01309864 System_Private_CoreLib!System.IO.StreamReader.ReadBuffer+0x63 08 00000088`3979ebb0 00007ffd`a2161d74 System_Private_CoreLib!System.IO.StreamReader.ReadLine+0x64 09 00000088`3979ec60 00007ffd`a2161949 CSG2025_Reversing_Challenge!CSG2025_Reversing_Challenge.CSG2025_RC_Srv.RemoteShell+0x404RemoteShell is calling ReadLine, which reaches the socket receive path. This suggests the thread was waiting for input when the dump was captured.
The RetAddr on the ReadLine row is 00007ffda2161d74. That is the return location in its caller, RemoteShell, so it gives us an address inside the application’s JIT-compiled method.
Resolve that code address with:
!ip2md 00007ffda2161d74Relevant output:
MethodDesc: 00007ffda2229398 Method Name: CSG2025_Reversing_Challenge.CSG2025_RC_Srv.RemoteShell(Int32) Class: 00007ffda2212528 MethodTable: 00007ffda22293d8 mdToken: 000000000600000C Module: 00007ffda21ee0a0 IsJitted: yes Current CodeAddr: 00007ffda2161970The field we need next is Module:
00007ffda21ee0a04. Export and decompile the assembly Inspect the module:
!dumpmodule 00007ffda21ee0a0Find its BaseAddress. Create C:\Analysis on your analysis machine if necessary, then replace BASE_ADDRESS below with the reported value:
!savemodule BASE_ADDRESS C:\Analysis\recovered.dllThe Module address from !ip2md identifies the runtime module structure. !savemodule needs the loaded image’s base address, which is reported by !dumpmodule.
Open recovered.dll in ILSpy or dnSpy, then trace:
Method or class What to inspect RemoteShell How commands are received and their results handled. CSG2025_RC_Crypto How crypto values are decoded and messages encrypted. CSG2025_RC_Com Where the message is stored and how it is sent. Microsoft documents the object, array, method, and module inspection commands in its SOS command reference.
5. Trace the Google Calendar message storage In the decompiler, open:
CSG2025_RC_Com → AppendTextToEvent()The method retrieves a Calendar event:
Event @event = service.Events.Get(text, eventId).Execute();The namespace import identifies the Event type:
using Google.Apis.Calendar.v3.Data;Its fully qualified name is:
Google.Apis.Calendar.v3.Data.EventThe method appends the message to the event’s description:
@event.Description = @event.Description + textToAppend + "\n";It then updates the Calendar event:
service.Events.Update(@event, text, eventId).Execute();@event is the local variable name. Event is its type. Searching the heap by the full type name lets us find event objects that may still contain the message.
These are decompiled code excerpts; we do not need to execute them or contact Google Calendar to read an event already present in the dump.
6. Recover the encrypted description Search for Calendar event objects:
!dumpheap -type Google.Apis.Calendar.v3.Data.EventFrom the results, identify the MethodTable for the exact Event type. In this dump it is 00007ffda2480c38.
List only the addresses of instances of that type:
!dumpheap -mt 00007ffda2480c38 -shortOutput:
0210af14b758 0210af1bcba0 0210af25d740Inspect the second event:
!do 0210af1bcba0Find the description’s backing field:
Value Name 00000210af1cc1b8 <Description>k__BackingFieldThe Value is a reference to a string object. Follow it:
!do 00000210af1cc1b8The recovered description contains this Base64 ciphertext:
xAYzbKdNTXbilYe1LgMrCwMvP0uu/6uhhT52MCnmzOTh2udnHKqJc/6iD+u9Bd3OIf one event has an empty or unrelated description, inspect the other event objects. A description can contain several appended lines; select the ciphertext line you intend to decrypt.
7. Decrypt the message The supplied script uses AES-CBC with a 24-byte key and a 16-byte IV. The key length makes this AES-192.
Install the dependency in your Python environment:
python -m pip install pycryptodomeSave this as decrypt.py:

title: Lro Rlo File Ext
content: #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Build the RLO/LRO filename pattern shown in the M2 lab writeup.""" from __future__ import annotations import argparse import json from pathlib import Path RLO = "\u202e" LRO = "\u202d" def build_name(display_name: str, extension: str, prefix: str | None) -> tuple[str, str]: if not extension.startswith(".") or len(extension) < 2: raise ValueError("--extension must include its leading dot, for example .exe") if prefix is None: marker_at = display_name.lower().find(extension.lower()) if marker_at <= 0: raise ValueError( f"{display_name!r} has no {extension!r} inside it; supply --prefix " "whose text is the start of the display name and ends in the real extension" ) prefix = display_name[: marker_at + len(extension)] if not display_name.startswith(prefix): raise ValueError("--prefix must match the beginning of the displayed name") if not prefix.lower().endswith(extension.lower()): raise ValueError("--prefix must end with the real extension") remainder = display_name[len(prefix) :] if not remainder: raise ValueError("the prefix must leave some displayed text after it") # RLO reverses the remainder for display. LRO then starts a left-to-right # run containing the prefix. That prefix is last in the stored name, so its # final extension remains the file's actual extension. stored_name = RLO + remainder[::-1] + LRO + prefix return stored_name, prefix def main() -> int: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser( description="Preview or apply the M2 lab RLO/LRO filename pattern." ) parser.add_argument("source", type=Path, help="Existing file, such as payload.exe") parser.add_argument("display_name", help="Name you want the UI to display") parser.add_argument( "--prefix", help="Displayed starting text ending with the source file's real extension; inferred when possible", ) parser.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true", help="Rename the source file") parser.add_argument( "--literal", action="store_true", help="Print the raw Unicode name too; bidi controls are invisible", ) args = parser.parse_args() if not args.source.is_file(): parser.error(f"source file does not exist or is not a regular file: {args.source}") if "/" in args.display_name or "\\" in args.display_name: parser.error("display_name must be a filename, without directory separators") extension = args.source.suffix if not extension: parser.error("source file has no extension to preserve") try: stored_name, prefix = build_name(args.display_name, extension, args.prefix) except ValueError as exc: parser.error(str(exc)) remainder = args.display_name[len(prefix) :] destination = args.source.with_name(stored_name) print(f"Displayed name: {args.display_name}") print(f"Source file: {args.source}") print(f"Real extension: {extension}") print(f"Split: {prefix!r} + {remainder!r}") print(f"Escaped name: {json.dumps(stored_name, ensure_ascii=True)}") print("Controls: U+202E RLO, then U+202D LRO") if args.literal: print("Literal destination name follows; bidi controls are invisible:") print(stored_name) if args.apply: if destination.exists(): parser.error(f"destination already exists: {destination!s}") args.source.rename(destination) print(f"Renamed to: {destination}") else: print("Preview only. Add --apply to rename the source file.") return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main())python script.py file.exe 'CSG2025.Exercise.doc' --apply

title: Triage · First Five Minutes
content:
Reversing triage Before decompiling: what format is it, what architecture, what runtime, and can this machine execute it? Preserve an original and analyze a copy.
1. Identify the file Linux/WSL examples, when these standard utilities are available:
sha256sum challenge file challenge xxd -l 64 challenge strings -a -n 5 challenge strings -a -e l -n 5 challenge-a scans all bytes; -n 5 sets minimum string length; GNU strings -e l selects 16-bit little-endian strings. A Windows strings implementation may use different flags. strings guide, xxd guide.
Header / structure Interpretation 7f 45 4c 46 ELF; inspect class, endianness and machine 4d 5a plus valid PE header Windows PE; may be native or managed cf fa ed fe / related Mach-O magic Apple binary; architecture from header 50 4b 03 04 ZIP container; possibly JAR/APK/Office/archive .pyc magic / Python bundle Version-specific bytecode/container analysis No recognizable header Raw blob, compressed/encrypted data or custom format A renamed extension is not format evidence. A PE file containing .NET strings is a hint; confirm the CLR runtime header/metadata in a managed-aware tool.
2. Inspect sections and imports objdump -f challenge objdump -h challenge objdump -x challenge objdump -d -M intel challenge-f: file/architecture header; -h: section headers; -x: all available headers; -d: code sections. -M intel is for x86 syntax. GNU objdump supports formats compiled into that installation; don’t expect it to read every Mach-O file. objdump.
Useful import hints:
Import / symbol Lead strcmp, memcmp, strncmp Input/expected comparison; inspect length and preprocessing fgets, scanf, read, ReadFile Input acquisition and buffer layout CryptDecrypt, EVP APIs Crypto path; arguments/IV/mode matter VirtualAlloc, VirtualProtect, mprotect Runtime code or unpacking possible ptrace, IsDebuggerPresent Debugger detection candidate GetProcAddress, dlsym Runtime import resolution Imports can be absent in static/inlined code; their absence does not exclude a behavior.
3. Can you run it? Target Suitable environment Linux ELF x86-64 Matching Linux runtime / WSL, subject to dependencies Windows PE x64 Matching Windows environment; x64dbg for native code .NET assembly Matching managed runtime and architecture; dnSpyEx for inspection macOS Mach-O Matching macOS/runtime; do static analysis elsewhere ARM firmware/raw code Correct loader/architecture; emulator needs memory/peripheral model An executable bit does not fix an architecture or OS mismatch. Missing ld-linux or libraries can look like “No such file” even when the binary exists. Runtime execution belongs in the challenge VM, not your everyday environment.
4. Search for anchors Search success/failure text, prompts, file paths, format strings, alphabet tables and crypto constants. For every promising string:
String location → all xrefs → printing caller → deciding branch → producer of compared valueA visible flag{...} might be a decoy. Determine whether a reachable path prints it and whether it matches the event’s actual flag format.
5. Packed or encrypted? Hints include a tiny import set, high-entropy data, an unusual entry stub and code written into an executable allocation. These are hints, not a definitive packer identification. Entropy alone cannot distinguish encryption from compression.
If Ghidra shows a short decoder followed by an indirect jump, inspect dynamic debugging and dump the produced code/data after initialization. Wrong language or image base can also produce nonsense disassembly; rule that out first.
6. Stop triage when you can state the plan Native PE x64, checked flag. Input from an edit box; failure string points to validate(). validate() compares 24 transformed bytes with a .rdata array. Next: export that array and model byte arithmetic.Do not read every startup function before identifying the challenge logic. Move to Ghidra, .NET or static analysis based on evidence.
References GNU objdump, GNU strings, Microsoft PE/COFF format.

title: 02 · HTTP / File Streams
content:
HTTP Requests, Responses, and Objects Flow: identify the HTTP version → locate request → match response → decode transport framing → export object → inspect bytes.
Tools: Wireshark, TShark, Burp Community, CyberChef, HxD.
1. Find the actual protocol http http2 tls tcp.port == 8080For plaintext HTTP on an unusual port, inspect the bytes for a request/status line, then use Analyze → Decode As → HTTP. A port alone is insufficient.
tshark -r traffic.pcapng -d tcp.port==8080,http -Y 'http.request'HTTP/2 uses binary frames and stream IDs. A TCP connection can contain many simultaneous HTTP/2 requests. Match an HTTP/2 stream within its connection; a tcp.stream value alone is not a single request.
2. Extract request metadata first tshark -r traffic.pcapng -Y 'http.request' -T fields \ -E header=y -E separator=/t \ -e frame.number -e tcp.stream -e http.request.method \ -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.user_agentUseful GUI filters:
http.request.method == "POST" http.request.uri contains "upload" http.request.uri contains "flag" http.authorization http.cookie http.set_cookie http.response.code >= 400Requests can reveal the endpoint, parameters, session cookie, file name, or password required elsewhere. Preserve duplicates and order when a later request depends on an earlier one.
3. Pair requests and responses Select the request in Wireshark. Expand the HTTP tree and follow the linked response frame when provided. Record request/response frame numbers and TCP stream. For redirects, inspect the destination and subsequent request. For downloads, inspect status, Content-Type, Content-Disposition, and body length. A 200 may be an error JSON wrapper or login page. A 302 may return to login. The response body determines whether the requested object was returned.
4. Export objects before hand-carving File -> Export Objects -> HTTP Choose object -> Save to an evidence directoryTShark equivalent:
tshark -r traffic.pcapng --export-objects http,http_objectsChoose a fresh directory to avoid filename collisions with earlier runs. Check the generated files and protocol tree. A recovered file may still be an archive, compressed payload, or encrypted application object.
Use xxd or HxD to inspect magic bytes:
xxd -l 64 http_objects/download.bin Header bytes Candidate 50 4b 03 04 ZIP-like container 1f 8b gzip stream 25 50 44 46 PDF 89 50 4e 47 PNG 7f 45 4c 46 ELF executable A signature is a lead. Validate by opening/parsing the object with the corresponding approved tool.
5. Separate framing from content An HTTP response can contain:
HTTP headers -> chunked transfer framing (HTTP/1.1 when selected) -> gzip/content encoding -> MIME or archive dataChunk lengths and CRLF separators are not part of the downloaded file. Content-Encoding: gzip differs from a gzip file intentionally downloaded as an object.
Do not Base64-decode the entire followed TCP stream. First isolate the actual encoded field or attachment. A raw bidirectional stream mixes client requests with server responses.
If object export produces invalid bytes, compare its size to reassembled data and check truncation, missing packets, and encryption. Avoid “fixing” a file by deleting unexplained bytes until framing explains them.
6. Forms and file uploads For a POST, inspect the request Content-Type:
Type Inspect application/x-www-form-urlencoded Percent encoding, + as space, duplicate keys application/json Nested values, escaped strings, literal JSON types multipart/form-data Boundary, part headers, filename, binary body application/octet-stream Raw bytes, known application framing A multipart file part begins after its part headers and ends before the next MIME boundary. Do not include the boundary text in an exported file.
Use Burp’s message editor/Decoder on the isolated request when reproducing a supplied challenge request. Preserve the original method, path, cookies, and content type.
7. Basic authentication and cookies Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNzThe Base64 value represents user:pass; it is encoding, not encryption. Decode the field in CyberChef. A cookie may instead be a session identifier, signed data, or encrypted state; a readable cookie does not imply forgery is possible.
For attack workflows following an observed HTTP lead, continue to Web Exploitation.
8. HTTPS / HTTP/2 / HTTP/3 caveats TLS must be decrypted before ordinary HTTP fields appear. HTTP/2 may require connection context and reassembly. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC/UDP; a TCP-only filter excludes it. Matching key material and supported dissectors matter; renaming a protocol with Decode As does not remove encryption. A capture started mid-connection can lack essential negotiated state. See TLS/SSH before attempting encrypted object export.
Final checks Record the parent capture, request frame, response frame, stream, exported filename, hash, and extraction method. Reopen the artifact and verify its intended structure. If only one direction was saved, record that choice.
Reference: Wireshark User’s Guide for stream-follow and object-export interfaces; TShark for export syntax.

title: AJCBBC Allowed Tools
content:
Tournament tool notes: what it is for → useful commands → CTF walkthrough → gotchas. One Markdown page per entry in the supplied 39-tool Windows approved list. Sidebar order follows the original list.
Each page now includes deeper CTF workflows and worked examples. CLI pages explain their options in tables; GUI pages explain the corresponding controls and how to move useful evidence into CLI tools.
Technique playbooks and visual guides Use these when you know the artifact or suspected vulnerability and need the next test:
Web payloads and database fingerprints Network captures and stateful protocols Steganography, images, documents and audio Reversing, Ghidra and debugger workflows Visual CyberChef recipes All 39 tools mapped to techniques Prepared Python snippet library Each individual tool page also links back to relevant playbooks.
For encoding and cryptography code, use the Python cookbook: Base encodings, XOR, classical ciphers, hashes/KDFs, AES modes, ChaCha20/XChaCha20, authenticated encryption and RSA.
Read a command before copying it # TShark example for a WSL installation, if supplied tshark -r traffic.pcapng -Y 'http.request' -T fields -e http.request.uri Piece Meaning tshark Executable -r traffic.pcapng Input capture -Y 'http.request' Display filter selecting HTTP requests -T fields Output selected fields rather than packet summaries -e http.request.uri Choose the URI field to print Options are tool-specific. Learn the operation and the option’s argument together:
Flag Different meanings across approved tools -r TShark/Zeek: read PCAP; xxd: reverse hex; fls/ExifTool: recurse; fsck.fat: repair; Volatility: renderer -d objdump: disassemble; xz/OpenSSL enc: decompress/decrypt; Zimmerman parsers: directory; cannelloni: debug categories -e binwalk: extract; TShark: output field; strings: encoding; RsaCtfTool: public exponent -l xz: list; xxd: byte limit; pdftotext: last page; cannelloni: local port -o Many tools: output; Sleuth Kit: filesystem sector offset; Volatility: output directory Uppercase/lowercase matters: -R and -r can be unrelated. Short flags can sometimes combine (xz -dk = -d -k), but do not assume every parser permits that.
Shell syntax used throughout Syntax Meaning > Redirect stdout to a file; replaces existing content >> Append stdout 2> Redirect stderr 2>&1 Send stderr to the current stdout destination A | B Pass A’s stdout into B # note Comment in Bash/PowerShell examples \ at Bash line end Continue the command on the next line Backtick at PowerShell line end Continue the command on the next line 'single quotes' Keep argument text literal under the shell’s quoting rules Keep binary output in binary-preserving paths. Text exporters can use text pipelines; packet captures, extracted streams and attachments need byte-exact handling.
Supporting shell flags used in the examples Utility / flag Meaning grep -i Ignore letter case grep -n Show matching text line numbers grep -E Use extended regular expressions grep -a Treat binary input as text for this search grep -C N Show N lines before/after each matching line sort -u Sort and remove duplicate lines; original order is lost diff -u Show differences with surrounding text head -n N Show only the first N lines mkdir -p DIR Create parent directories as needed; existing directory is accepted ls -l -a -h Detailed listing, including dotfiles, with readable sizes sha256sum FILE Hash the file’s bytes with SHA-256 For dd, if= is input, of= is output, bs= is block size, skip= skips input blocks, and count= limits copied blocks. Multiply block counts by block size to get byte positions. Every example using these supporting utilities explains its immediate goal.
Tournament setup Windows: GUI tools and TShark, as listed below. WSL: Linux CLI tools; Burp and Ghidra require a working GUI/display setup. Browser: CyberChef and browser-only exercises. Library rule from the supplied list: Python/uv may add libraries except AI/ML related packages. Installing AI related libraries or sub-tools is prohibited for extensible tools generally. Most versions are listed as “latest”; the actual PC’s --help and installed build determine available options. The supplied list specifies Ghidra 12.1.4 and Burp 2026.4.x. These are listed versions, not a claim that they are current upstream releases. How to read the commands bash blocks run inside WSL. powershell blocks run in Windows PowerShell. text blocks show GUI recipes, filters or debugger commands; their heading tells you where to enter them.
Paths such as /path/to/, C:\CTF\, sample offsets, PIDs and 192.0.2.10 are placeholders. Replace them with your challenge values. flag{demo} is an example, not a tournament result.
Common shell utilities in examples (grep, dd, cp, etc.) are supporting commands; the supplied list does not separately establish their competition approval or availability.

title: Ghidra Cheatsheet · From Strings to Check
content:
Ghidra cheatsheet One useful route: import → confirm processor → analyze → success/failure string → xrefs → validator → types/constants → verified input. Menus and shortcuts can differ by release/keymap; use the action’s context menu or Help if a shortcut differs.
Annotated layout diagram, not a captured screenshot. Panels are conceptual and can be docked differently in your installation.
1. Import correctly Launch the supplied Ghidra installation and create a Non-Shared Project. Import a working copy of the binary. Confirm loader, language, bitness and byte order in the import summary. Open it in CodeBrowser; run Auto Analyze with sensible defaults. Save the project after analysis and as meaningful annotations accumulate. For a raw blob, Ghidra cannot infer the intended load address/processor reliably. Select the documented architecture and base from the challenge/device model. A wrong choice can produce plausible-looking nonsense.
2.
